Exam Preparation

Focused Exam Workflows

Workflow: Journalizing Transactions

The Fastest Exam Workflow

  1. Mark perpetual or periodic.
  2. Identify buyer or seller.
  3. Write calculations beside the transaction.
  4. Record entries chronologically.
  5. Maintain AP/AR balances mentally or in T-accounts.
  6. Calculate discounts only after returns/allowances.
  7. Adjust for inventory shrinkage at the end.
🚨 Errors That Cost Marks:
  • 1 Entry for Perpetual Sale: Forgetting the COGS/Inventory entry.
  • Selling Price in COGS: COGS uses original cost, not selling price!
  • Discounting Freight: Discounts generally apply to merchandise, not freight.
  • Restoring Inv. on Allowance: An allowance does not return physical goods.

Workflow: Inventory Costing

The 10-Step Subjective Approach

  1. Identify System: Perpetual or Periodic.
  2. List Layers: e.g., 5 @ $100, 8 @ $110.
  3. Calculate Totals: Total units & cost available.
  4. Calculate Units: Avail − Sold = Ending Units.
  5. Apply Method: FIFO, LIFO, or WA.
  6. Calculate COGS: Do not skip dates if perpetual!
  7. Calculate Ending Inv: List exact remaining layers.
  8. Control Check: COGS + End Inv = Goods Available.
  9. Calculate Profit: Sales − COGS = Gross Profit.
  10. Financial Effect: Rising prices? FIFO = higher profit.

🚨 Common Exam Mistakes

  • Selling Price in Inventory: Costing uses purchase cost, NOT selling price.
  • Simple Average for WA: Do not just average the prices. Divide Total Cost by Total Units.
  • Recalculating WA after a sale: Under perpetual WA, recalculate the average ONLY after a purchase.
  • Skipping Beg. Inventory: It is part of goods available!
  • Periodic vs Perpetual LIFO: Don't apply LIFO only at year-end if the system is perpetual.

Workflow: Bank Reconciliation

  1. Identify: Who already recorded each item? Adjust the side that hasn't.
  2. Bank Side: Add deposits in transit, subtract outstanding cheques. Fix bank errors.
  3. Book Side: Add collections/EFT receipts. Subtract charges/NSF/EFT payments. Fix book errors.
  4. Balance: Confirm both adjusted balances agree. Never stop until they match.
  5. Journalize: Journalize ONLY book-side adjustments and book errors.

Workflow: Cash Flows

  1. Compare Balance Sheets: Calculate changes in every account.
  2. Operating (Indirect): Start with Net Income. Add non-cash items (Depreciation). Reverse gains (subtract) and losses (add). Adjust Working Capital.
  3. Investing: Use T-accounts for Long-term Assets. Asset Disposal = Book Value + Gain (- Loss).
  4. Financing: Trace changes in long-term debt and equity. Dividends Paid: Beg RE + Net Income − End RE.
  5. Check Ending Cash: Beginning Cash + Net Change = Ending Cash.

Chapter 1

Assumptions, Principles & Business Forms

📐 4 Core Assumptions & Principles

Economic Entity

Business activities are recorded separately from the owner's personal activities. Owner's RM5,000 personal cash + business's RM20,000 ≠ RM25,000 of business cash.

Cost Principle

Assets/services are recorded at actual historical cost, not estimated market value — even if the owner believes it's worth more.

Going Concern

Assumes the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future — why equipment is a long-term resource, not something to sell immediately.

Monetary Unit

Only transactions measurable in monetary terms are recorded — "employee talent" isn't an asset because it can't be objectively measured.

Chapter 1

The Accounting Equation

The Foundation

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

Every business resource is financed by either creditors (liabilities) or the owner (equity).

Assets

Economic resources expected to benefit the business in future. "What resources does the business have?"

Cash, AR, Inventory, Supplies, Furniture, Equipment, Land

Liabilities

Debts owed to creditors. "What does the business owe?"

Accounts Payable, Notes Payable, Salaries Payable, Utilities Payable

Equity

Owner's claim on assets after liabilities are deducted.

Equity = Assets − Liabilities

➕➖ Expanded Accounting Equation

Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue − Expenses − Withdrawals

Increases Equity

  • Owner Contribution — owner invests assets into the business.
  • Revenue — business earns revenue from goods/services.

Decreases Equity

  • Expense — costs incurred to earn revenue.
  • Withdrawal — owner takes business assets for personal use (not an expense — doesn't affect net income).

Net Income vs. Net Loss

Net Income = Revenue − Expenses

If Revenue > Expenses → Net Income (Equity ↑). If Expenses > Revenue → Net Loss (Equity ↓).

Full Intuitive Explanation

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

Chapter 1 is not really six unrelated topics. It follows one story:

A business carries out activities → Accounting records them → Financial statements summarize them → People use the information to make decisions

For a subjective exam, you will probably need to do two things:

  1. Explain concepts clearly.
  2. Apply the accounting equation, prepare simple statements, or calculate ROA.

The chapter covers accounting users, governing rules, business organizations, the accounting equation, transaction analysis, financial statements, and return on assets.

1. What accounting actually does

Accounting is an information system that:

Measures business activities → Processes the information → Communicates results

Imagine you own a tutoring business. During the month, you:

  • Invest cash.
  • Buy equipment.
  • Earn service revenue.
  • Pay rent.
  • Borrow money.
  • Allow customers to pay later.

Accounting turns all those events into useful reports. So accounting is not merely recording numbers — its final purpose is to help people decide:

  • Is the business profitable?
  • Can it repay its debts?
  • Does it have enough cash?
  • Should an investor invest?
  • Should management expand?

Good theoretical answer

Accounting is an information system that measures business activities, processes the information into reports, and communicates the results to decision-makers. It helps internal and external users evaluate the financial performance and financial position of a business.

2. Financial accounting versus managerial accounting

The easiest distinction is based on who uses the information.

Financial accounting

Financial accounting mainly serves people outside the business. External users include: investors, creditors or lenders, tax authorities, government agencies.

"Should I invest in this company?" / "Can this company repay its loan?"

Managerial accounting

Managerial accounting serves people inside the business. Internal users include: managers, employees, department heads, business owners making operating decisions.

"Should we increase prices?" / "Which department is costing too much?" / "Can we afford another branch?"

Strong comparison answer

Financial accounting provides information mainly to external users such as investors, creditors, and taxing authorities. Managerial accounting provides information to internal users such as managers and employees for planning, controlling, and decision-making.

3. Organizations and accounting rules

Accounting needs common rules because businesses would otherwise record the same transaction differently whenever convenient. Imagine two companies buy identical equipment for RM50,000. One records RM50,000. The other records RM90,000 because management feels "confident about its value." Comparing the businesses would become rather pointless.

  • FASB — the Financial Accounting Standards Board oversees the creation and governance of accounting standards in the United States.
  • SEC — the Securities and Exchange Commission oversees US financial markets.
  • IASB — the International Accounting Standards Board publishes IFRS.
  • IFRS — International Financial Reporting Standards are global accounting guidelines.
  • GAAP — Generally Accepted Accounting Principles are the accounting guidelines used to prepare financial information consistently.

Relationship

FASB → Accounting standards under US GAAP
IASB → IFRS
SEC → Oversees US financial markets

4. Useful accounting information

Accounting information should be both relevant and faithfully represented.

Relevant

Relevant information can affect a user's decision. Example: Revenue, Profit, Debt, Cash balance. These can influence investment or lending decisions.

Faithfully represented

Information should reflect what actually happened. It should be complete, neutral, and free from error.

A useful exam distinction: Relevance concerns whether information helps decisions. Faithful representation concerns whether the information accurately represents reality.

5. Accounting assumptions and principles

These are popular theoretical questions because lecturers can easily ask: "Identify and explain the accounting assumption involved."

Economic entity assumption

The business is treated separately from its owner. Suppose the owner has RM5,000 personally and the business has RM20,000 — the business does not have RM25,000. The owner's personal transactions and business transactions must be kept separate. Example: the owner buys a personal phone using personal money — this is not a business transaction. If the owner takes cash from the business for personal use, it is recorded as a withdrawal.

Model answer

The economic entity assumption requires the activities of the business to be recorded separately from the personal activities of its owner.

Cost principle

Assets and services are generally recorded at their actual cost. Suppose land is purchased for RM100,000 — even if the owner believes it is worth RM150,000, the transaction is initially recorded based on the actual cost.

Model answer

The cost principle requires acquired assets and services to be recorded at their actual historical cost rather than an estimated market value.

Going concern assumption

The business is assumed to continue operating for the foreseeable future. This is why assets such as equipment are treated as resources to be used over time rather than assumed to be sold immediately.

Model answer

The going concern assumption assumes that the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.

Monetary unit assumption

Only transactions that can be measured in monetary terms are recorded. A skilled employee may be valuable, but "employee talent" is not recorded as an asset because it cannot be objectively measured as a business-owned monetary amount.

Model answer

The monetary unit assumption requires financial statement items to be measured and reported using a monetary unit.

6. Forms of business organization

Sole proprietorship

  • One owner
  • Owner is personally liable for business debts
  • Usually used by smaller businesses
  • Business may terminate when the owner chooses or dies

Partnership

  • Two or more owners
  • Owners are called partners
  • Partners generally share profits
  • Partners may be personally liable

Corporation

  • Separate legal entity
  • Owned by stockholders
  • Stockholders generally have limited liability
  • Has indefinite life
  • Corporation is a separate taxable entity

Limited-liability company

  • One or more members
  • Members generally have limited liability
  • Often combines partnership and corporation features

Likely comparison question

"Differentiate between a sole proprietorship and corporation."

Good answer

A sole proprietorship has one owner, and the owner is personally liable for business debts. A corporation is a separate legal entity owned by stockholders, and stockholders are generally not personally liable for the corporation's debts. A corporation also has an indefinite life, while a sole proprietorship may terminate when the owner dies or chooses to stop operating.

7. Ethics, audits, and internal controls

Audit

An audit is an examination of a company's financial statements and accounting records. Its purpose is to evaluate whether the information is properly presented and supported.

Sarbanes-Oxley Act

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires companies to review internal controls.

PCAOB

The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board monitors the work of independent accountants who audit public companies.

Simple relationship

SOX → Stronger internal-control requirements
PCAOB → Oversight of public-company auditors

8. The accounting equation

This is the foundation of the calculation questions:

Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity

It means that every business resource is financed by either creditors (represented by liabilities) or the owner (represented by equity).

Assets

Assets are economic resources expected to benefit the business in the future. Examples: Cash, Accounts Receivable, Inventory, Supplies, Furniture, Equipment, Land. Assets answer: "What resources does the business have?"

Liabilities

Liabilities are debts owed to creditors. Examples: Accounts Payable, Notes Payable, Salaries Payable, Utilities Payable. Liabilities answer: "What does the business owe?"

Equity

Equity is the owner's claim on the business assets after liabilities are deducted.

Equity = Assets − Liabilities

Example: Assets = RM90,000, Liabilities = RM30,000 → Equity = RM90,000 − RM30,000 = RM60,000

9. Expanded accounting equation

Equity changes because of: owner contributions, revenue, expenses, withdrawals. The expanded equation is:

Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue − Expenses − Withdrawals

An alternative arrangement is:

Assets = Liabilities + Capital − Withdrawals + Revenue − Expenses

Both tell the same story.

What increases equity?

Owner contribution — the owner invests assets into the business. (Contribution ↑ ⇒ Equity ↑)

Revenue — the business earns revenue by providing goods or services. (Revenue ↑ ⇒ Equity ↑)

What decreases equity?

Expense — costs incurred to earn revenue. (Expense ↑ ⇒ Equity ↓)

Withdrawal — the owner takes business assets for personal use. (Withdrawal ↑ ⇒ Equity ↓)

A withdrawal is not an expense. That distinction matters because expenses affect net income, while withdrawals do not affect net income.

10. Net income and net loss

Net Income = Revenue − Expenses

If Revenue > Expenses, the business earns net income. If Expenses > Revenue, the business records a net loss. Net income increases equity. Net loss decreases equity.

11. Calculation type 1: Find the missing amount

Example 1: Find equity

Given: Assets = RM150,000, Liabilities = RM60,000
Assets = Liabilities + Equity → RM150,000 = RM60,000 + Equity → Equity = RM90,000

Example 2: Find liabilities

Given: Assets = RM120,000, Equity = RM75,000
Liabilities = Assets − Equity → RM120,000 − RM75,000 = RM45,000

Example 3: Find assets

Given: Liabilities = RM40,000, Equity = RM70,000
Assets = RM40,000 + RM70,000 = RM110,000

12. Calculation type 2: Transaction analysis

For each transaction, use three questions: (1) Which accounts are affected? (2) Does each account increase or decrease? (3) Does the accounting equation remain balanced?

#TransactionEffect
1Owner invests RM30,000 cashCash (Asset) +30,000; Capital (Equity) +30,000
2Buy equipment for RM10,000 cashEquipment +10,000, Cash −10,000 — an asset exchange, not an expense; total assets unchanged
3Buy supplies on account RM2,000Supplies (Asset) +2,000; Accounts Payable (Liability) +2,000
4Earn RM5,000 cash revenueCash (Asset) +5,000; Revenue (Equity) +5,000
5Earn RM3,000 revenue on accountAccounts Receivable (Asset) +3,000; Revenue (Equity) +3,000
6Pay RM1,200 rentCash (Asset) −1,200; Rent Expense causes Equity −1,200
7Pay RM500 Accounts PayableCash (Asset) −500; Accounts Payable (Liability) −500 — settles a debt, not a new expense
8Collect RM1,000 Accounts ReceivableCash +1,000, Accounts Receivable −1,000 — total assets unchanged; not new revenue (already recorded when earned)
9Owner withdraws RM800Cash (Asset) −800; Withdrawals cause Equity −800

TransactionEffect

Borrow cashAssets ↑, Liabilities ↑

Buy asset on accountAssets ↑, Liabilities ↑

14. Calculation type 3: Expanded equation

Suppose a business has: Beginning capital = RM40,000, Owner contribution = RM10,000, Revenue = RM25,000, Expenses = RM12,000, Withdrawals = RM3,000, Liabilities = RM20,000.

Ending Equity = 40,000 + 10,000 + 25,000 − 12,000 − 3,000 = RM60,000

Assets = Liabilities + Equity = RM20,000 + RM60,000 = RM80,000

15. Financial statements

Chapter 1 introduces four financial statements. They answer different questions.

StatementMain question
Income statementWas the business profitable?
Statement of owner's equityWhy did capital change?
Balance sheetWhat does the business own and owe?
Statement of cash flowsWhere did cash come from and go?

16. Income statement

The income statement reports revenue, expenses, and net income or loss for a period.

Revenue − Expenses = Net Income

Example: Service Revenue = RM18,000; Rent Expense = RM4,000; Salaries Expense = RM6,000; Utilities Expense = RM1,000.
Total expenses = RM4,000 + RM6,000 + RM1,000 = RM11,000.
Net income = RM18,000 − RM11,000 = RM7,000

Format

Ammar Services — Income Statement — For the Month Ended 31 December 2025
Service Revenue18,000
Less: Rent Expense4,000
Salaries Expense6,000
Utilities Expense1,000
Total Expenses11,000
Net Income7,000
The income statement covers a period, so use: "For the month/year ended…"

17. Statement of owner's equity

This statement explains changes in capital.

Ending Capital = Beginning Capital + Contributions + Net Income − Withdrawals

Example: Beginning Capital = RM30,000; Contribution = RM5,000; Net Income = RM7,000; Withdrawals = RM2,000.
RM30,000 + RM5,000 + RM7,000 − RM2,000 = RM40,000

Format

Ammar Services — Statement of Owner's Equity — For the Month Ended 31 December 2025
Beginning Capital30,000
Add: Owner Contribution5,000
Add: Net Income7,000
Less: Owner Withdrawals(2,000)
Ending Capital40,000

18. Balance sheet

The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at one specific date.

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

Suppose — Assets: Cash RM20,000, Accounts Receivable RM8,000, Supplies RM2,000, Equipment RM30,000 → Total Assets = RM60,000. Liabilities: Accounts Payable RM12,000, Notes Payable RM8,000 → Total Liabilities = RM20,000. Equity: Owner's Capital = RM40,000. Check: RM60,000 = RM20,000 + RM40,000.

Format

Ammar Services — Balance Sheet — As at 31 December 2025
AssetsRM
Cash20,000
Accounts Receivable8,000
Supplies2,000
Equipment30,000
Total Assets60,000
Liabilities and Owner's EquityRM
Accounts Payable12,000
Notes Payable8,000
Owner's Capital40,000
Total Liabilities and Owner's Equity60,000
The balance sheet is a snapshot, so use "As at…" — never "For the year ended…"

19. Statement of cash flows

The statement of cash flows reports cash receipts and cash payments for a period. It groups cash flows into:

  • Operating activities — day-to-day business activities. E.g. cash received from customers, rent paid, salaries paid.
  • Investing activities — buying or selling long-term assets. E.g. buying equipment, buying land.
  • Financing activities — transactions involving owners and lenders. E.g. owner contribution, owner withdrawal, borrowing money.

20. Relationship among financial statements

The statements should be prepared in this logical order:

Income Statement → Statement of Owner's Equity → Balance Sheet

Why?

  1. The income statement calculates net income.
  2. Net income goes into the statement of owner's equity.
  3. Ending capital goes into the balance sheet.

Also: ending cash from the statement of cash flows should agree with Cash on the balance sheet.

21. Calculation type 4: ROA

Return on assets measures how profitably a company uses its assets.

ROA = Net Income ÷ Average Total Assets
Average Total Assets = (Beginning Total Assets + Ending Total Assets) ÷ 2

Example

Given: Net Income = RM24,000; Beginning Total Assets = RM180,000; Ending Total Assets = RM220,000.
Average assets = (RM180,000 + RM220,000) ÷ 2 = RM200,000.
ROA = RM24,000 ÷ RM200,000 = 0.12 = 12%

Interpretation

The business generated RM0.12 of net income for every RM1 invested in average assets.

A higher ROA generally indicates more efficient use of assets, but it should be compared with previous periods, similar businesses, and industry averages.

22. Likely theoretical subjective questions

Question: Explain why accounting is important

Good structure: (1) Define accounting. (2) Explain that it measures and processes business activities. (3) Explain that reports communicate information. (4) Identify users and decisions.

Model answer

Accounting is important because it measures business activities, processes the information into reports, and communicates the results to decision-makers. External users such as investors and creditors use accounting information to evaluate profitability and debt-paying ability, while internal users such as managers use it for planning and controlling business operations.

Question: Differentiate financial and managerial accounting

Model answer

Financial accounting mainly provides standardized information to external users such as investors, creditors, and government authorities. Managerial accounting provides information to internal users such as managers and employees. Financial accounting focuses mainly on reporting overall business performance, while managerial accounting supports internal planning, control, and decision-making.

Question: Explain the accounting equation

Model answer

The accounting equation is Assets equals Liabilities plus Owner's Equity. Assets are the economic resources of the business, liabilities are obligations owed to creditors, and owner's equity is the owner's residual claim on the assets. Every transaction must keep the equation balanced because business assets are financed either by creditors or by the owner.

Question: Explain the expanded accounting equation

Model answer

The expanded accounting equation separates owner's equity into capital, revenue, expenses, and withdrawals. Owner contributions and revenues increase equity, while expenses and withdrawals decrease equity. Therefore, Assets equal Liabilities plus Capital plus Revenue minus Expenses minus Withdrawals.

23. Full mixed practice question

A business completed the following transactions:

  1. Owner invested RM40,000 cash.
  2. Purchased equipment for RM12,000 cash.
  3. Purchased supplies of RM3,000 on account.
  4. Earned RM10,000 service revenue in cash.
  5. Earned RM5,000 service revenue on account.
  6. Paid rent of RM2,000.
  7. Paid RM1,000 to the supplier.
  8. Collected RM3,000 from customers.
  9. Owner withdrew RM2,500.

Transaction effects

TransactionAssetsLiabilitiesEquity
Owner investment+40,000—+40,000
Equipment for cashNo net change——
Supplies on account+3,000+3,000—
Cash revenue+10,000—+10,000
Revenue on account+5,000—+5,000
Pay rent−2,000—−2,000
Pay supplier−1,000−1,000—
Collect receivableNo net change——
Withdrawal−2,500—−2,500

Ending balances

Cash = 40,000 − 12,000 + 10,000 − 2,000 − 1,000 + 3,000 − 2,500 = RM35,500

Accounts Receivable = RM5,000 − RM3,000 = RM2,000

Supplies = RM3,000 | Equipment = RM12,000

Total assets = RM35,500 + RM2,000 + RM3,000 + RM12,000 = RM52,500

Accounts Payable = RM3,000 − RM1,000 = RM2,000

Equity = RM40,000 + RM15,000 − RM2,000 − RM2,500 = RM50,500

Check: RM52,500 = RM2,000 + RM50,500 → Balanced.

Income statement

Revenue = RM10,000 + RM5,000 = RM15,000. Expense = RM2,000. Net income = RM15,000 − RM2,000 = RM13,000

Statement of owner's equity

RM40,000 + RM13,000 − RM2,500 = RM50,500

Balance sheet check

Assets = RM52,500. Liabilities + Equity = RM2,000 + RM50,500 = RM52,500. ✓

24. Common subjective-exam mistakes

  • Treating all cash payments as expenses — buying equipment for cash is not immediately an expense; it exchanges one asset for another.
  • Treating cash collection as new revenue — collecting Accounts Receivable is not new revenue; the revenue was recorded when earned.
  • Treating withdrawal as an expense — withdrawal reduces equity but not net income.
  • Confusing Accounts Receivable and Accounts Payable — Receivable: customer owes the business → asset. Payable: business owes someone else → liability.
  • Using ending assets instead of average assets for ROA — ROA uses (Beginning Assets + Ending Assets) ÷ 2.
  • Using the wrong date wording — Income statement, owner's equity statement, and cash flow statement: for a period. Balance sheet: at a specific date.

25. Final revision sheet

Core formulas

Assets = Liabilities + Equity
Equity = Assets − Liabilities
Net Income = Revenue − Expenses
Ending Capital = Beginning Capital + Contributions + Net Income − Withdrawals
Average Assets = (Beginning Assets + Ending Assets) ÷ 2
ROA = Net Income ÷ Average Total Assets

Core relationships

Revenue and contributions → Increase equity
Expenses and withdrawals → Decrease equity
Net income → Statement of Owner's Equity
Ending Capital → Balance Sheet

The one idea to carry into the exam

Do not begin by asking: "Is this debit or credit?" — that belongs to Chapter 2.

For Chapter 1, begin by asking: "What resource, debt, or ownership claim changed?" Once that is clear, the accounting equation usually becomes straightforward.

📒 What Is an Account?

A detailed record of all increases and decreases in one specific item during a period. Every account answers: "What happened to this particular item, and what is its current balance?"

💰 Asset Accounts

Cash

Money the business controls — bank balances, notes, coins, cheques.

Accounts Receivable

Customers owe the business. Clue: "performed services on account."

Notes Receivable

A formal written promise to pay a fixed principal, usually with interest, by a set date.

Prepaid Expense

Paid in advance for a future benefit (e.g. Prepaid Rent, Prepaid Insurance) — an asset until used.

Supplies

Purchased for future use. An asset until used, then becomes an expense.

Long-term Assets

Land, Building, Equipment, Furniture, Fixtures.

📉 Liability Accounts

Accounts Payable

Arises when the business purchases something on account — received the goods, hasn't paid yet.

Notes Payable

A formal written promise made by the business to repay a debt, usually with interest.

Accrued Liabilities

Owed but not yet paid — Salaries, Utilities, Taxes, Rent Payable.

Unearned Revenue

Cash received before the goods/services are provided — the business still owes a service (or refund).

SituationAccount

🧾 Equity Accounts

Owner, Capital ↑ Equity

The owner's investment and accumulated claim in the business.

Revenue ↑ Equity

Results from delivering goods/services — e.g. Service Revenue, Rent Revenue.

Owner, Withdrawals ↓ Equity

Assets taken by the owner for personal use. Not an expense.

Expenses ↓ Equity

Costs incurred to earn revenue — e.g. Rent, Salaries, Utilities Expense.

Double-Entry Accounting

↔️ What Debit & Credit Really Mean

Debit

Left side

Credit

Right side

Debit does not automatically mean increase, cash received, or "good." Credit does not automatically mean decrease, cash paid, or "bad." Whether a debit increases an account depends entirely on the account type.

⭐ The Debit & Credit Rules (Memorize This)

Account TypeIncreaseDecreaseNormal Balance
AssetsDebitCreditDebit

RevenueCreditDebitCredit

Debit-normal

Credit-normal

🧠 Why These Rules Work

Assets = Liabilities + Equity
  • Assets sit on the left of the equation → they increase with debits.
  • Liabilities and Capital sit on the right → they increase with credits. Revenue increases equity, so it also increases with credits.
  • Expenses and Withdrawals reduce equity, so they move on the opposite side from normal equity — they increase with debits.

"Normal" doesn't mean an account can never appear on the opposite side — it means its expected ending balance is normally on that side.

⚠️ What a Balanced Trial Balance Does NOT Prove

A balanced trial balance only proves total debit balances equal total credit balances — not that every transaction is correct. It can still balance even when:

  • A transaction is completely omitted.
  • The wrong account is used (e.g. debiting Equipment instead of Supplies).
  • Both debit and credit contain the same wrong amount.
  • Two errors cancel each other.
  • A transaction is recorded twice.

📉 Debt Ratio Calculator

Debt Ratio = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Assets — the proportion of assets financed by liabilities.

Debt Ratio

40.0%

The business financed 40% of its assets using liabilities. The remaining 60% is financed through equity.

Higher ratio: greater reliance on creditors, more debt, higher financial risk, smaller equity portion.
Lower ratio: less reliance on debt, more owner financing, greater protection for creditors.

"Lower is always better" is too simplistic — debt can help a business expand. Compare against previous years, competitors, and industry norms.

Chapter 2

Full Intuitive Explanation

📚

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

Chapter 1 explained what accounting information means. Chapter 2 explains how that information enters the accounting system. The complete story is:

Transaction → Source Document → Journal → Ledger → Unadjusted Trial Balance

For a mixed theoretical and calculation exam, you should be ready to:

  • Explain accounts, debits, credits, journals, ledgers, and trial balances.
  • Analyse transactions.
  • Prepare journal entries.
  • Calculate balances using T-accounts.
  • Prepare an unadjusted trial balance.
  • Calculate and interpret the debt ratio.

1. The big idea of Chapter 2

Imagine a business receives RM10,000 from its owner. Chapter 1 would say:

Assets increase = Equity increases

Chapter 2 records the same effect more precisely:

Cash10,000
Owner, Capital10,000

So Chapter 2 takes the broad accounting equation and divides it into individual accounts. Instead of recording only "Assets," the business records: Cash, Accounts Receivable, Supplies, Land, Equipment. Instead of recording only "Liabilities," it records: Accounts Payable, Notes Payable, Salaries Payable, Unearned Revenue.

2. What is an account?

An account is a detailed record of all increases and decreases in one specific item during a period. For example, the Cash account records: cash received from customers, cash invested by the owner, cash borrowed from a bank, cash paid for expenses, cash used to purchase assets, cash withdrawn by the owner.

Each account answers: "What happened to this particular item, and what is its current balance?"

3. Main account categories

The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Each section contains separate accounts.

Assets

Assets are economic resources expected to benefit the business in the future. Common asset accounts in the chapter include:

Cash — money controlled by the business, including bank balances, notes, coins, and cheques.

Accounts Receivable — money customers owe the business for goods or services already provided. The clue is usually "performed services on account." The business has earned revenue, but the customer will pay later.

Notes Receivable — a formal written promise by another party to pay a fixed principal amount, usually interest, by a specified date.

Prepaid Expense — a payment made in advance for a future benefit (e.g. Prepaid Rent, Prepaid Insurance). It is initially an asset because the benefit has not yet been used.

Supplies — items purchased for future business use. Initially assets; they become expenses when used.

Long-term assets — Land, Building, Equipment, Furniture, Fixtures.

4. Liability accounts

Liabilities are obligations the business owes to outsiders.

Accounts Payable

Usually arises when the business purchases something on account.

"Purchased supplies for RM2,000 on account." The business received supplies but has not paid yet — Supplies increase, Accounts Payable increases.

Notes Payable

A formal written promise made by the business to repay a debt, usually with interest. Example: "Purchased a RM60,000 building by signing a note."

Building60,000
Notes Payable60,000

Accrued liabilities

An amount owed but not yet paid — Salaries Payable, Utilities Payable, Taxes Payable, Rent Payable. Example: "The business received a RM100 telephone bill that will be paid next month."

Utilities Expense100
Utilities Payable100

Unearned Revenue

Occurs when the business receives cash before providing the promised goods or services. Example: a customer pays RM600 now for a service to be provided later.

Cash600
Unearned Revenue600

Unearned Revenue is a liability because the business still owes the customer a service or possibly a refund.

SituationAccount
Customer owes the businessAccounts Receivable
Business owes service to customerUnearned Revenue

5. Equity accounts

Owner, Capital — represents the owner's investment and accumulated claim in the business. It increases equity.

Owner, Withdrawals — records assets taken by the owner for personal use. It decreases equity. Withdrawals are not expenses because they are not costs incurred to earn revenue.

Revenue — results from delivering goods or services (e.g. Service Revenue, Rent Revenue). Revenue increases equity.

Expenses — costs incurred to earn revenue (e.g. Rent Expense, Salaries Expense, Utilities Expense). Expenses decrease equity.

6. Chart of accounts versus ledger

These terms sound similar, but they are not the same.

Chart of accounts

An organized list of all accounts used by the business:

NumberAccount
101Cash
111Accounts Receivable
121Supplies
201Accounts Payable
301Owner, Capital
401Service Revenue
501Rent Expense

The account numbers help keep the system organized.

Ledger

The ledger contains the actual accounts, transactions, and balances.

Chart of accounts = list of account names. Ledger = actual record of the accounts. The chart is like the contents page. The ledger is the full book.

7. Double-entry accounting

Under double-entry accounting, every transaction affects at least two accounts. Example: a business buys RM3,000 of equipment for cash. Two effects occur: (1) Equipment increases. (2) Cash decreases. The fundamental rule is:

Total Debits = Total Credits

This does not mean there must always be one debit and one credit. A transaction may have one debit and two credits, two debits and one credit, or several debits and several credits. Only the total amounts must be equal.

8. What debit and credit really mean

A debit means the left side of an account. A credit means the right side.

Account
Debit (Left) | Credit (Right)
Debit does not automatically mean Increase, Cash received, or Good. Credit does not automatically mean Decrease, Cash paid, or Bad. Whether a debit increases an account depends on the account type.

9. Debit and credit rules

This is one of the most important tables for the exam.

Account typeIncreaseDecreaseNormal balance
AssetsDebitCreditDebit
ExpensesDebitCreditDebit
Owner, WithdrawalsDebitCreditDebit
LiabilitiesCreditDebitCredit
RevenueCreditDebitCredit
Owner, CapitalCreditDebitCredit
Debit-normal accounts: Assets, Expenses, Withdrawals
Credit-normal accounts: Liabilities, Revenue, Capital

10. Why these rules work

Start with the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are on the left side of the equation, so assets increase with debits. Liabilities and equity are on the right side, so liabilities increase with credits, capital increases with credits, and revenue increases with credits because revenue increases equity. Expenses and withdrawals reduce equity, so they follow the opposite side from normal equity — expenses increase with debits, and withdrawals increase with debits.

11. Normal balance

The normal balance is the side on which an account normally increases.

AccountTypeNormal balance
CashAssetDebit
Accounts ReceivableAssetDebit
EquipmentAssetDebit
Accounts PayableLiabilityCredit
Notes PayableLiabilityCredit
Service RevenueRevenueCredit
Owner, CapitalEquityCredit
Rent ExpenseExpenseDebit
Owner, WithdrawalsEquity reductionDebit
"Normal" does not mean the account can never appear on the opposite side. It means its expected ending balance is normally on that side.

12. T-accounts

A T-account is a simplified form of a ledger account. Suppose Cash contains:

Cash
Debit     |     Credit
30,000   |   20,000
5,500    |   3,200
2,000    |   5,000

Total debit = RM30,000 + RM5,500 + RM2,000 = RM37,500

Total credit = RM20,000 + RM3,200 + RM5,000 = RM28,200

Ending balance = RM37,500 − RM28,200 = RM9,300. Cash therefore has a debit balance of RM9,300.

How to calculate a T-account balance

  1. Add the debit side.
  2. Add the credit side.
  3. Subtract the smaller total from the larger total.
  4. The balance belongs on the larger side.

13. Source documents

A transaction should be supported by evidence. Common source documents include purchase invoices, sales invoices, receipts, bank cheques, bank records, and payroll records. The general flow is:

Transaction → Source Document → Accounting Record

Source documents help determine the transaction date, the amount, the accounts involved, and the nature of the transaction.

14. Journal versus ledger

Journal

The journal records transactions in chronological order. It answers: "What happened on each date?"

Ledger

The ledger organizes transactions by account. It answers: "What happened to Cash, Revenue, Accounts Payable, and every other account?"

JournalLedger
Organized by dateOrganized by account
Shows complete transactionsShows individual account histories
First place transaction is recordedReceives amounts through posting

15. Journalizing

Journalizing means recording a transaction in the journal. A journal entry normally includes: (1) Date, (2) Debit account, (3) Debit amount, (4) Credit account, (5) Credit amount, (6) Explanation.

Nov. 1

Cash30,000
Owner, Capital30,000

Owner contributed cash to the business.

The debit account is written first. The credit account is normally indented.

16. Posting

Posting means transferring information from the journal into individual ledger accounts. Example journal entry:

Cash5,500
Service Revenue5,500

Posting means RM5,500 is placed on the debit side of Cash, and RM5,500 is placed on the credit side of Service Revenue.

Journalize first → Post second

17. Five-step transaction analysis

Step 1: Identify the accounts — "Which accounts are affected?"

Step 2: Identify the account types — Are they Assets? Liabilities? Capital? Revenue? Expense? Withdrawal?

Step 3: Decide whether each account increases or decreases. Do not jump directly to debit or credit yet.

Step 4: Apply the debit and credit rules — translate the increases and decreases into debits and credits.

Step 5: Check the entry — confirm Total Debits = Total Credits.

18. Common journal entries

These transaction patterns are essential for calculation questions.

Transaction 1: Owner contributes cash

The owner invests RM30,000 cash. Cash: asset increases → Debit. Owner, Capital: equity increases → Credit.

Cash30,000
Owner, Capital30,000

Owner contribution.

Accounting equation effect: Assets increase = Equity increases.

Transaction 2: Purchase land for cash

RM20,000 cash. Land: asset increases → Debit. Cash: asset decreases → Credit.

Land20,000
Cash20,000

Purchased land for cash.

This is not an expense — the business exchanged one asset for another.

Transaction 3: Purchase supplies on account

RM500 of supplies, will pay later. Supplies: asset increases → Debit. Accounts Payable: liability increases → Credit.

Office Supplies500
Accounts Payable500

Purchased supplies on account.

Transaction 4: Earn cash revenue

Performs services, receives RM5,500 cash. Cash increases → Debit. Service Revenue increases → Credit.

Cash5,500
Service Revenue5,500

Performed services for cash.

Transaction 5: Earn revenue on account

RM3,000 of services; customer will pay later. Accounts Receivable increases → Debit. Service Revenue increases → Credit.

Accounts Receivable3,000
Service Revenue3,000

Performed services on account.

The revenue is recorded because the work was completed.

Transaction 6: Pay expenses

Pays Rent RM2,000 and Salaries RM1,200.

Rent Expense2,000
Salaries Expense1,200
Cash3,200

Paid rent and salaries.

This is a compound journal entry because it contains more than two accounts. Check: RM2,000 + RM1,200 = RM3,200.

Transaction 7: Pay Accounts Payable

Pays RM300 to a supplier. Accounts Payable decreases → Debit. Cash decreases → Credit.

Accounts Payable300
Cash300

Paid amount owed to supplier.

This is not an expense — the expense or asset was recorded when the original purchase occurred.

Transaction 8: Collect Accounts Receivable

Collects RM2,000 from a customer. Cash increases → Debit. Accounts Receivable decreases → Credit.

Cash2,000
Accounts Receivable2,000

Collected cash on account.

This is not new revenue — revenue was recorded when the service was performed.

Transaction 9: Owner withdraws cash

Owner withdraws RM5,000. Owner, Withdrawals increases → Debit. Cash decreases → Credit.

Owner, Withdrawals5,000
Cash5,000

Owner withdrawal.

A withdrawal is not an expense.

Transaction 10: Pay rent in advance

Prepays three months of rent for RM3,000. Prepaid Rent increases → Debit. Cash decreases → Credit.

Prepaid Rent3,000
Cash3,000

Paid rent in advance.

It is an asset because future benefit remains.

Transaction 11: Purchase building using a note

Purchases a RM60,000 building and signs a note. Building increases → Debit. Notes Payable increases → Credit.

Building60,000
Notes Payable60,000

Purchased building by signing a note.

No cash is involved, but it is still a transaction.

Transaction 12: Owner contributes furniture

Furniture valued at RM18,000. Furniture increases → Debit. Owner, Capital increases → Credit.

Furniture18,000
Owner, Capital18,000

Owner contributed furniture.

An owner contribution does not have to be cash.

Transaction 13: Utility bill received but unpaid

RM100 utility bill, will pay later. Utilities Expense increases → Debit. Utilities Payable increases → Credit.

Utilities Expense100
Utilities Payable100

Recorded utility expense owed.

Transaction 14: Customer pays in advance

Customer pays RM600 before service is provided. Cash increases → Debit. Unearned Revenue increases → Credit.

Cash600
Unearned Revenue600

Received cash for future services.

It is not Service Revenue yet because the service has not been performed.

This normally creates an expense and a payable:

20. Calculation type 1: Determine debit and credit

Example: the business purchases equipment for RM15,000 cash.

Step 1 — Accounts: Equipment, Cash.

Step 2 — Account types: both are assets.

Step 3 — Changes: Equipment increases, Cash decreases.

Step 4 — Apply rules: asset increase = Debit; asset decrease = Credit.

Equipment15,000
Cash15,000

21. Calculation type 2: Determine T-account balances

Suppose Accounts Payable has: RM3,000 credit from purchases, RM1,000 debit from payment, RM500 credit from another purchase.

Accounts Payable
Debit     |     Credit
1,000    |   3,000
       |   500

Credit total = RM3,000 + RM500 = RM3,500

Debit total = RM1,000

Balance = RM3,500 − RM1,000 = RM2,500. Accounts Payable has a RM2,500 credit balance.

22. Calculation type 3: Prepare an unadjusted trial balance

A trial balance is a list of all ledger accounts and their balances at a specific date. The usual order is: (1) Assets, (2) Liabilities, (3) Equity, (4) Revenue, (5) Expenses.

AccountDebit RMCredit RM
Cash20,000—
Accounts Receivable4,000—
Supplies2,000—
Equipment10,000—
Accounts Payable—3,000
Notes Payable—8,000
Owner, Capital—20,000
Owner, Withdrawals1,000—
Service Revenue—10,000
Rent Expense2,000—
Salaries Expense2,000—
Total41,00041,000

Because Total Debits = Total Credits, the trial balance is mathematically balanced.

23. What does a balanced trial balance prove?

A balanced trial balance proves that recorded debit balances equal recorded credit balances. It does not prove that every transaction is correct. For example, suppose the business purchased Supplies but incorrectly debited Equipment:

Equipment1,000
Cash1,000

The entry balances, but the wrong asset was used. A trial balance may still balance when: a transaction is completely omitted; the wrong account is used; both debit and credit contain the same wrong amount; two errors cancel each other; a transaction is recorded twice.

Strong theoretical answer

A trial balance helps verify that total debit balances equal total credit balances. However, it does not guarantee that all transactions are correct because some errors, such as using the wrong account or omitting an entire transaction, may still leave the trial balance balanced.

24. Unadjusted trial balance

It is called unadjusted because it is prepared before period-end adjusting entries. Adjustments such as these have not yet been included: supplies used, prepaid rent expired, depreciation, salaries owed, interest accrued, unearned revenue earned. Those are dealt with in Chapter 3.

25. The accounting cycle at the Chapter 2 stage

The accounting cycle is the process used to produce financial statements. At the Chapter 2 level, the process is:

Transaction → Source Document → Journal → Ledger → Unadjusted Trial Balance

Later chapters add:

Adjusting Entries → Adjusted Trial Balance → Financial Statements → Closing Entries

26. Debt ratio

The debt ratio measures the proportion of a company's assets financed by liabilities.

Debt Ratio = Total Liabilities ÷ Total Assets

Example

Total liabilities = RM60,000; Total assets = RM150,000.
Debt Ratio = RM60,000 ÷ RM150,000 = 0.40 = 40%

Interpretation

The business financed 40% of its assets using liabilities. The remaining 60% is financed through equity.

27. Interpreting the debt ratio

A higher debt ratio generally indicates greater reliance on creditors, more debt obligations, higher financial risk, and a smaller owner's equity portion. A lower debt ratio generally indicates less reliance on debt, more financing from owners, and greater protection for creditors.

But "lower is always better" is too simplistic. Debt may help a business expand and earn additional returns. The ratio should be compared with previous years, competitors, industry norms, and the company's ability to generate cash.

28. Likely theoretical subjective questions

Question: Explain double-entry accounting

Model answer

Double-entry accounting is a system in which every transaction affects at least two accounts. The dual effects of each transaction are recorded using debits and credits, and total debits must always equal total credits. A debit refers to the left side of an account, while a credit refers to the right side. Assets, expenses, and withdrawals increase with debits, while liabilities, revenues, and owner's capital increase with credits.

Question: Differentiate between journal and ledger

Model answer

A journal records transactions in chronological order and shows the complete debit and credit effects of each transaction. A ledger groups transactions according to individual accounts and shows the changes and balances of each account. Transactions are first journalized and then posted from the journal to the ledger.

Question: Explain the purpose of a trial balance

Model answer

A trial balance is a list of all ledger accounts and their balances at a particular date. Its main purpose is to verify that total debit balances equal total credit balances after transactions have been posted. However, a balanced trial balance does not guarantee that all transactions are correct because some errors may not affect the equality of debits and credits.

Question: Explain normal balance

Model answer

The normal balance of an account is the side on which the account normally increases. Assets, expenses, and withdrawals have normal debit balances, while liabilities, revenues, and owner's capital have normal credit balances.

32. Common subjective-exam mistakes

  • Assuming debit means decrease — debit means left; its effect depends on the account type.
  • Debiting Cash whenever cash is paid — Cash decreases with a credit because Cash is an asset.
  • Recording collection from a customer as revenue — collection of Accounts Receivable is Dr Cash / Cr Accounts Receivable, not Service Revenue again.
  • Recording payment of Accounts Payable as an expense — payment is Dr Accounts Payable / Cr Cash; the original purchase was already recorded.
  • Treating owner withdrawal as an expense — withdrawals reduce equity but do not affect net income.
  • Treating prepaid rent as an immediate expense — if the payment provides future benefit, it's Dr Prepaid Rent / Cr Cash.
  • Treating a customer advance as revenue — before service is provided, it's Dr Cash / Cr Unearned Revenue.
  • Forgetting that non-cash transactions are recorded — buying a building by signing a note still affects assets and liabilities.
  • Assuming a balanced trial balance means no errors — some errors still preserve debit-credit equality.

The main exam strategy

For every transaction, do not begin with: "Is it debit or credit?" Begin with: (1) What happened? (2) Which accounts changed? (3) What type is each account? (4) Did each account increase or decrease? (5) What debit-credit rule applies?

Account → Account Type → Increase/Decrease → Debit/Credit
Once the first three are correct, the debit and credit usually stop looking like black magic.
Chapter 3

The Adjusting Process

🧩 The Main Problem Chapter 3 Solves

A business pays RM12,000 for one year of insurance on 1 January. Cash is paid immediately, but the benefit lasts 12 months. Recording all RM12,000 as January's expense would make:

Jan expense too high
Feb–Dec expense too low
Jan profit too low
Later profits too high

The cash payment happened once, but the benefit is used gradually — that's what adjusting entries fix.

⚖️ Cash-Basis vs. Accrual-Basis Accounting

Cash-Basis Not GAAP

Revenue recorded when cash is received; expense recorded when cash is paid.

Service performed in December, paid in January → December revenue = RM0, January revenue = RM5,000. January wrongly reports December's work.

Accrual-Basis Required by GAAP

Revenue recorded when earned; expense recorded when incurred — regardless of cash timing.

Accounts Receivable5,000
Service Revenue5,000

⏳ Time-Period Concept & Fiscal Year

The life of a business is divided into smaller reporting periods (month, quarter, year) — but some activities cross period boundaries: rent paid for several months, salaries paid after month-end, interest accumulating over time, services provided across multiple months.

A fiscal year is any consecutive 12-month accounting period — it may or may not follow the calendar year (e.g. 1 Jul–30 Jun).

🧮 Matching Principle

Expenses are recorded when incurred and matched with the revenue of the same period. Employees work in December, paid in January → salary expense belongs in December.

Revenue for the period − Expenses for the same period = Net Income

Revenue Recognition Principle — 5 Steps

1. Identify contract

Creates enforceable rights and obligations.

2. Identify obligations

A promise to provide a distinct good/service.

3. Determine price

Amount the business expects to receive.

4. Allocate price

Split price among multiple obligations.

5. Recognize revenue

When each obligation is satisfied.

Revenue is recorded when the business has completed the work or delivered the promised good — not automatically when cash is received.

Chapter 3

The 4 Adjustment Types

Key rule: Adjusting entries normally do NOT involve Cash. Cash was either recorded earlier, or will be recorded later — the adjustment fixes timing, not cash movement.

Deferrals

Cash first, recognition later

Accruals

Recognition first, cash later

Deferred Revenue Clues

Accrued Expense Clues

  • Incurred but unpaid

  • Interest accumulated
  • Utilities used

Accrued Revenue Clues

  • Earned but not collected
  • Work completed, not billed
  • Revenue receivable
  • Customer will pay later

"Remaining" vs. "Used"

Supplies: Unadjusted RM1,500, remaining RM400.

Used = 1,500 − 400 = 1,100

The adjustment uses the amount used, not the amount remaining.

"Earned" vs. "Still Unearned"

Unearned Revenue balance RM4,000; RM1,500 remains unearned.

Earned = 4,000 − 1,500 = 2,500

Read the wording carefully — the question may give either the transferred amount or the remaining balance.

Chapter 3

Full Intuitive Explanation

📚

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

Chapter 2 records transactions when they occur. Chapter 3 deals with a less convenient reality:

Cash may be received or paid in one period, while the related revenue or expense belongs to another period.

Therefore, accounts often need to be corrected at the end of the accounting period before financial statements are prepared. The chapter covers cash versus accrual accounting, the time-period concept, revenue recognition, matching, deferrals, accruals, depreciation, adjusted trial balance, the effects of missing adjustments, the accounting cycle, and the worksheet. The full flow is:

Unadjusted Trial Balance → Adjusting Entries → Adjusted Trial Balance → Financial Statements

1. The main problem Chapter 3 solves

Suppose a business pays RM12,000 for one year of insurance on 1 January. Cash is paid immediately, but the insurance benefit lasts for 12 months. Recording all RM12,000 as January expense would make: January expense too high; February to December expense too low; January profit too low; later profits too high. The cash payment happened once, but the benefit is used gradually.

So accounting must ask: How much revenue was actually earned, and how much expense was actually incurred during this period? That is the purpose of adjusting entries.

2. Cash-basis accounting versus accrual-basis accounting

Cash-basis accounting

Revenue is recorded when cash is received; expense is recorded when cash is paid. Easier to use, but the chapter states that it is not allowed under GAAP. Example: a business provides RM5,000 of services in December but receives payment in January. Under cash basis, December revenue = RM0, January revenue = RM5,000. The problem: January reports revenue from work performed in December.

Accrual-basis accounting

Revenue is recorded when earned; expense is recorded when incurred. Using the same example, the revenue belongs in December because that is when the service was performed.

Accounts Receivable5,000
Service Revenue5,000

Cash may arrive later, but the revenue has already been earned.

Strong theoretical answer

Cash-basis accounting records revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. Accrual-basis accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid. Accrual accounting provides a more accurate picture of business performance because revenues and expenses are reported in the correct accounting period.

3. Insurance example: cash basis versus accrual basis

A business pays RM1,200 on 1 May for six months of insurance. Monthly insurance cost = RM1,200 ÷ 6 = RM200.

Cash-basis treatment: the entire RM1,200 is recorded as expense when paid.

Accrual-basis treatment — initial entry:

Prepaid Insurance1,200
Cash1,200

Then each month:

Insurance Expense200
Prepaid Insurance200

The payment begins as an asset because future insurance protection remains. As the protection is used, the asset becomes expense.

4. Revenue received before it is earned

Suppose a business receives RM600 on 30 April for six months of service from May to October. Monthly revenue = RM600 ÷ 6 = RM100. Initial entry:

Cash600
Unearned Revenue600

Each month:

Unearned Revenue100
Service Revenue100
The business does not earn all RM600 merely because the customer paid early. Apparently receiving money and deserving it are not always the same event.

5. The time-period concept

Assumes the life of a business can be divided into smaller reporting periods (month, quarter, year), allowing financial statements to be prepared regularly. The problem: some activities cross period boundaries — rent paid for several months, salaries paid after month-end, interest accumulating over time, services provided across multiple months. Adjusting entries divide those amounts between the correct periods.

Fiscal year

Any consecutive 12-month accounting period. May or may not follow the calendar year — e.g. 1 January to 31 December, or 1 July to 30 June.

6. Revenue recognition principle

Determines when revenue should be recorded. Five steps:

  1. Identify the contract with the customer — creates enforceable rights and obligations.
  2. Identify the performance obligations — a promise to provide a distinct good or service.
  3. Determine the transaction price — the amount the business expects to receive.
  4. Allocate the transaction price — if the contract contains several obligations, allocate the price among them.
  5. Recognize revenue when each obligation is satisfied — when the promised good or service is transferred to the customer.
Simple explanation: Revenue is recorded when the business has completed the work or delivered the promised good, not automatically when cash is received.

7. Matching principle

Guides the recognition of expenses. It requires expenses to be recorded when incurred and matched with the revenue of the same period. Example: employees work during December but are paid in January — the salary expense belongs in December because the employees helped generate December revenue.

Salaries ExpenseXXX
Salaries PayableXXX

The goal is to calculate accurate net income:

Revenue for the period − Expenses for the same period = Net Income

8. What are adjusting entries?

Made at the end of the accounting period to: record revenue in the period earned; record expense in the period incurred; update asset balances; update liability balances; calculate accurate net income or net loss; prepare accurate financial statements.

A common feature: Adjusting entries normally do not involve Cash. Cash was either recorded earlier, or will be recorded later — the adjustment fixes timing rather than cash movement.

9. Two major categories of adjustments

Deferrals

Cash happens first. Revenue or expense recognition happens later.

Cash first, recognition later

Two types: (1) Deferred expenses, (2) Deferred revenues.

Accruals

Revenue or expense recognition happens first. Cash happens later.

Recognition first, cash later

Two types: (1) Accrued expenses, (2) Accrued revenues.

10. The four adjusting-entry patterns

This is the most important table in Chapter 3.

Adjustment typeDebitCredit
Deferred expenseExpenseAsset
Deferred revenueLiabilityRevenue
Accrued expenseExpenseLiability
Accrued revenueAssetRevenue

Expanded

Expense

Revenue

11. Deferred expenses

Occurs when cash is paid before the related expense is incurred. Also called a prepaid expense. Examples: Prepaid Rent, Prepaid Insurance, Office Supplies, Depreciation-related asset usage. Initially the payment is recorded as an asset; as the benefit is consumed, part of the asset becomes expense.

ExpenseXXX
Prepaid AssetXXX

12. Prepaid rent

Smart Touch Learning pays RM3,000 on 1 December for three months of rent (December, January, February). Monthly rent = RM3,000 ÷ 3 = RM1,000.

Initial entry:

Prepaid Rent3,000
Cash3,000

Adjustment on 31 December — one month expired:

Rent Expense1,000
Prepaid Rent1,000

After adjustment: Rent Expense = RM1,000; Prepaid Rent remaining = RM2,000 (covers January and February).

13. Supplies adjustment

Office Supplies before adjustment = RM500; supplies remaining at year-end = RM100. Supplies used = RM500 − RM100 = RM400.

Supplies Expense400
Office Supplies400

After adjustment: Supplies Expense = RM400; Office Supplies asset = RM100.

Supplies Used = Unadjusted Supplies Balance − Supplies Remaining

The adjustment uses the amount used, not the amount remaining.

14. Depreciation

Property, plant, and equipment are long-lived tangible assets used in business operations — buildings, equipment, furniture. Depreciation allocates the cost of a depreciable asset over its useful life. It is not simply a guess about the asset's market value.

Straight-line depreciation formula

Annual Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life

Residual value is the expected value of the asset at the end of its useful life.

15. Depreciation calculation

Furniture costs RM18,000, residual value = RM0, useful life = 5 years.
Annual depreciation = (RM18,000 − RM0) ÷ 5 = RM3,600.
Monthly depreciation = RM3,600 ÷ 12 = RM300.

Depreciation Expense—Furniture300
Accumulated Depreciation—Furniture300

16. Accumulated depreciation

Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset account. A contra account (1) is linked to another account, (2) has the opposite normal balance. Furniture is an asset with a normal debit balance; Accumulated Depreciation—Furniture therefore has a normal credit balance.

AccountNormal balance
FurnitureDebit
Accumulated Depreciation—FurnitureCredit

17. Why the asset itself is not credited

The Furniture account stays at its original cost. Instead of reducing Furniture directly, accounting records the total depreciation separately. This allows users to see original cost, total accumulated depreciation, and remaining book value.

18. Book value

Book Value = Asset Cost − Accumulated Depreciation

For the furniture: RM18,000 − RM300 = RM17,700

Furniture18,000
Less: Accumulated Depreciation(300)
Book Value17,700

Book value is an accounting amount, not necessarily market value.

19. Deferred revenue

Occurs when cash is received before goods or services are provided. Also called Unearned Revenue.

CashXXX
Unearned RevenueXXX

Unearned Revenue is a liability because the business still owes goods, services, or a refund. When the service is provided:

Unearned RevenueXXX
Service RevenueXXX

20. Unearned-revenue calculation

A customer pays RM600 for 30 days of service. By 31 December, 10 days have been completed. Fraction earned = 10/30 = 1/3. Revenue earned = RM600 × 1/3 = RM200.

Unearned Revenue200
Service Revenue200

Remaining liability = RM600 − RM200 = RM400. The RM400 remains unearned because 20 days of service are still owed.

21. Accrued expenses

An expense that has been incurred but not yet paid — Salaries Expense, Interest Expense, Utilities Expense.

ExpenseXXX
PayableXXX

The expense is debited because expenses increase with debits; the payable is credited because liabilities increase with credits.

22. Accrued salaries

Smart Touch Learning pays RM2,400 monthly salary: RM1,200 on the 15th, RM1,200 on the first day of the next month. The first half was already paid and recorded. By 31 December, employees have earned the second RM1,200.

Salaries Expense1,200
Salaries Payable1,200

At 31 December: Total December Salaries Expense = RM2,400; Salaries Payable = RM1,200.

Payment in January — when the liability is paid:

Salaries Payable1,200
Cash1,200
Do not debit Salaries Expense again — the expense was already recognized in December. January merely pays the liability.

23. Accrued interest

Interest = Principal × Annual Rate × Time

Suppose Principal = RM60,000, Annual rate = 2%, Time = one month.
RM60,000 × 2% × 1/12 = RM100.

Interest Expense100
Interest Payable100

Cash is not credited because the interest has not yet been paid.

24. Time fraction for interest

Because the rate is annual:

TimeFraction
1 month1/12
3 months3/12
6 months6/12
9 months9/12
1 year12/12

Example

A RM100,000 loan is borrowed on 1 July at 8% annually. Adjustment date: 31 December. Time = 6/12. Interest = RM100,000 × 8% × 6/12 = RM4,000.

Interest Expense4,000
Interest Payable4,000

25. Accrued revenues

Occurs when revenue has been earned but cash has not yet been collected.

Accounts ReceivableXXX
Service RevenueXXX

The business records an asset because the customer owes money, and revenue because the service has been performed.

26. Accrued-revenue calculation

Smart Touch Learning earns RM1,600 monthly for services beginning 16 December. By 31 December, half a month has been completed. Revenue earned = RM1,600 × 1/2 = RM800.

Accounts Receivable800
Service Revenue800

When the customer later pays:

Cash800
Accounts Receivable800

No additional revenue is recorded for that RM800 because it was already recognized.

27. How to identify the four adjustment types

Deferred expense clues: paid in advance, prepaid, expired, used, supplies remaining, insurance coverage, depreciation.

Deferred revenue clues: cash received in advance, Unearned Revenue, customer deposit, portion now earned, future service.

Accrued expense clues: incurred but unpaid, owed, not yet paid, salaries payable, interest accumulated, utilities used.

Accrued revenue clues: earned but not collected, work completed but not billed, revenue receivable, customer will pay later.

28. "Remaining" versus "used"

Questions may give the ending balance rather than the adjustment amount.

Supplies: Unadjusted = RM1,500, remaining = RM400. Used = RM1,500 − RM400 = RM1,100.

Supplies Expense1,100
Supplies1,100

Prepaid rent: Prepaid Rent = RM6,000, RM2,000 remains unused. Expired = RM6,000 − RM2,000 = RM4,000.

Rent Expense4,000
Prepaid Rent4,000

29. "Earned" versus "still unearned"

Suppose Unearned Revenue has a RM4,000 balance.

If RM1,500 has been earned:

Unearned Revenue1,500
Service Revenue1,500

Remaining liability = RM4,000 − RM1,500 = RM2,500.

If RM1,500 remains unearned: earned amount = RM4,000 − RM1,500 = RM2,500.

Unearned Revenue2,500
Service Revenue2,500
Read the wording. The question may give either the transferred amount or the remaining balance.

30. Adjusted trial balance

After adjusting entries are journalized and posted to the ledger, the business prepares the adjusted trial balance — a list of all accounts with their corrected balances. Its purposes: confirm total debits equal total credits; show updated asset and liability balances; provide amounts for preparing financial statements.

Financial statements are prepared from the adjusted trial balance, not the unadjusted one.

31. How adjusted balances are calculated

Same side: add

Service Revenue: Unadjusted = RM10,000 Credit; Adjustment = RM2,000 Credit. Adjusted = RM12,000 Credit.

Opposite side: subtract

Prepaid Rent: Unadjusted = RM6,000 Debit; Adjustment = RM2,000 Credit. Adjusted = RM4,000 Debit.

Unearned Revenue: Unadjusted = RM5,000 Credit; Adjustment = RM1,500 Debit. Adjusted = RM3,500 Credit.

32. Effect of missing adjustments

This is important for theoretical questions.

Deferred expense omitted — missing: Dr Expense / Cr Asset. Effect: Expense understated, Asset overstated, Net income overstated, Equity overstated.

Deferred revenue omitted — missing: Dr Unearned Revenue / Cr Revenue. Effect: Revenue understated, Liability overstated, Net income understated, Equity understated.

Accrued expense omitted — missing: Dr Expense / Cr Liability. Effect: Expense understated, Liability understated, Net income overstated, Equity overstated.

Accrued revenue omitted — missing: Dr Asset / Cr Revenue. Effect: Asset understated, Revenue understated, Net income understated, Equity understated.

33. Summary of omitted-adjustment effects

Missing adjustmentExpense/RevenueAsset/LiabilityNet incomeEquity
Deferred expenseExpense understatedAsset overstatedOverstatedOverstated
Deferred revenueRevenue understatedLiability overstatedUnderstatedUnderstated
Accrued expenseExpense understatedLiability understatedOverstatedOverstated
Accrued revenueRevenue understatedAsset understatedUnderstatedUnderstated

Useful shortcut

Missing expense ⇒ Net income too high
Missing revenue ⇒ Net income too low

34. Accounting cycle in Chapter 3

By the end of Chapter 3, the accounting cycle includes:

  1. Analyse transactions.
  2. Journalize transactions.
  3. Post to the ledger.
  4. Prepare the unadjusted trial balance.
  5. Journalize and post adjusting entries.
  6. Prepare the adjusted trial balance.

Financial statements follow from the adjusted trial balance.

35. Worksheet

A worksheet is an internal document that helps organize the adjusting process. The Chapter 3 worksheet contains four main sections: (1) Account names, (2) Unadjusted trial balance, (3) Adjustments, (4) Adjusted trial balance.

Unadjusted Balance + Adjustment = Adjusted Balance

However, when the adjustment is on the opposite side, subtract rather than blindly add.

36. Likely theoretical subjective questions

Question: Explain why adjusting entries are needed

Model answer

Adjusting entries are needed because cash receipts and payments do not always occur in the same accounting period as the related revenues and expenses. Under accrual accounting, revenue must be recorded when earned and expenses when incurred. Adjusting entries update revenue, expense, asset, and liability accounts so that net income and financial position are correctly reported before financial statements are prepared.

Question: Differentiate between deferrals and accruals

Model answer

Deferrals occur when cash is paid or received before the related expense or revenue is recognized. Examples include prepaid expenses and unearned revenue. Accruals occur when an expense or revenue is recognized before cash is paid or received. Examples include accrued salaries, accrued interest, and accrued revenue.

Question: Explain accumulated depreciation

Model answer

Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset account that records the total depreciation recognized on an asset to date. It has a credit normal balance, which is opposite to the debit balance of the related asset. The asset's book value is calculated by subtracting accumulated depreciation from its original cost.

Question: Explain the adjusted trial balance

Model answer

The adjusted trial balance is a list of all accounts and their balances after adjusting entries have been journalized and posted. Its purpose is to confirm that total debits equal total credits and to provide the corrected account balances used to prepare financial statements.

37. Full mixed calculation practice

At 31 December, the following information is available:

  1. Prepaid Rent has a balance of RM6,000 covering six months beginning 1 October.
  2. Supplies has a balance of RM1,500. Supplies remaining are RM400.
  3. Furniture cost RM24,000, has no residual value, and a useful life of four years. One month's depreciation is required.
  4. Employees have earned RM2,000 but have not been paid.
  5. A RM50,000 loan carries 6% annual interest. Three months of interest have accrued.
  6. Unearned Revenue has a balance of RM4,000. RM1,500 has now been earned.
  7. RM900 of service revenue has been earned but not recorded.

Adjustment 1 — Prepaid rent: Monthly rent = RM6,000 ÷ 6 = RM1,000. October to December = 3 months. Expired = RM1,000 × 3 = RM3,000.

Rent Expense3,000
Prepaid Rent3,000

Adjustment 2 — Supplies: Used = RM1,500 − RM400 = RM1,100.

Supplies Expense1,100
Supplies1,100

Adjustment 3 — Depreciation: Annual = (RM24,000 − RM0) ÷ 4 = RM6,000. Monthly = RM6,000 ÷ 12 = RM500.

Depreciation Expense—Furniture500
Accumulated Depreciation—Furniture500

Adjustment 4 — Accrued salaries:

Salaries Expense2,000
Salaries Payable2,000

Adjustment 5 — Accrued interest: RM50,000 × 6% × 3/12 = RM750.

Interest Expense750
Interest Payable750

Adjustment 6 — Unearned revenue earned:

Unearned Revenue1,500
Service Revenue1,500

Adjustment 7 — Accrued revenue:

Accounts Receivable900
Service Revenue900

38. Overall effect of the adjustments

Expenses added = RM3,000 + RM1,100 + RM500 + RM2,000 + RM750 = RM7,350

Revenue added = RM1,500 + RM900 = RM2,400

Net effect on income = RM2,400 − RM7,350 = −RM4,950

Therefore, the adjustments reduce net income by RM4,950 compared with the unadjusted amount. They did not make the business worse. They merely stopped the unadjusted records from exaggerating profit by RM4,950.

39. Common subjective-exam mistakes

  • Using Cash in an adjusting entry — adjusting entries normally do not involve Cash.
  • Recording the amount remaining as expense — for supplies: Used = Balance before adjustment − Remaining.
  • Crediting the depreciable asset — credit Accumulated Depreciation, not Furniture or Building.
  • Forgetting the time fraction for interest — annual rates must be multiplied by the fraction of the year.
  • Treating Unearned Revenue as revenue immediately — it remains a liability until the service is provided.
  • Recording revenue again when cash is collected — if accrued revenue was already recorded, later collection reduces Accounts Receivable.
  • Recording expense again when the payable is paid — if accrued expense was already recognized, later payment reduces the payable.
  • Preparing statements from the unadjusted trial balance — financial statements use adjusted balances.

40. Final revision table

SituationAdjustment
Prepaid asset has been usedDr Expense, Cr Asset
Supplies have been consumedDr Supplies Expense, Cr Supplies
Depreciation is requiredDr Depreciation Expense, Cr Accumulated Depreciation
Customer advance has been earnedDr Unearned Revenue, Cr Revenue
Expense incurred but unpaidDr Expense, Cr Payable
Revenue earned but uncollectedDr Accounts Receivable, Cr Revenue

Core formulas

Supplies Used = Supplies Before Adjustment − Supplies Remaining
Straight-Line Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life
Book Value = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation
Interest = Principal × Rate × Time

The main exam strategy

For every adjustment, ask these questions in order: (1) What has already been recorded? (2) What has actually happened by period-end? (3) What amount should remain in the asset or liability account? (4) What amount must be recognized as revenue or expense? (5) Which debit and credit will create those correct balances?

Cash timing ≠ Revenue and expense timing

Adjusting entries exist to repair that difference.

Closing Entries

⚽ Temporary Accounts

Relate to one accounting period and are closed at the end of it — like the scoreboard for one football match. At the end of the match, the score resets.

Revenues, Expenses, Income Summary, Owner, Withdrawals.

🏟️ Permanent Accounts

Assets, Liabilities, Owner, Capital.

Income Summary is a temporary account used only during closing. It receives revenue and expense balances, shows net income or net loss, then transfers that result to Owner, Capital. It never appears in the final financial statements.

The Worksheet

Chapter 3 introduced: (1) Account names, (2) Unadjusted trial balance, (3) Adjustments, (4) Adjusted trial balance. Chapter 4 adds: (5) Income Statement columns, (6) Balance Sheet columns, (7) Net income or net loss.

Income Statement Columns

Debit: Rent, Salaries, Supplies, Depreciation, Interest Expense.

Credit: Service Revenue, Rent Revenue, other revenues.

Balance Sheet Columns

Assets, Contra assets, Liabilities, Owner Capital, Owner Withdrawals. Withdrawals go here because they affect equity, not net income.

Worksheet Placement Rule

ResultIncome StatementBalance Sheet
Net incomeDebitCredit
Net lossCreditDebit

Net income increases equity, so it goes to the Balance Sheet Credit side (and balances the Income Statement columns on the Debit side). A net loss does the opposite. This is only a worksheet balancing amount — it is not yet a journal entry.

Adjusting EntriesClosing Entries

Produce adjusted trial balanceProduce post-closing trial balance
