Chapter 6

Calculation-Focused Explanation

📚

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

Chapter 6 is mainly about one calculation problem:

When identical goods were purchased at different costs, which costs should be assigned to Cost of Goods Sold and which costs should remain in Ending Inventory?

The physical number of units does not change between methods. What changes is the cost assigned to those units. This affects:

COGS → Gross Profit → Net Income
Ending Inventory → Current Assets → Total Assets

For a subjective exam, the most important areas are: (1) FIFO, (2) LIFO, (3) Weighted-average, (4) Perpetual versus periodic calculations, (5) Financial-statement effects, (6) Lower-of-cost-or-market, (7) Inventory errors, (8) Inventory turnover and days in inventory.

1. The equation behind the whole chapter

Every inventory question is based on:

Cost of Goods Available for Sale = Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases

That total cost must be divided into:

Cost of Goods Available for Sale = COGS + Ending Inventory

Therefore:

COGS = Cost of Goods Available for Sale − Ending Inventory

This equation is your built-in error check. For example, if total goods available cost RM10,000, COGS + Ending Inventory = RM10,000. If your answer totals RM9,700, congratulations — RM300 of inventory has vanished into the accounting void.

2. The chapter's main example

DateTransactionUnitsCost per unit
August 1Beginning inventory2RM350
August 5Purchase4RM360
August 15Sale4—
August 26Purchase12RM380
August 31Sale10—

Total units available = 2 + 4 + 12 = 18 units

Units sold = 4 + 10 = 14 units

Ending units = 18 − 14 = 4 units

Total cost available = (2 × RM350) + (4 × RM360) + (12 × RM380) = RM700 + RM1,440 + RM4,560 = RM6,700

No matter which method is used: COGS + Ending Inventory = RM6,700

3. Cost layers

When purchases occur at different prices, treat each purchase as a separate cost layer.

Layer 1: 2 units @ RM350
Layer 2: 4 units @ RM360
Layer 3: 12 units @ RM380

FIFO, LIFO and weighted-average differ only in how they consume or combine these layers.

Part A: Perpetual Inventory System

Under perpetual inventory, COGS is calculated every time a sale occurs. You cannot simply wait until the end and apply the method once — you must update inventory after each transaction.

4. Perpetual FIFO

FIFO means: First cost in → First cost out. COGS uses the oldest available costs; ending inventory contains the newest costs. Think of a queue — the oldest cost layer leaves first.

August 1 beginning inventory: 2 units @ RM350 (Total RM700)

August 5 purchase: 4 × RM360 = RM1,440. Balance: 2 @ RM350, 4 @ RM360 = 6 units, RM2,140.

Merchandise Inventory1,440
Accounts Payable1,440

August 15 sale of four units: FIFO removes the oldest units first — 2 @ RM350 + 2 @ RM360 = RM700 + RM720 = RM1,420.

Cost of Goods Sold1,420
Merchandise Inventory1,420

Remaining: 2 units @ RM360 (RM720).

August 26 purchase: 12 × RM380 = RM4,560. Available: 2 @ RM360, 12 @ RM380 = 14 units, RM5,280.

August 31 sale of ten units: 2 @ RM360 + 8 @ RM380 = RM720 + RM3,040 = RM3,760. Remaining: 4 units @ RM380 = RM1,520.

Final FIFO: Total COGS = RM1,420 + RM3,760 = RM5,180. Ending Inventory = RM1,520. Check: RM5,180 + RM1,520 = RM6,700.

5. Perpetual LIFO

LIFO means: Last cost in → First cost out. COGS uses the newest available costs; ending inventory contains older costs. Think of a stack — the newest layer on top leaves first.

August 15 sale of four units: Before the sale: 2 @ RM350, 4 @ RM360. LIFO removes the newest units: 4 × RM360 = RM1,440. Remaining: 2 units @ RM350 (RM700).

August 26 purchase: Add 12 × RM380 = RM4,560. Available: 2 @ RM350, 12 @ RM380.

August 31 sale of ten units: The newest units are RM380 each: 10 × RM380 = RM3,800. Remaining: 2 @ RM350 + 2 @ RM380 = RM700 + RM760 = RM1,460.

Final perpetual LIFO: COGS = RM1,440 + RM3,800 = RM5,240. Ending Inventory = RM1,460. Check: RM5,240 + RM1,460 = RM6,700.

6. Perpetual weighted-average

Calculate a new average cost after every purchase — also called the moving-average method.

Average Cost per Unit = Total Cost Available ÷ Total Units Available
Do not recalculate the average after a sale. Recalculate it after a purchase.

Average after Aug 5 purchase: (2 units, RM700) + (4 units, RM1,440) = 6 units, RM2,140. Average = RM2,140 ÷ 6 = RM356.6667 → RM356.67.

Aug 15 sale of 4 units: 4 × RM356.67 = RM1,426.68 → RM1,427. Remaining cost = RM2,140 − RM1,427 = RM713; remaining qty = 6 − 4 = 2 units.

New average after Aug 26 purchase: RM713 (2 units) + RM4,560 (12 units) = RM5,273, 14 units. New average = RM5,273 ÷ 14 = RM376.6429 → RM376.64.

Aug 31 sale of 10 units: 10 × RM376.64 = RM3,766.40 (rounded RM3,766). Remaining qty = 14 − 10 = 4. Ending inventory = 4 × RM376.64 = RM1,506.56 → RM1,507.

Final perpetual weighted-average: COGS = RM1,427 + RM3,766 = RM5,193. Ending Inventory = RM1,507. Check: RM5,193 + RM1,507 = RM6,700. Rounding may cause a RM1 difference — follow the rounding policy stated in the question.

7. Specific identification

Assigns the actual cost of the specific unit sold. Suitable for cars, houses, jewellery, unique machinery, and other high-value individual products. Suppose four units sold were specifically identified as 1 unit at RM350 and 3 units at RM360.

COGS = (1 × RM350) + (3 × RM360) = RM350 + RM1,080 = RM1,430. There is no FIFO or LIFO assumption — the actual units are known. This method is usually less calculation-heavy unless the question tells you exactly which units were sold.

Part B: Comparing Financial Statement Effects

8. Comparison using the chapter's figures

Assume 14 units were sold at RM500 each. Sales revenue = 14 × RM500 = RM7,000.

MethodCOGSGross ProfitEnding Inventory
Specific identification5,2001,8001,500
FIFO5,1801,8201,520
LIFO5,2401,7601,460
Weighted-average5,1931,8071,507

Gross Profit = Sales − COGS. For FIFO: RM7,000 − RM5,180 = RM1,820. For LIFO: RM7,000 − RM5,240 = RM1,760.

9. When costs are rising

In the example: RM350 → RM360 → RM380.

FIFO sends older, cheaper costs to COGS. Therefore: COGS lower, gross profit higher, net income higher, ending inventory higher.

LIFO sends newer, more expensive costs to COGS. Therefore: COGS higher, gross profit lower, net income lower, ending inventory lower.

Weighted-average usually falls between FIFO and LIFO.

During rising costsFIFOWeighted-averageLIFO
COGSLowestMiddleHighest
Gross profitHighestMiddleLowest
Net incomeHighestMiddleLowest
Ending inventoryHighestMiddleLowest

10. When costs are falling

The relationship reverses.

During falling costsFIFOWeighted-averageLIFO
COGSHighestMiddleLowest
Gross profitLowestMiddleHighest
Net incomeLowestMiddleHighest
Ending inventoryLowestMiddleHighest
Do not blindly memorise tables. Ask: (1) Which cost does the method send to COGS? (2) Are those costs higher or lower?

Part C: Full Worked Perpetual Question

A business uses a perpetual inventory system:

DateTransaction
May 1Beginning inventory: 5 units at RM100
May 4Purchased 8 units at RM110
May 10Sold 7 units
May 18Purchased 10 units at RM125
May 25Sold 9 units

Required: (1) Calculate COGS and ending inventory using FIFO. (2) Using LIFO. (3) Using weighted-average.

11. First calculate unit quantities

Units available = 5 + 8 + 10 = 23

Units sold = 7 + 9 = 16

Ending units = 23 − 16 = 7

Total cost available = (5 × RM100) + (8 × RM110) + (10 × RM125) = RM500 + RM880 + RM1,250 = RM2,630. Therefore COGS + Ending Inventory = RM2,630.

12. Perpetual FIFO solution

May 10 sale of 7 units: Available: 5 @ RM100, 8 @ RM110. FIFO COGS = (5 × RM100) + (2 × RM110) = RM500 + RM220 = RM720. Remaining: 6 units @ RM110.

May 18 purchase: Add 10 @ RM125. Available: 6 @ RM110, 10 @ RM125.

May 25 sale of 9 units: FIFO COGS = (6 × RM110) + (3 × RM125) = RM660 + RM375 = RM1,035. Remaining: 7 units @ RM125.

Final FIFO: Total COGS = RM720 + RM1,035 = RM1,755. Ending Inventory = 7 × RM125 = RM875. Check: RM1,755 + RM875 = RM2,630.

13. Perpetual LIFO solution

May 10 sale of 7 units: Available: 5 @ RM100, 8 @ RM110. Newest units first: 7 × RM110 = RM770. Remaining: 5 @ RM100, 1 @ RM110.

May 18 purchase: Add 10 @ RM125. Available: 5 @ RM100, 1 @ RM110, 10 @ RM125.

May 25 sale of 9 units: Newest units first: 9 × RM125 = RM1,125. Remaining: 5 @ RM100, 1 @ RM110, 1 @ RM125.

Ending inventory = (5 × RM100) + (1 × RM110) + (1 × RM125) = RM500 + RM110 + RM125 = RM735.

Final LIFO: COGS = RM770 + RM1,125 = RM1,895. Check: RM1,895 + RM735 = RM2,630.

14. Perpetual weighted-average solution

Average after May 4 purchase: Total units = 5 + 8 = 13. Total cost = RM500 + RM880 = RM1,380. Average = RM1,380 ÷ 13 = RM106.1538 → RM106.15.

May 10 sale of 7 units: 7 × RM106.15 = RM743.05 → COGS = RM743.05. Remaining units = 13 − 7 = 6. Remaining cost using unrounded calculation = RM1,380 − RM743.0769 = RM636.9231. (It is safer to keep unrounded values internally.)

New average after May 18 purchase: Remaining cost RM636.9231 + new purchase RM1,250 = RM1,886.9231. Total units = 6 + 10 = 16. New average = RM1,886.9231 ÷ 16 = RM117.9327 → RM117.93.

May 25 sale of 9 units: 9 × RM117.9327 = RM1,061.3943 → RM1,061.39.

Total weighted-average COGS: RM743.0769 + RM1,061.3943 = RM1,804.47.

Ending inventory: 7 units × RM117.9327 = RM825.53. Check: RM1,804.47 + RM825.53 = RM2,630.

15. Comparison of the worked example

MethodCOGSEnding Inventory
FIFO1,755875
LIFO1,895735
Weighted-average1,804.47825.53

Because costs increased from RM100 to RM125: FIFO produced the lowest COGS, LIFO produced the highest COGS, and weighted-average fell between them.

Part D: Periodic Inventory System

Under periodic inventory, the company waits until the end of the period. It calculates COGS = Goods Available − Ending Inventory. The timing of individual sales is generally ignored when assigning costs.

16. Periodic FIFO

Periodic FIFO leaves the newest costs in ending inventory. Using the chapter example, four units remain — the newest units cost RM380: 4 × RM380 = RM1,520. COGS = RM6,700 − RM1,520 = RM5,180.

FIFO gives the same result under perpetual and periodic. Why? Both approaches leave the newest costs in ending inventory.

17. Periodic LIFO

Periodic LIFO assigns the newest costs from the entire period to COGS. The four ending units therefore come from the oldest layers: 2 units at RM350, 2 units at RM360. Ending inventory = (2 × RM350) + (2 × RM360) = RM700 + RM720 = RM1,420. COGS = RM6,700 − RM1,420 = RM5,280.

SystemLIFO COGS
PerpetualRM5,240
PeriodicRM5,280

They differ because perpetual LIFO applies LIFO at each sale date, while periodic LIFO applies it once at period-end.

18. Periodic weighted-average

Calculate one average using all units available for the entire period. Average Cost = RM6,700 ÷ 18 = RM372.22. Ending inventory = 4 × RM372.22 = RM1,488.88 → RM1,489. COGS = 14 × RM372.22 = RM5,211.08 → RM5,211.

19. Perpetual versus periodic summary

MethodPerpetual COGSPeriodic COGS
FIFO5,1805,180
LIFO5,2405,280
Weighted-average5,1935,211

What to remember

  • FIFO: normally same under both systems.
  • LIFO: may differ.
  • Weighted-average: may differ.
  • Perpetual weighted-average recalculates after purchases.
  • Periodic weighted-average calculates once at period-end.

Part E: Lower-of-Cost-or-Market

20. Lower-of-cost-or-market calculation

Inventory should be reported at the lower of historical cost or market value.

Reported Inventory = min(Cost, Market)

Suppose Historical cost = RM30,000, Market value = RM24,000. Reported inventory = RM24,000. Write-down = RM30,000 − RM24,000 = RM6,000.

Cost of Goods Sold6,000
Merchandise Inventory6,000

Effects: Inventory decreases RM6,000; COGS increases RM6,000; Gross profit decreases RM6,000; Net income decreases RM6,000; Total assets decrease RM6,000.

21. Lower-of-cost-or-market item-by-item example

ItemCostMarketLower Amount
A8,0007,0007,000
B5,0006,0005,000
C10,0008,5008,500

Reported inventory = RM7,000 + RM5,000 + RM8,500 = RM20,500. Original cost = RM8,000 + RM5,000 + RM10,000 = RM23,000. Write-down = RM23,000 − RM20,500 = RM2,500.

Cost of Goods Sold2,500
Merchandise Inventory2,500
Do not increase Item B from RM5,000 to RM6,000. Lower-of-cost-or-market permits losses, not imaginary gains.

Part F: Inventory Errors

22. The key inventory-error formula

COGS = Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory

Because ending inventory is subtracted: ending inventory and COGS move oppositely; ending inventory and profit move together.

23. Ending inventory overstated

Suppose ending inventory is overstated by RM4,000. Because too much is subtracted: COGS is understated by RM4,000. Then gross profit is overstated by RM4,000, net income is overstated by RM4,000. Balance-sheet effects: Inventory overstated RM4,000, Total assets overstated RM4,000, Equity overstated RM4,000.

Account or measureEffect
Ending InventoryOverstated
COGSUnderstated
Gross ProfitOverstated
Net IncomeOverstated
Total AssetsOverstated
EquityOverstated

24. Ending inventory understated

Suppose ending inventory is understated by RM3,000. Because too little is subtracted: COGS is overstated by RM3,000. Therefore: gross profit understated RM3,000, net income understated RM3,000, total assets understated RM3,000, equity understated RM3,000.

25. Fast inventory-error rule

Ending Inventory and Net Income move together

Inventory overstated → income overstated. Inventory understated → income understated.

Ending Inventory and COGS move oppositely

Inventory overstated → COGS understated. Inventory understated → COGS overstated.

26. Why the error reverses next year

Ending inventory for Year 1 becomes beginning inventory for Year 2. Suppose Year 1 ending inventory is overstated by RM5,000.

Year 1: Ending inventory too high — COGS understated RM5,000, Net income overstated RM5,000.

Year 2: Beginning inventory now too high — COGS overstated RM5,000, Net income understated RM5,000.

ErrorYear 1 incomeYear 2 income
Ending inventory overstatedOverstatedUnderstated
Ending inventory understatedUnderstatedOverstated
The two-year total income eventually corrects itself, assuming no new errors. That does not mean Year 1 was acceptable. Investors generally prefer financial statements that are correct before the error quietly reverses next year.

27. Full inventory-error calculation

Suppose: Beginning inventory = RM20,000; Purchases = RM90,000; Correct ending inventory = RM25,000; Reported ending inventory = RM29,000; Sales = RM140,000.

Correct COGS = RM20,000 + RM90,000 − RM25,000 = RM85,000

Incorrect COGS = RM20,000 + RM90,000 − RM29,000 = RM81,000

COGS is understated by RM85,000 − RM81,000 = RM4,000

Correct gross profit = RM140,000 − RM85,000 = RM55,000

Incorrect gross profit = RM140,000 − RM81,000 = RM59,000

Gross profit is overstated by RM4,000.

Part G: Inventory Turnover

28. Inventory turnover formula

Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) ÷ 2

The ratio estimates how many times the company sells and replaces its average inventory during the year.

29. Inventory turnover example

Suppose COGS = RM480,000; Beginning inventory = RM70,000; Ending inventory = RM90,000. Average inventory = (RM70,000 + RM90,000) ÷ 2 = RM80,000. Inventory turnover = RM480,000 ÷ RM80,000 = 6 times.

Interpretation: the company sold an amount equivalent to its average inventory approximately six times during the year.

30. Days' sales in inventory

Days' Sales in Inventory = 365 ÷ Inventory Turnover

Using turnover of six: 365 ÷ 6 = 60.83 → ≈61 days.

Interpretation: inventory remains in the business for approximately 61 days before being sold.

31. Interpreting turnover carefully

Higher turnover may mean: inventory sells quickly, less cash is tied up, less risk of obsolescence. But extremely high turnover may mean: inventory levels are too low, frequent stockouts occur, customers cannot obtain products.

Lower turnover may mean: inventory is slow-moving, products are obsolete, too much inventory was purchased. But some industries naturally sell slowly.

Do not compare a convenience store with a luxury car dealership and then announce that the dealership has apparently forgotten how selling works.

Part H: Subjective-Exam Workflow

32. Step-by-step approach for costing questions

  1. Identify the system: write clearly "Perpetual" or "Periodic."
  2. List all inventory layers (e.g. 5 @ RM100, 8 @ RM110, 10 @ RM125).
  3. Calculate total goods available — both total units and total cost.
  4. Calculate units sold and ending units: Units Available − Units Sold = Ending Units.
  5. Apply the costing method — FIFO (oldest costs sold first), LIFO (newest costs sold first), Weighted-average (blend costs).
  6. Calculate COGS for each sale if perpetual — do not skip sale dates.
  7. Calculate ending inventory — list the exact remaining layers.
  8. Perform the control check: COGS + Ending Inventory = Cost of Goods Available.
  9. Calculate gross profit if required: Sales − COGS.
  10. Explain the financial effect — if prices rise: FIFO → higher profit, LIFO → lower profit.

33. Recommended inventory record format

DatePurchasesCOGSInventory Balance
Beginning——5 @ RM100
Purchase8 @ RM110—5 @ RM100; 8 @ RM110
Sale—CalculationRemaining layers
Purchase10 @ RM125—Updated layers
Sale—CalculationEnding layers

This is much safer than doing everything inside one heroic line of arithmetic.

34. Common exam mistakes

  • Using selling price in inventory calculations — inventory costing uses purchase cost, not selling price. Selling price matters only when calculating Sales Revenue and Gross Profit.
  • Applying FIFO or LIFO only at year-end under perpetual — perpetual requires the method to be applied at every sale.
  • Recalculating weighted-average after a sale — under perpetual weighted-average, recalculate after purchases, not sales.
  • Taking a simple average — wrong: (RM100 + RM125) ÷ 2. Correct: Total cost of all units ÷ Total number of units.
  • Forgetting beginning inventory — it is part of goods available for sale.
  • Mixing units and ringgit — always show quantity, cost per unit, and total cost.
  • Forgetting the final check: COGS + Ending Inventory = Goods Available.
  • Assuming highest profit means best method — the method changes cost allocation, not actual cash collected from customers.
  • Confusing perpetual weighted-average with periodic weighted-average — Perpetual → several moving averages. Periodic → one average for the entire period.

35. Formulas to memorise

Goods Available for Sale = Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases
COGS = Goods Available − Ending Inventory
Gross Profit = Net Sales − COGS
Weighted-Average Cost = Total Cost Available ÷ Total Units Available
Lower-of-Cost-or-Market = min(Cost, Market)
Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) ÷ 2
Days in Inventory = 365 ÷ Inventory Turnover

36. Final mental map

FIFO

Old costs → COGS
New costs → Ending Inventory

During rising costs: lower COGS, higher profit, higher inventory.

LIFO

New costs → COGS
Old costs → Ending Inventory

During rising costs: higher COGS, lower profit, lower inventory.

Weighted-average

Blend all available costs — usually falls between FIFO and LIFO.

Inventory errors

Ending Inventory ↑ → COGS ↓ → Profit ↑
Ending Inventory ↓ → COGS ↑ → Profit ↓

The most important control equation

COGS + Ending Inventory = Cost of Goods Available for Sale

For subjective Chapter 6 questions, most marks come from showing the cost layers clearly, applying the method at the correct time, and proving that COGS plus ending inventory equals the total cost available.

Chapter 6

Full Intuitive Explanation

🧠

Open the complete intuitive explanation

The conceptual, reasoning-first companion to the Calc-Focused tab — all content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

Chapter 5 explained how inventory transactions are recorded. Chapter 6 asks a more awkward question:

When identical goods were purchased at different prices, which purchase cost should be assigned to the goods sold?

Suppose a shop buys one tablet for RM350, another for RM360, and another for RM380. The tablets may look identical, but their recorded costs differ. If one tablet is sold, accounting must decide whether its Cost of Goods Sold is RM350, RM360 or RM380.

That decision affects: Cost of Goods Sold, Gross profit, Net income, Ending inventory, Total assets. This is the central issue behind FIFO, LIFO, weighted-average and specific identification.

1. The chapter's central equation

Regardless of the costing method used:

Cost of Goods Available for Sale = Beginning Inventory + Net Cost of Inventory Purchased

That total cost must eventually be divided into two places:

Cost of Goods Available for Sale = Cost of Goods Sold + Ending Inventory

Imagine inventory cost as one large cake. At the end of the period, the portion already eaten becomes Cost of Goods Sold, and the portion remaining becomes Ending Inventory. Every inventory costing method divides the same cake differently — none of the methods changes the total cost available.

2. Physical flow versus cost flow

An inventory costing method does not always describe which physical item was actually sold. For example, FIFO assumes the oldest costs are assigned to Cost of Goods Sold — it does not necessarily mean employees physically searched for the oldest item and sold that exact one. The costing method is mainly a rule for deciding which costs go to COGS and which costs remain in ending inventory.

This distinction matters because students often imagine FIFO and LIFO as warehouse arrangements. They are primarily cost-flow assumptions, not mandatory physical-flow descriptions.

3. Accounting principles related to inventory

Consistency

A business should normally use the same inventory method from one accounting period to another — it should not use FIFO this year, LIFO next year, and weighted-average the year after merely because each method produces the most flattering profit that year. Consistency allows investors to make meaningful comparisons. A method may be changed, but the change and its effects should be disclosed.

Disclosure

Financial statements should provide enough important information for users to understand how the figures were prepared. For inventory, the notes may disclose the inventory costing method used, how inventory is valued, and whether any write-downs occurred.

A figure without context is not especially useful. Reporting RM1 million of inventory while quietly omitting that half of it is obsolete would be creative storytelling, not faithful accounting.

Materiality

Materiality asks whether an item is large enough to affect someone's decision. RM10,000 may be material to a small business earning RM100,000 annually; the same RM10,000 might be insignificant to a multinational company earning billions. Materiality is therefore relative — there is no universal amount that is always material.

The practical question is: would knowing this information reasonably change a user's decision?

Conservatism

When there are two reasonable estimates, conservatism encourages the business not to overstate assets or profit. Its basic attitude: do not recognise uncertain gains too early; recognise probable losses when evidence supports them; avoid presenting inventory at an unrealistically high value. This principle supports the lower-of-cost-or-market rule discussed later.

Conservatism does not mean deliberately making the company look terrible. That would simply replace optimism with another form of distortion.

4. Inventory controls

Inventory can be stolen, damaged, misplaced or recorded incorrectly. A computer balance is not magical truth merely because it appears on a screen. Useful inventory controls include: requiring authorisation before purchases, checking goods when they are received, maintaining receiving documents, separately recording damaged goods, recording every inventory sale and removal, and conducting regular physical counts.

Even under a perpetual system, a physical count is still required. The count checks whether the accounting records agree with reality.

5. The example used throughout the chapter

DateActivityQuantityUnit cost
August 1Beginning inventory2 unitsRM350
August 5Purchase4 unitsRM360
August 15Sale4 units—
August 26Purchase12 unitsRM380
August 31Sale10 units—

Total units available = 2 + 4 + 12 = 18 units

Total units sold = 4 + 10 = 14 units

Ending units = 18 − 14 = 4 units

Total cost available = (2 × RM350) + (4 × RM360) + (12 × RM380) = RM700 + RM1,440 + RM4,560 = RM6,700. Therefore, whichever method is used: COGS + Ending Inventory = RM6,700. The method merely determines how that RM6,700 is divided.

6. Specific identification

Tracks the actual cost of every individual item. Suitable when products are individually distinguishable, expensive, few in number, and easy to track separately — cars, jewellery, property, unique machinery.

Suppose a car dealer has Car A costing RM80,000, Car B costing RM85,000, Car C costing RM90,000. If Car B is sold, RM85,000 becomes Cost of Goods Sold — there is no assumption involved because the exact unit is known.

In the chapter's example, specific identification produces COGS = RM5,200, Ending Inventory = RM1,500. Check: RM5,200 + RM1,500 = RM6,700.

Its weakness is that it is impractical for thousands of identical low-value goods. Nobody sensibly assigns a unique accounting identity to every packet of biscuits in a supermarket.

7. FIFO: First-In, First-Out

FIFO assumes the oldest costs are sold first. COGS receives older costs; ending inventory contains newer costs. Think of a queue — the costs that entered first leave first.

August 15 sale of four units: Before the sale: 2 @ RM350, 4 @ RM360. FIFO sells the oldest costs first: (2 × RM350) + (2 × RM360) = RM700 + RM720 = RM1,420. Remaining: 2 units @ RM360.

August 26 purchase: Add 12 @ RM380. Inventory now: 2 @ RM360, 12 @ RM380.

August 31 sale of ten units: FIFO again uses the oldest costs: (2 × RM360) + (8 × RM380) = RM720 + RM3,040 = RM3,760.

Total FIFO COGS = RM1,420 + RM3,760 = RM5,180

FIFO ending inventory — four of the newest RM380 units remain: 4 × RM380 = RM1,520. Check: RM5,180 + RM1,520 = RM6,700.

FIFO journal entry

The sales revenue entry is unaffected by the inventory method. For the August 15 sale of four units at RM500 each:

Accounts Receivable2,000
Sales Revenue2,000

The inventory method changes only the second entry:

Cost of Goods Sold1,420
Merchandise Inventory1,420

The RM2,000 uses the selling price. The RM1,420 uses the FIFO cost.

8. LIFO: Last-In, First-Out

LIFO assumes the newest costs are sold first. COGS receives recent costs; ending inventory contains older costs. Think of a stack — the latest cost placed on top is the first cost removed.

August 15 sale of four units: Before the sale: 2 @ RM350, 4 @ RM360. The newest units are the RM360 units: 4 × RM360 = RM1,440. Remaining: 2 units @ RM350.

August 26 purchase: Add 12 @ RM380. Inventory now: 2 @ RM350, 12 @ RM380.

August 31 sale of ten units: The newest units are RM380 each: 10 × RM380 = RM3,800.

Total perpetual LIFO COGS = RM1,440 + RM3,800 = RM5,240

Ending inventory — remaining: 2 @ RM350, 2 @ RM380 = RM700 + RM760 = RM1,460. Check: RM5,240 + RM1,460 = RM6,700.

9. Weighted-average under a perpetual system

A new average cost is calculated after every purchase — also called a moving-average method.

Average cost per unit = Total cost of units available ÷ Total units available

It is a weighted average because it considers how many units exist at each cost. Simply averaging RM350 and RM360 would be wrong because there may not be equal quantities at each price.

Average after the August 5 purchase: 2 units (RM700) + 4 units (RM1,440) = 6 units, RM2,140. Average = RM2,140 ÷ 6 = RM356.67 per unit.

August 15 sale: 4 × RM356.67 ≈ RM1,427. Approximately two units remain, with a total rounded cost of RM713.

New average after the August 26 purchase: Remaining cost RM713 + new purchase (12 × RM380) RM4,560 = RM5,273. Total units = 2 + 12 = 14. New average = RM5,273 ÷ 14 ≈ RM376.64.

August 31 sale: 10 × RM376.64 ≈ RM3,766.

Total weighted-average COGS = RM1,427 + RM3,766 = RM5,193

Ending inventory = 4 × RM376.64 ≈ RM1,507. Small differences can arise because of rounding.

10. Comparison of the four methods

Using the chapter's figures:

MethodCOGSEnding InventoryGross Profit
Specific identification5,2001,5001,800
FIFO5,1801,5201,820
LIFO5,2401,4601,760
Weighted-average5,1931,5071,807
Sales revenue is RM7,000 under every method. The goods did not magically sell for different amounts. Only the cost assigned to those sales changed.

11. Effects when inventory costs are rising

In the example, costs rise: RM350 → RM360 → RM380.

FIFO sends the older, cheaper costs to COGS. Therefore: COGS lower, gross profit higher, net income higher, ending inventory higher because recent expensive costs remain.

LIFO sends newer, more expensive costs to COGS. Therefore: COGS higher, gross profit lower, net income lower, ending inventory lower because older cheap costs remain. Weighted-average generally falls between FIFO and LIFO.

MeasureFIFOWeighted-averageLIFO
COGSLowestMiddleHighest
Net incomeHighestMiddleLowest
Ending inventoryHighestMiddleLowest

12. Effects when inventory costs are falling

When costs decline, the pattern reverses. Suppose costs move RM380 → RM360 → RM350. FIFO sends the older expensive costs to COGS, while LIFO sends the newer cheaper costs.

MeasureFIFOWeighted-averageLIFO
COGSHighestMiddleLowest
Net incomeLowestMiddleHighest
Ending inventoryLowestMiddleHighest
Do not memorise two separate tables. Ask: does this method send old costs or new costs to COGS, and are those costs currently higher or lower? That reasoning survives exam questions better than memorising arrows with no idea why they point anywhere.

13. The inventory method does not change cash

Choosing FIFO instead of weighted-average does not change how many units were bought, how many units were sold, the selling price, the cash paid to suppliers, or the cash collected from customers. It changes how accounting allocates historical costs between COGS and ending inventory.

However, because reported profit changes, inventory methods may indirectly affect items linked to accounting income, such as taxes or performance evaluation.

14. Lower-of-cost-or-market

Inventory is initially recorded at historical cost. However, suppose goods cost RM3,000 but can now be replaced for only RM2,200 because they are damaged, outdated or declining in value.

Reported inventory = min(Historical cost, Market value)

Therefore: min(RM3,000, RM2,200) = RM2,200. The loss is RM3,000 − RM2,200 = RM800.

Cost of Goods Sold800
Merchandise Inventory800

After the adjustment: Inventory decreases by RM800; COGS increases by RM800; Gross profit decreases by RM800; Net income decreases by RM800.

Why use the lower amount?

Because reporting the inventory at RM3,000 would overstate the economic value of an asset that can now be replaced for only RM2,200. This applies conservatism:

Do not continue reporting inventory at an amount that is no longer reasonably recoverable.

If market value exceeds cost, inventory generally remains at historical cost. An unrealised gain is not recorded merely because replacement prices increased.

15. Inventory errors

The key formula is:

COGS = Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory

Ending inventory is subtracted. Therefore, ending inventory and COGS move in opposite directions.

Ending inventory is overstated

Suppose ending inventory should be RM20,000 but is mistakenly recorded as RM25,000. The business subtracts RM5,000 too much when calculating COGS. Therefore: Ending Inventory overstated RM5,000; COGS understated RM5,000; Gross Profit overstated RM5,000; Net Income overstated RM5,000; Total Assets overstated RM5,000; Owner's Equity overstated RM5,000.

Intuition: the business claims too many unsold goods remain. If more goods supposedly remain unsold, fewer goods supposedly became COGS. Lower COGS then creates artificially higher profit.

Ending inventory is understated

Suppose RM20,000 exists, but only RM18,800 is recorded — understated by RM1,200. Therefore: Ending Inventory understated RM1,200; COGS overstated RM1,200; Gross Profit understated RM1,200; Net Income understated RM1,200; Total Assets understated RM1,200; Owner's Equity understated RM1,200.

Fast memory rule

Ending Inventory and Profit move together

Ending inventory overstated → profit overstated. Ending inventory understated → profit understated. Meanwhile: Ending Inventory and COGS move oppositely.

16. Why inventory errors reverse in the following period

One period's ending inventory becomes the next period's beginning inventory. Suppose Year 1 ending inventory is overstated by RM5,000.

Year 1: because ending inventory is subtracted — COGS is understated; profit is overstated.

Year 2: the overstated ending inventory becomes overstated beginning inventory. Because beginning inventory is added — COGS is overstated; profit is understated. Therefore, the error reverses across two periods.

Error in Year 1 ending inventoryYear 1 profitYear 2 profit
OverstatedOverstatedUnderstated
UnderstatedUnderstatedOverstated
The two-year total profit eventually becomes correct, assuming no further errors. That does not make the original mistake harmless. Each individual year's statements were still wrong, and users may have made decisions based on them.

17. Inventory turnover

Measures how many times, approximately, the business sells and replaces its average inventory during the year.

Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) ÷ 2

Using the chapter's PepsiCo example: Average Inventory = (RM4,172 + RM4,347) ÷ 2 = RM4,259.5. Inventory Turnover = RM37,075 ÷ RM4,259.5 ≈ 8.70 times.

Interpretation: the company sold and replenished an amount equivalent to its average inventory around 8.7 times during the year.

Is high turnover always good?

Generally, high turnover may indicate goods sell quickly, less cash is trapped in inventory, and obsolescence risk is lower. But an extremely high turnover could also mean inventory levels are too low, the company frequently runs out of stock, and customers cannot buy what they want. Likewise, low turnover might indicate obsolete or unpopular inventory, but some industries naturally hold inventory for longer.

A jewellery retailer and a fresh-food shop should not be judged using the same turnover expectation.

18. Days' sales in inventory

Converts turnover into an average number of days.

Days' Sales in Inventory = 365 ÷ Inventory Turnover

Using turnover of 8.70: 365 ÷ 8.70 ≈ 42 days.

Interpretation: on average, inventory remains with the company for approximately 42 days before being sold. A lower number generally means faster movement, but again, industry context matters. For perishable food, 100 days would probably be a disaster. For specialised machinery, it may be entirely normal.

19. Perpetual versus periodic costing

The costing methods can be used with either inventory system, but their calculations may differ.

Perpetual system

Costs are assigned whenever a sale occurs. For weighted-average, a new moving average is calculated after every purchase. For LIFO, the latest costs available at each sale date are used.

Periodic system

The company waits until the end of the period. It knows total units available, total units sold, and ending units counted. The costing method is then applied to the entire period.

20. Periodic FIFO

Under periodic FIFO, ending inventory contains the newest costs and COGS contains the oldest costs. Four units remain, so ending inventory = 4 × RM380 = RM1,520. COGS = RM6,700 − RM1,520 = RM5,180.

FIFO produces the same ending inventory and COGS under both perpetual and periodic systems in this example. More generally, FIFO perpetual and FIFO periodic produce the same result because both ultimately leave the newest costs in ending inventory.

21. Periodic LIFO

Under periodic LIFO, the newest costs from the entire period are assigned to COGS. Four ending units are taken from the oldest layers: 2 units at RM350, 2 units at RM360. Ending inventory = (2 × RM350) + (2 × RM360) = RM700 + RM720 = RM1,420. COGS = RM6,700 − RM1,420 = RM5,280.

Compare: Perpetual LIFO COGS = RM5,240; Periodic LIFO COGS = RM5,280. The results differ because perpetual LIFO applies LIFO at each sale date, while periodic LIFO looks at the entire period at once.

22. Periodic weighted-average

Calculates one average using all goods available during the entire period. Average cost = RM6,700 ÷ 18 ≈ RM372.22 per unit. Ending inventory = 4 × RM372.22 ≈ RM1,489. COGS = 14 × RM372.22 ≈ RM5,211.

This differs from perpetual weighted-average because perpetual uses a new moving average after each purchase, while periodic uses one average at period-end.

23. Perpetual versus periodic results

MethodPerpetual COGSPeriodic COGS
FIFO5,1805,180
LIFO5,2405,280
Weighted-average5,1935,211

FIFO matches. LIFO and weighted-average may differ because the timing of purchases and sales matters under perpetual accounting.

24. Important typo in the slides

Pages 59 and 60 label Cost of Goods Available for Sale as containing 28 units. Based on the transactions: 2 + 4 + 12 = 18 units. Therefore, 28 units is a slide typo — the RM6,700 total and the later calculations correctly correspond to 18 units, not 28.

Final mental map

When prices rise

FIFO: Old cheap costs → COGS; New expensive costs → Ending Inventory
Therefore: lower COGS, higher profit, higher inventory
LIFO: New expensive costs → COGS; Old cheap costs → Ending Inventory
Therefore: higher COGS, lower profit, lower inventory
Weighted-average: Blends the costs
Therefore: normally between FIFO and LIFO

Inventory error rule

Ending Inventory overstated → COGS understated → Profit overstated
Ending Inventory understated → COGS overstated → Profit understated

Ratios

Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
Days in Inventory = 365 ÷ Turnover

One equation tying the entire chapter together

Beginning Inventory + Purchases = COGS + Ending Inventory
Every costing method is simply a different, rule-based answer to: how much of the available inventory cost should be treated as sold, and how much should remain as an asset?
Chapter 7

Control Concepts

🛡️ The 5 Layers of Defense (Components)

1. Control Env.

The "tone at the top." Does management actually care about ethics, or just pretend to?

2. Risk Assess.

Identifying what could go wrong (e.g., cash theft, data leaks) and how serious it is.

3. Procedures

The actual actions: passwords, alarms, required approvals, and physical counts.

4. Info System

Ensuring the accounting system safely captures and communicates accurate data.

5. Monitoring

Internal/external audits and reviews. Controls must be continuously checked.

⚖️ 3-Duty Rule (Separation)

  • 1. Authorization: Who approves it.
  • 2. Custody: Who physically holds it.
  • 3. Recording: Who enters it in books.
Limitation: Separation fails if employees engage in Collusion (cooperating to bypass controls).

📑 3-Way Match (Payments)

  1. Purchase Order: What was authorized.
  2. Receiving Report: What actually arrived.
  3. Supplier Invoice: What they are charging.

🔍 Internal vs. External Audit

Internal AuditorExternal Auditor
Employee of the companyIndependent outsider
Reviews operations and controlsAudits financial statements
Helps management improve systemsProvides assurance to external users

An audit reduces risk, but it does not guarantee that every fraud will be found.

⚠️ Limitations of Internal Control

Controls provide reasonable assurance, not perfect assurance. They can fail due to human error, carelessness, management override, collusion, or cost limitations.

Collusion: two or more employees cooperate to bypass controls — separation of duties is less effective when the separated employees work together in the fraud.

Cost-benefit: a company shouldn't spend RM10,000 protecting RM100 — the benefit should reasonably exceed the cost.

📜 Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) Provisions

  • Management must take responsibility for internal controls.
  • Public companies must issue an internal control report.
  • External auditors must evaluate internal controls.
  • The PCAOB oversees auditors of public companies.
  • Auditors face restrictions on consulting services for audit clients.
  • Serious penalties apply for fraudulent reporting.

❓ The One Question That Solves Every Reconciling Item

"Who has already recorded it?"

Company recorded it, bank hasn't → adjust the bank side (deposits in transit, outstanding cheques). No journal entry needed.
Bank recorded it, company hasn't → adjust the book side (fees, interest, EFT, NSF). Journal entry required.

Both adjusted balances agree at RM19,720 — that agreement is the whole point of the exercise.
