Chapter 7 is titled Internal Control and Cash. Although much of the chapter is theory, the calculation-heavy areas are quite concentrated: (1) Petty cash, (2) Cash Short and Over, (3) Credit-card processing fees, (4) Bank reconciliation, (5) Journal entries arising from bank reconciliation, (6) Cash ratio.

The most likely long subjective question is a bank reconciliation with related journal entries. Petty cash is another common calculation because it is easy to test and surprisingly easy to get wrong by debiting Petty Cash every time money disappears from the box.

Part A: What you need to know before calculating

1. Internal control in one sentence

Internal control is the system used to safeguard assets, produce reliable records, encourage compliance with policies, and improve operating efficiency. For a subjective question, the examiner may give a situation and ask you to identify the weakness. The central principle is:

Authorization, custody and recording should be separated

For example, one employee should not receive cash, record the cash, deposit the cash, and prepare the bank reconciliation. That person could steal the cash and modify the records.

Perhaps they are perfectly honest, but designing an accounting system around optimism is not much of a control strategy.

2. Important separation of duties

FunctionMeaning
AuthorizationApproving the transaction
CustodyPhysically controlling the asset
RecordingEntering the transaction in the accounting records
ReconciliationComparing independent records

For cash: Cashier handles cash. Accountant records cash. Another employee prepares the bank reconciliation. Manager reviews the reconciliation.

Part B: Petty Cash

3. What is petty cash?

A small cash fund used for minor payments such as postage, small office supplies, taxi or delivery charges, minor repairs. The fund normally operates under an imprest system.

Cash remaining + Petty cash tickets = Authorized petty cash fund

If they do not equal, there is a shortage or overage.

4. Establishing a petty cash fund

Suppose a company creates a RM500 petty cash fund.

Petty Cash500
Cash500

This is not an expense. The company is merely moving cash from the bank account to the petty cash box. Total assets remain unchanged.

5. Ordinary petty cash payments

Suppose the petty cash custodian pays RM40 for delivery. At the time of payment: cash leaves the petty cash box, a petty cash ticket is prepared, and normally no journal entry is made immediately. The expense is recorded when the fund is replenished — this avoids recording a journal entry every time someone buys RM6 worth of envelopes.

6. Replenishing petty cash with no shortage or overage

Suppose: Authorized fund = RM500; Cash remaining = RM170; Petty cash tickets = RM330 (Office Supplies RM200, Delivery Expense RM80, Repairs Expense RM50).

Check: RM170 + RM330 = RM500 — no shortage or overage exists. Cash needed to replenish = RM500 − RM170 = RM330.

Office Supplies200
Delivery Expense80
Repairs Expense50
Cash330
Important: do not debit Petty Cash during ordinary replenishment. The Petty Cash account remains at RM500.

7. Why Petty Cash is not used during replenishment

The Petty Cash account represents the authorized size of the fund, not the physical notes currently inside the box. Even when the box contains only RM170: RM170 exists as physical cash, RM330 has been replaced by tickets — together they still represent the RM500 fund. The account changes only when the authorized fund changes.

8. Petty cash shortage

Suppose: Authorized fund = RM500; Cash remaining = RM168; Tickets = RM330. Total accounted for = RM168 + RM330 = RM498. Shortage = RM500 − RM498 = RM2. Cash required to restore the box to RM500 = RM500 − RM168 = RM332.

Assume tickets are Office Supplies RM200, Delivery Expense RM80, Repairs Expense RM50 (total RM330).

Office Supplies200
Delivery Expense80
Repairs Expense50
Cash Short and Over2
Cash332

The shortage is debited because it behaves like an expense or loss.

9. Petty cash overage

Suppose: Cash remaining = RM175; Tickets = RM330. Total accounted for = RM175 + RM330 = RM505. Overage = RM505 − RM500 = RM5. Cash required to restore the box to RM500 = RM500 − RM175 = RM325.

Office Supplies200
Delivery Expense80
Repairs Expense50
Cash Short and Over5
Cash325

Cash Short and Over is credited because the fund contains RM5 more than expected — it behaves like other income or a reduction of expense.

10. Petty cash formulas

Total Accounted For = Cash Remaining + Petty Cash Tickets
Shortage = Fund Balance − Total Accounted For (when total accounted for is lower)
Overage = Total Accounted For − Fund Balance (when total accounted for is higher)
Replenishment Cheque = Fund Balance − Cash Remaining

11. Increasing the petty cash fund

Suppose the fund increases from RM500 to RM700. Increase = RM700 − RM500 = RM200.

Petty Cash200
Cash200

Now the Petty Cash account balance becomes RM700.

12. Decreasing the petty cash fund

Suppose the fund decreases from RM700 to RM500. Decrease = RM700 − RM500 = RM200.

Cash200
Petty Cash200

The excess cash is returned to the company's main bank account or cash balance.

13. Petty cash account rule

Use Petty Cash only when: establishing the fund, increasing the fund, decreasing the fund.

Do not use Petty Cash when: recording ordinary petty cash expenses, replenishing the existing fund, recording shortages or overages.

Part C: Full Petty Cash Question

On 1 March, Zeta Trading established a petty cash fund of RM400. On 31 March, the fund contained RM96 cash and tickets: Office Supplies RM145, Delivery Expense RM80, Postage Expense RM75. On 1 April, the fund was increased to RM550.

Required: (1) Record the establishment. (2) Determine whether a shortage or overage exists. (3) Record the replenishment. (4) Record the increase in the fund.

Step 1 — Establish the fund:

Mar. 1

Petty Cash400
Cash400

Step 2 — Calculate total tickets: RM145 + RM80 + RM75 = RM300. Total accounted for = RM96 + RM300 = RM396. Shortage = RM400 − RM396 = RM4.

Step 3 — Calculate replenishment amount: RM400 − RM96 = RM304.

Mar. 31

Office Supplies145
Delivery Expense80
Postage Expense75
Cash Short and Over4
Cash304

Step 4 — Increase fund to RM550: Increase needed = RM550 − RM400 = RM150.

Apr. 1

Petty Cash150
Cash150

Part D: Credit and Debit Card Transactions

14. Credit-card processing fee

Suppose card sale = RM8,000, processor fee = 3%. Processing fee = RM8,000 × 3% = RM240. Net cash = RM8,000 − RM240 = RM7,760.

The chapter discusses two methods — net method and gross method. These concern how the payment processor deposits the money, not whether the company feels emotionally gross or net about the transaction.

15. Credit-card sale using the net method

The processor immediately deducts the fee.

Cash7,760
Credit Card Expense240
Sales Revenue8,000

Check: RM7,760 + RM240 = RM8,000. If the business uses a perpetual inventory system, also record COGS separately — suppose the goods cost RM5,000:

Cost of Goods Sold5,000
Merchandise Inventory5,000
The slides sometimes say to ignore COGS in examples merely to focus on the card fee. In a complete merchandising question, do not conveniently forget the second entry.

16. Credit-card sale using the gross method

Under the gross method, the full RM8,000 is deposited first.

Cash8,000
Sales Revenue8,000

Later, the processor deducts RM240:

Credit Card Expense240
Cash240

Net cash effect = RM8,000 − RM240 = RM7,760. Both methods ultimately produce: Sales Revenue = RM8,000; Credit Card Expense = RM240; Net cash received = RM7,760. The difference is timing.

17. Credit-card calculation workflow

Step 1 — Calculate the fee: Card Fee = Sales × Fee Rate

Step 2 — Calculate net cash: Net Cash = Sales − Fee

Step 3 — Identify the method: Net → record Cash and Expense together. Gross → record full Cash first and Expense later.

Part E: Bank Reconciliation

18. Why bank and book balances differ

A business has two cash records: the company's Cash account and the bank statement. They differ because some transactions have been recorded by only one side. The purpose of bank reconciliation is to calculate:

Adjusted Bank Balance = Adjusted Book Balance

These adjusted amounts represent the correct cash balance.

19. The most important bank-reconciliation question

Ask: "Who has already recorded the item?"

Company recorded it, bank has not → adjust the bank side (deposit in transit, outstanding cheque).

Bank recorded it, company has not → adjust the book side (service charge, interest revenue, EFT, NSF cheque, bank collection).

This is safer than memorising a list and then panicking when the wording changes slightly.

20. Bank-side items

The bank side starts with the balance on the bank statement.

Deposit in transit — recorded by the company, not yet recorded by the bank → Add to bank balance.

Outstanding cheque — recorded by the company, not yet paid by the bank → Subtract from bank balance.

Bank error — adjust according to whether the error made the bank balance too high or too low.

21. Book-side items

The book side starts with the Cash balance in the general ledger.

Add to book balance: bank collection from customer, interest revenue, EFT receipt, correction of book error that understated Cash.

Subtract from book balance: bank service charge, NSF cheque, EFT payment, correction of book error that overstated Cash.

22. Bank-reconciliation format

Balance per bank statement
Add: Deposits in transit
Add/Subtract: Bank errors
Less: Outstanding cheques
= Adjusted bank balance
Balance per Cash account
Add: Bank collections, interest, EFT receipts
Add/Subtract: Book errors
Less: Service charges, NSF cheques, EFT payments
= Adjusted book balance

The two adjusted balances must agree.

23. Deposit in transit

Suppose a RM12,000 deposit was recorded by the company on 31 December but appears on the January bank statement. At 31 December: Add RM12,000 to the bank balance. No journal entry is made — the company already recorded Dr Cash / Cr Relevant Account. Recording it again would duplicate the cash receipt.

24. Outstanding cheque

Suppose cheque number 208 for RM4,500 was issued and recorded by the company but has not yet cleared. At month-end: Subtract RM4,500 from the bank balance. No journal entry is made — the company already recorded Dr Relevant Account / Cr Cash.

25. Bank service charge

Suppose the bank deducts RM60. The bank has recorded the reduction, but the company has not. Subtract from the book balance.

Bank Expense60
Cash60

Some questions may use Bank Service Charge Expense instead of Bank Expense. Use the account title given by the lecturer.

26. Interest earned

Suppose the bank credits RM90 interest. Add to the book balance.

Cash90
Interest Revenue90

27. EFT receipt

Suppose a customer pays RM1,800 directly into the company's bank account. The bank has increased the account, but the company has not recorded it. Add to the book balance.

Cash1,800
Accounts Receivable1,800

The credit account depends on why the money was received.

28. EFT payment

Suppose the bank automatically pays RM700 rent. Subtract from the book balance.

Rent Expense700
Cash700

If the payment settles Accounts Payable instead, debit Accounts Payable. Read the transaction rather than automatically using an expense account.

29. NSF cheque

NSF means nonsufficient funds. Suppose a customer's RM2,000 cheque is returned unpaid. The original receipt may have been Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Accounts Receivable 2,000. Because the cheque is worthless, the customer still owes the money.

Accounts Receivable2,000
Cash2,000

Subtract the NSF cheque from the book balance. Do not debit Bad Debt Expense automatically — an NSF cheque does not prove the customer will never pay.

30. Bank collection of a note

Suppose the bank collects: Note principal = RM5,000; Interest = RM200; Collection fee = RM50. Net cash deposited = RM5,000 + RM200 − RM50 = RM5,150.

Cash5,150
Bank Expense50
Notes Receivable5,000
Interest Revenue200

Add RM5,150 to the book balance if that is the net amount credited by the bank. Read the bank advice carefully — some questions may show the gross collection and fee separately.

Part F: Errors in Bank Reconciliation

31. Book error: cheque recorded too high

Suppose a cheque was correctly issued for RM540 but recorded in the books as RM590. The company reduced Cash by RM50 too much. Difference = RM590 − RM540 = RM50. Therefore: Add RM50 to book balance.

Assume the cheque paid Accounts Payable:

Cash50
Accounts Payable50

Why credit Accounts Payable? The original entry probably debited Accounts Payable by RM590 when it should have been RM540. The company reduced the liability RM50 too much, so the liability must be restored.

32. Book error: cheque recorded too low

Suppose a RM920 cheque was recorded as RM290. Cash was reduced by only RM290 instead of RM920. Difference = RM920 − RM290 = RM630. Therefore: Subtract RM630 from book balance.

If the cheque paid Accounts Payable:

Accounts Payable630
Cash630

33. Book error: receipt recorded too low

Suppose a cash receipt of RM6,400 was recorded as RM4,600. Cash is understated by RM6,400 − RM4,600 = RM1,800. Add RM1,800 to the book balance.

If it was collected from a customer:

Cash1,800
Accounts Receivable1,800

34. Bank error

Suppose the bank deducts another company's RM750 cheque from your account. The bank balance is RM750 too low. Therefore: Add RM750 to the bank side. No journal entry is made by the company because its books are already correct.

The bank must fix its own error. For once, accounting allows someone else to clean up their own mess.

Part G: Full Bank Reconciliation Question

The following information relates to Alpha Trading on 31 May: Balance per bank statement RM25,600; Balance per Cash account RM24,130; Deposit in transit RM4,800; Outstanding cheques RM3,250; Bank service charge RM80; EFT receipt from customer RM1,500; Interest earned RM40; NSF customer cheque RM600; a cheque for RM720 paid to a supplier was recorded in the books as RM270; the bank incorrectly deducted another customer's cheque of RM300 from Alpha Trading's account.

Required: (1) Prepare the bank reconciliation. (2) Prepare the related journal entries.

35. Bank side

Beginning bank balance = RM25,600. Add deposit in transit = +RM4,800. Subtract outstanding cheques = −RM3,250. Add bank error = +RM300.

Adjusted bank balance = RM25,600 + RM4,800 − RM3,250 + RM300 = RM27,450

36. Book error calculation

The cheque should have reduced Cash by RM720 but reduced it by only RM270. Cash is overstated by RM720 − RM270 = RM450. Therefore, subtract RM450 from the book balance.

37. Book side

Beginning book balance = RM24,130. Add: EFT receipt RM1,500, Interest RM40. Subtract: Service charge RM80, NSF cheque RM600, Book error RM450.

Calculation: RM24,130 + RM1,500 + RM40 − RM80 − RM600 − RM450 = RM24,540.

This does not equal the adjusted bank balance of RM27,450. That means the data, as presented, do not reconcile. The unreconciled difference is RM27,450 − RM24,540 = RM2,910. In a real exam, this means one of three things: another reconciling item was omitted, one amount was copied incorrectly, or the opening balance is wrong. Do not force both sides to agree by inventing RM2,910 of "miscellaneous adjustment." Accounting markers tend not to reward fiction.

Corrected version for a fully balanced illustration

Suppose the Cash account balance was RM27,040 instead of RM24,130. Then: RM27,040 + RM1,500 + RM40 − RM80 − RM600 − RM450 = RM27,450. Now both sides agree.

38. Journal entries from the corrected example

EFT receipt:

Cash1,500
Accounts Receivable1,500

Interest earned:

Cash40
Interest Revenue40

Bank service charge:

Bank Expense80
Cash80

NSF cheque:

Accounts Receivable600
Cash600

Book error on supplier cheque (understated by RM450):

Accounts Payable450
Cash450

39. Items with no journal entries

Do not journalize: Deposit in transit, Outstanding cheques, Bank error. Why? Deposit and cheque were already recorded by the company. The bank must correct its own error.

Note: the source notes continue into a further worked example ("Part H: Another Fully Worked Bank Reconciliation") that was cut off before it could be captured in full — the reasoning above already covers every reconciling-item pattern that a second worked example would use.
Chapter 7

Full Intuitive Explanation

🧠

Open the complete intuitive explanation

The conceptual, reasoning-first companion to the Calc-Focused tab — all content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

This chapter is really about one uncomfortable fact:

Cash is easy to steal, easy to misuse and easy to record incorrectly.

A business therefore cannot rely entirely on employees being honest, careful and awake. Internal controls are designed so that errors and fraud are either prevented or detected quickly. The chapter covers: internal controls, controls over cash received and paid, petty cash, debit and credit card transactions, bank reconciliations, cash ratio.

The slides call the learning objectives "Chapter 8," although the title page identifies this as Chapter 7. That appears to be a numbering error in the slides rather than a secret bonus chapter.

1. What is internal control?

Internal control refers to the policies and procedures a company uses to: (1) protect its assets, (2) encourage employees to follow company policies, (3) improve operational efficiency, (4) produce accurate accounting records.

An internal control is not merely a locked safe. It includes the entire system surrounding a transaction: who approves it, who handles the asset, who records it, what documents support it, who checks the work afterward.

Simple example

Suppose one employee is allowed to receive cash from customers, record the cash received, deposit it in the bank, and prepare the bank reconciliation. That employee could steal RM500 and alter the records to hide it.

The problem is not necessarily that the employee is dishonest. The problem is that the system gives one person enough control to steal and conceal the theft. A good internal control system reduces that opportunity.

2. The five components of internal control

The chapter identifies five broad components — think of them as layers of defence: Control environment, Risk assessment, Control procedures, Information system, Monitoring.

A. Control environment

The overall attitude of management toward honesty, responsibility and control.

It answers: does management genuinely care about proper controls, or does it merely display an impressive policy manual that nobody follows?

Examples: management behaving ethically, clear organizational structure, hiring competent employees, disciplinary action for violations, management not pressuring employees to manipulate results. The attitude at the top affects everyone below it — if managers ignore controls whenever they become inconvenient, employees quickly learn that the controls are decorative.

B. Risk assessment

The business identifies possible problems and considers how serious they are — cash may be stolen, inventory may disappear, customer information may be leaked, a fake supplier invoice may be paid, accounting data may be lost. The company then decides which controls are needed.

Risk assessment is basically asking: what could go wrong, and what would happen if it did?

C. Control procedures

The actual actions used to prevent or detect problems — requiring approval before purchases, separating duties, using numbered documents, conducting physical counts, requiring passwords, reviewing transactions, reconciling bank accounts. These are the practical part of internal control.

D. Information system

The company needs a system that captures transactions, records them correctly, communicates information to relevant employees, and produces useful reports. For example, a sale should be recorded in Sales Revenue, Cash or Accounts Receivable, Inventory, and Cost of Goods Sold. A poorly designed accounting system may allow transactions to disappear, duplicate or be recorded in the wrong accounts.

E. Monitoring

Controls must be checked over time — a control that worked five years ago may be useless today. Monitoring can include internal audits, external audits, management reviews, surprise cash counts, reviewing unusual transactions.

Internal control is not a machine that is installed once and then admired forever. It must be tested.

3. Important internal control procedures

Competent and ethical employees

Even a good system can fail when employees do not understand their responsibilities. Businesses should hire qualified staff, train them properly, check references, set ethical expectations, evaluate performance. Competence reduces errors, while ethical conduct reduces deliberate fraud.

Assignment of responsibility

Each duty should be clearly assigned to a specific person. Instead of saying "someone in accounting should check this," the company should specify "the accounts payable supervisor must approve the payment."

When responsibility is unclear, everyone can blame everyone else. A wonderfully efficient arrangement for avoiding accountability.

4. Separation of duties

Dividing important responsibilities among different people, to prevent one employee from both committing and hiding an error or fraud. Two major separations are important.

A. Separate operations from accounting

The employee performing the transaction should not be the only person recording it. Example: sales staff sell goods, accounting staff record sales. If the same person performs and records everything, that person can alter the records to cover mistakes or theft.

B. Separate custody of assets from accounting

The person physically controlling an asset should not control its accounting records. Example: cashier handles cash, accountant records cash, another employee prepares the bank reconciliation. If the cashier also maintains the cash records, missing money can be concealed by changing the accounting balance.

The three-duty rule

For important assets, try to separate: (1) Authorization — who approves the transaction, (2) Custody — who holds the asset, (3) Recording — who records the transaction. One person should not control all three.

5. Internal and external audits

Internal audit

Performed by employees of the company. Its purpose is to test controls, identify weaknesses, improve procedures, detect unusual activity. Because internal auditors work for the company, they understand its systems in detail.

External audit

Performed by independent accountants outside the company. Its purpose is mainly to provide an independent opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented.

Internal auditorExternal auditor
Employee of the companyIndependent outsider
Reviews operations and controlsAudits financial statements
Helps management improve systemsProvides assurance to external users

An audit reduces risk, but it does not guarantee that every fraud will be found.

6. Documents as controls

Documents create evidence that transactions occurred — sales invoices, purchase orders, receiving reports, cheques, bank deposit slips, petty cash tickets. Good documents should often be pre-numbered, properly approved, stored securely, and matched with related documents.

Pre-numbering makes missing documents easier to detect. For example, if receipts jump from number 140 to number 142, someone should ask where receipt 141 went.

7. Electronic controls

Modern controls include: passwords, PINs, firewalls, encryption, digital signatures, access logs, inventory sensors, multi-factor authentication.

Encryption converts readable information into an unreadable format unless the user has the correct key.

Firewall limits unauthorized access to a network.

Access restriction — employees should only access the information needed for their jobs. A cashier probably does not need permission to alter employee payroll records.

8. Other controls

The chapter lists controls such as: fireproof vaults, alarms, fidelity bonds, mandatory vacations, job rotation, loss-prevention employees.

Why mandatory vacations can detect fraud

Some fraud schemes require continuous concealment. When the responsible employee takes leave, another employee performs the job and may discover irregularities.

Why job rotation helps

Fraud becomes harder when duties regularly change and another person reviews the work.

9. Limitations of internal control

Internal control provides reasonable assurance, not perfect assurance. Controls can fail because of human error, carelessness, management override, collusion, cost limitations.

Collusion

Two or more employees cooperate to bypass controls. For example: one employee approves a fake supplier, another employee creates the invoice, both share the payment. Separation of duties is less effective when separated employees cooperate in the fraud.

Cost-benefit limitation

Controls cost money. A company should not spend RM10,000 on a control designed to protect RM100. The benefit should reasonably exceed the cost. This does not mean ignoring small thefts — it means selecting controls appropriate to the risk.

10. Sarbanes–Oxley Act

Commonly called SOX, introduced after major accounting scandals involving public companies. The chapter emphasizes several provisions: management must take responsibility for internal controls; public companies must issue an internal control report; external auditors must evaluate internal controls; the PCAOB oversees auditors of public companies; auditors face restrictions on providing certain consulting services to audit clients; serious penalties apply for fraudulent reporting.

The basic idea is: senior executives cannot simply blame junior accountants when the financial reports are false.

11. Controls over cash receipts

Cash receipts mainly arise from cash sales, customer payments, bank collections, electronic receipts. The business must ensure that all cash received is recorded, deposited, and matched with supporting records.

Cash sales at a store

Useful controls include: a point-of-sale terminal, a receipt issued for every sale, cash counted at the end of the shift, cash register totals compared with actual cash, cash deposited daily, different people handling cash and reviewing records.

Example

The register reports RM4,000 of sales. Cash in the drawer is RM3,950. There is a RM50 shortage.

The difference should be investigated rather than casually blamed on "the system," a phrase that has protected many questionable cash drawers.

12. Cash receipts by mail

The diagram on page 20 separates incoming cheques from the accounting information. This reduces the ability of one employee to steal a cheque and hide the missing payment. The process works like this:

Step 1 — Mailroom: the mailroom employee opens the mail. Cheques go to the treasurer or cashier. Remittance advices go to accounting. A remittance advice explains who paid, how much was paid, and which account or invoice the payment relates to.

Step 2 — Treasurer or cashier: the cheques are deposited in the bank. The bank provides a deposit receipt.

Step 3 — Accounting department: accounting uses the remittance advices to record:

Cash
Accounts Receivable

Step 4 — Controller: the controller compares the bank deposit total with the amount recorded as a debit to Cash. The amounts should agree.

Why split the cheque and remittance advice?

Suppose the employee opening the mail receives both the cheque and the customer account information. That employee could steal the cheque and alter the records to make it appear that the customer never paid. Separating the documents makes concealment more difficult.

13. Lock-box system

Allows customers to send payments directly to a post office box controlled by the bank. The bank opens the box, processes the payments, deposits them directly, and sends payment information to the company. Benefits: faster deposits, less employee access to cash, reduced theft risk, improved processing speed. The disadvantage is that the bank charges a fee.

14. Controls over cash payments

Most large payments should be made using cheques, electronic payments, or authorized banking systems — these provide a record of the payment. Before paying a supplier, the company should confirm: (1) the purchase was authorized, (2) the goods were actually received, (3) the invoice amount is correct, (4) the payment has not already been made.

15. The payment packet and three-way matching

Pages 26–27 show three documents used before paying a supplier — often called a three-way match: (1) Purchase order, (2) Receiving report, (3) Supplier invoice.

Purchase order shows what the company authorized: product, quantity, agreed price, supplier.

Receiving report shows what actually arrived: product received, quantity received, condition of goods.

Supplier invoice shows what the supplier is charging: items, quantity, price, total amount owed.

Why match all three?

Suppose the purchase order authorizes 100 units, the receiving report confirms only 80 arrived, and the invoice charges for 100.

The business should not blindly pay for 100 merely because the supplier managed to produce a professional-looking invoice. Payment should normally be based on the authorized quantity actually received.

16. Evaluated receipts settlement and EDI

Evaluated receipts settlement simplifies payment by comparing the purchase order with the receiving report. The company calculates the amount owed without waiting for a traditional supplier invoice.

Electronic data interchange allows the buyer's and supplier's computer systems to exchange transaction information directly — purchase orders, shipping information, invoices, payment details.

It reduces paperwork and processing time, although automated nonsense remains nonsense if the underlying data is wrong.

17. Petty cash

A small amount of cash kept for minor payments — postage, small office supplies, taxi fares, minor delivery costs. It avoids issuing a cheque for every RM5 purchase.

18. Establishing a petty cash fund

Suppose the company creates a RM200 petty cash fund.

Petty Cash200
Cash200

This does not reduce the company's total cash — it merely transfers cash from the bank account to the petty cash box. Both Cash and Petty Cash are assets.

19. The imprest petty cash system

Under an imprest system, the authorized petty cash fund remains at a fixed amount. At any time:

Cash on hand + Petty cash tickets = Authorized fund balance

Suppose the authorized fund is RM200. If RM60 has been spent: cash remaining should be RM140, tickets should total RM60. RM140 + RM60 = RM200. The petty cash tickets replace the physical cash that was spent.

20. Why petty cash payments are not immediately journalized

When the custodian pays RM20 for delivery: a petty cash ticket is prepared, but no journal entry is made immediately. The expenses are recorded when the fund is replenished — this avoids making dozens of tiny journal entries throughout the month. The Petty Cash account itself normally remains at the authorized balance.

21. Replenishing petty cash with a shortage

The chapter gives: Authorized fund RM200; Cash remaining RM118; Tickets RM80. Total accounted for = RM118 + RM80 = RM198. Shortage = RM200 − RM198 = RM2. Cash needed to restore the box to RM200 = RM200 − RM118 = RM82.

Suppose the tickets consist of Office Supplies RM60, Delivery Expense RM20.

Office Supplies60
Delivery Expense20
Cash Short and Over2
Cash82

Why debit Cash Short and Over? A shortage behaves like an expense or loss — the company has RM2 less cash than it should have.

22. Replenishing petty cash with an overage

Suppose Cash remaining RM118, Tickets RM90. Total accounted for = RM118 + RM90 = RM208. The authorized fund is only RM200, so there is an RM8 overage. The amount needed to restore physical cash remains RM200 − RM118 = RM82.

Office Supplies60
Delivery Expense30
Cash Short and Over8
Cash82

Why credit Cash Short and Over? An overage behaves like other income or a reduction of expense — there is RM8 more value than expected.

23. Petty Cash account rule

The Petty Cash account is normally used only when establishing the fund, increasing the fund, or decreasing the fund. It is not used for ordinary replenishment. This is a common exam trap.

Ordinary replenishment:
Dr Expenses
Dr/Cr Cash Short and Over
   Cr Cash

Do not debit Petty Cash again unless the authorized fund itself changes.

24. Increasing the petty cash fund

Suppose the fund increases from RM200 to RM300. Increase needed = RM300 − RM200 = RM100.

Petty Cash100
Cash100

Now the Petty Cash account balance is RM300.

25. Debit and credit card sales

Businesses accepting card payments should protect customer information. Controls include: using approved POS terminals, encrypting cardholder data, not printing the full card number, restricting access to stored card information, training employees, separating refunds from reconciliation, maintaining firewalls, minimizing data storage. The business normally pays a fee to the card processor.

26. Credit card sale using the net method

Suppose Sale = RM3,000; Processing fee = 4%. Fee = RM3,000 × 4% = RM120. Cash received = RM3,000 − RM120 = RM2,880.

Cash2,880
Credit Card Expense120
Sales Revenue3,000

The processor deposits the net amount after deducting its fee.

27. Credit card sale using the gross method

Under the gross method, the full sale amount is deposited first. On the sale date:

Cash3,000
Sales Revenue3,000

When the processor later deducts its fee:

Credit Card Expense120
Cash120
Net methodGross method
Fee deducted immediatelyFull sales amount deposited
One entry includes feeFee recorded separately later
Cash initially RM2,880Cash initially RM3,000

Both methods eventually produce: Sales Revenue of RM3,000; Credit Card Expense of RM120; Net cash increase of RM2,880. The difference is timing.

28. Bank account as a control device

A bank account provides an independent record of cash transactions. The company has its own Cash account; the bank independently records deposits, cheques, electronic transfers, fees, collections. These two records can be compared — that independence is what makes the bank useful as a control.

29. Common bank documents

Signature card shows who is authorized to sign cheques or operate the account.

Deposit ticket lists the money being deposited.

Cheque is an instruction to the bank to pay a specified amount. Important parties: Maker (person or company issuing the cheque), Payee (person or company receiving payment), Bank (institution ordered to pay). The cheque diagram on page 49 also identifies the routing number, account number and cheque serial number.

30. Bank statement

A bank statement normally shows: beginning balance, deposits, cheques, EFT receipts, EFT payments, bank charges, interest, ending balance. The bank statement and the company's Cash account will often disagree at month-end — this does not automatically mean somebody stole the money. Usually, the difference is caused by timing or transactions recorded by only one party.

31. Bank reconciliation

A bank reconciliation explains why the bank's cash balance and the company's Cash account balance are different. The objective is to calculate the correct adjusted cash balance. Both sides must end at the same amount:

Adjusted bank balance = Adjusted book balance

32. The two sides of a bank reconciliation

Bank side

Begins with the balance on the bank statement. Adjust for items that the company already recorded but the bank has not. Typical items: deposits in transit, outstanding cheques, bank errors.

Book side

Begins with the Cash balance in the company's general ledger. Adjust for items that the bank already recorded but the company has not. Typical items: bank collections, interest revenue, EFT receipts, service charges, EFT payments, NSF cheques, book errors.

33. Deposits in transit

A deposit in transit has been recorded by the company but not yet recorded by the bank. Example: the company deposits RM9,000 on 30 April after the bank's processing cut-off. The company already increased Cash, but the bank statement does not yet include it.

Therefore: Add deposit in transit to bank balance. It is not added to the book balance because the company already recorded it.

34. Outstanding cheques

An outstanding cheque has been written and recorded by the company but not yet processed by the bank. Example: the company issued a RM2,000 cheque. The company already reduced Cash, but the bank has not yet reduced the account.

Therefore: Subtract outstanding cheque from bank balance. It is not deducted from the book balance again — doing so would record the payment twice.

35. Bank collections and EFT receipts

Suppose the bank collects RM100 from a customer on behalf of the company. The bank has increased the account, but the company has not yet recorded it.

Therefore: Add to book balance.

Cash100
Accounts Receivable100

36. Interest revenue

Suppose the bank credits RM30 of interest. The bank already added it, but the company has not recorded it.

Therefore: Add to book balance.

Cash30
Interest Revenue30

37. Bank service charge

Suppose the bank deducts a RM20 monthly fee. The bank has already reduced the account, but the company has not yet recorded it.

Therefore: Subtract from book balance.

Bank Expense20
Cash20

38. EFT payment

Suppose the bank automatically pays a RM40 utility bill. The bank reduced the account, but the company has not recorded it.

Therefore: Subtract from book balance.

Utilities Expense40
Cash40

39. NSF cheque

NSF means nonsufficient funds. Suppose a customer pays RM1,200 by cheque. The company initially records:

Cash1,200
Accounts Receivable1,200

Later, the bank discovers the customer does not have enough money and reverses the deposit. The company has not really received cash — the customer still owes the amount. Correction:

Accounts Receivable1,200
Cash1,200

An NSF cheque is not automatically a bad debt. The customer may still pay later — the receivable is restored.

40. Complete bank reconciliation example

Bank balance: RM12,720. Add deposit in transit: +RM9,000. Subtract outstanding cheque: −RM2,000. Adjusted bank balance = RM12,720 + RM9,000 − RM2,000 = RM19,720.

Book balance: RM20,850. Add: EFT receipt RM100, Interest revenue RM30. Subtract: Service charge RM20, EFT utility payment RM40, NSF cheque RM1,200. RM20,850 + RM100 + RM30 − RM20 − RM40 − RM1,200 = RM19,720. Both adjusted balances agree.

41. The most important bank reconciliation rule

Items on the bank side usually do not require journal entries. Why? Because deposits in transit and outstanding cheques have already been recorded in the company's books.

Items on the book side usually do require journal entries. Why? Because the company has not yet recorded them.

Journalize book-side adjustments, not ordinary bank-side timing differences

Bank errors are corrected by the bank. Book errors are corrected by the company.

42. Fast bank reconciliation guide

Bank statement balance
+ Deposits in transit
− Outstanding cheques
± Bank errors
= Adjusted bank balance
Book Cash balance
+ Bank collections
+ Interest
+ EFT receipts
− Service charges
− NSF cheques
− EFT payments
± Book errors
= Adjusted book balance

The two adjusted amounts must agree.

43. How to decide whether an item belongs on the bank or book side

Ask: "Who has already recorded it?"

Company recorded it, bank has not → adjust the bank side. Examples: deposit in transit, outstanding cheque.

Bank recorded it, company has not → adjust the book side. Examples: bank fee, interest, NSF cheque, EFT.

That one question is more reliable than memorizing a random list without understanding it.

44. Book errors

Suppose the company writes a cheque for RM540 but records it as RM450. The company reduced Cash by RM90 too little. Correction required = RM540 − RM450 = RM90. Subtract RM90 from the book balance. The related journal entry depends on the original transaction — for example:

Accounts Payable90
Cash90

The bank did nothing wrong, so the bank side is not adjusted.

45. Bank errors

Suppose the bank mistakenly deducts another customer's RM500 cheque from the company's account. The bank balance is RM500 too low. Add RM500 on the bank side. No journal entry is made by the company because the company's books were already correct. The bank must correct its own mistake.

46. Cash ratio

The cash ratio measures whether a company can pay its current liabilities using only its most liquid resources.

Cash Ratio = (Cash + Cash Equivalents) ÷ Current Liabilities

Cash equivalents are highly liquid short-term investments generally convertible into cash within three months or less — e.g. treasury bills, money market instruments, very short-term deposits.

47. Cash ratio example

The chapter gives: Cash and cash equivalents = RM5,596 million; Current liabilities = RM26,220 million. Cash Ratio = RM5,596 ÷ RM26,220 = 0.21.

Interpretation: the company has approximately RM0.21 of cash and cash equivalents for every RM1 of current liabilities. This does not necessarily mean the company can pay only 21% of its liabilities overall — it may also collect receivables, sell inventory, or generate operating cash before those liabilities become due.

48. Is a higher cash ratio always better?

A higher ratio suggests stronger immediate liquidity. However, an extremely high cash ratio may indicate that too much cash is sitting idle, the company is not investing productively, or management lacks useful expansion opportunities.

A lower ratio may be risky, but it can be normal for businesses with stable daily cash collections, fast inventory turnover, reliable access to credit. The ratio should be compared with previous years, competitors, industry averages, and the company's business model.

One ratio without context is just a number wearing a tie.

49. Final mental map

Internal control

Protect assets
+ Follow policies
+ Improve efficiency
+ Reliable accounting records

Separation of duties

Authorization
Custody
Recording

Keep these duties with different people where practical.

Petty cash

Cash remaining + Petty cash tickets
= Authorized fund

Use Petty Cash only when establishing or changing the fund.

Bank reconciliation

Bank side:
+ Deposits in transit
− Outstanding cheques
± Bank errors
Book side:
+ Collections, interest, EFT receipts
− Fees, NSF cheques, EFT payments
± Book errors

Journal entries

Record book-side adjustments. Do not record ordinary deposits in transit or outstanding cheques again.

Cash ratio

Cash Ratio = (Cash + Cash Equivalents) ÷ Current Liabilities
The main idea tying the chapter together is: do not allow one person, one document or one accounting record to be the only evidence that cash is correct.
Chapter 8

Cash Flows Core Concepts

🤔 Why Net Income ≠ Cash

  • Credit Sales (Revenue ↑, Cash = 0).
  • Depreciation (Net Income ↓, Cash = 0).
  • Equipment purchase (Uses cash, Income unchanged).

💸 Free Cash Flow (FCF)

Operating Cash Flow − Planned CapEx − Cash Dividends
= Free Cash Flow

🧮 The Logic of Indirect Adjustments

The indirect method begins with accrual-based profit, then removes everything that did not represent operating cash.

Adding Back Depreciation

Depreciation reduced net income without reducing current-period cash. Adding it back cancels out the deduction. (It does not mean depreciation creates cash).

Subtracting Gains

The gain inflated net income, but the full cash proceeds belong in the Investing section. Subtracting the gain removes it from Operating so it isn't double-counted.

Adding Back Losses

A loss reduced net income, but the disposal is an investing activity — the loss itself is not an operating cash payment, so it's added back.

🚨 Common Exam Traps

  • Trap: Reporting only the gain from an asset sale under Investing.
    Fact: Report the FULL cash proceeds.
  • Trap: Putting loan repayments entirely under Operating.
    Fact: Principal = Financing. Interest = Operating.
  • Trap: Treating equipment purchases as Operating expenses.
    Fact: Equipment is a long-term asset (Investing).

🗺️ Balance-Sheet Shortcut

Account CategoryUsually Linked To
Current assetsOperating
Current liabilitiesOperating
Long-term assetsInvesting
Long-term liabilitiesFinancing
EquityFinancing

A useful starting point, not a mindless rule — e.g. dividends reduce retained earnings but are financing.

📋 Non-Cash Investing & Financing Activities

Major transactions that affect investing/financing accounts but use no cash — e.g. building acquired by issuing shares, land acquired via a note payable, debt converted to shares.

Building300,000
Common Stock300,000

Cash effect = RM0 → disclosed separately, never inside the main cash-flow totals.

Chapter 8

Classification

⚙️ Operating
  • + Collections
  • + Interest/Div Rcvd
  • − Pay Suppliers
  • − Pay Employees
  • − Pay Interest/Tax
🏭 Investing
  • + Sell Equip/Land
  • + Sell Long-term Investments
  • − Buy Equip/Land
  • − Loans Made to Others
🏦 Financing
  • + Borrow / Issue Stock
  • − Repay Principal
  • − Pay Dividends
  • − Buy Treasury Stock

Long-term assets → Investing

Long-term debt and equity → Financing

💡 The Interest/Dividend Trap

Under this chapter's classification, interest and dividends split by whether they're received or paid:

ItemClassification
Interest receivedOperating
Dividend income receivedOperating
Interest paidOperating
Dividends paid to shareholdersFinancing

Apparently one payment (a loan repayment) was not complicated enough — accounting splits it: principal → financing, interest → operating.
