Chapter 8

Calculation-Focused Explanation

🧮

Open the complete calculation-focused explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

This treats Appendix B: Statement of Cash Flows as Chapter 8. For a subjective calculation exam, this chapter mainly tests whether you can take information from two balance sheets, one income statement, and additional transaction information, and convert it into a complete statement of cash flows.

The most likely calculation areas: (1) Classifying transactions as operating, investing or financing, (2) Preparing operating cash flow using the indirect method, (3) Calculating cash paid for long-term assets, (4) Calculating cash received from disposal of assets, (5) Calculating financing cash flows, (6) Finding dividends paid, (7) Preparing non-cash disclosures, (8) Calculating free cash flow, (9) Preparing operating cash flow using the direct method.

Part A: The logic behind the statement

1. Net income is not cash

Suppose a company makes a RM20,000 credit sale:

Accounts Receivable20,000
Sales Revenue20,000

Net income increases, but Cash does not. Now suppose the company records RM5,000 depreciation:

Depreciation Expense5,000
Accumulated Depreciation5,000

Net income decreases, but no cash leaves the company. Therefore:

Net income ≠ cash generated

The statement of cash flows explains the difference.

2. The final cash equation

The entire statement must satisfy:

Operating Cash Flow + Investing Cash Flow + Financing Cash Flow = Net Change in Cash

Then:

Beginning Cash + Net Change in Cash = Ending Cash

The ending cash must agree with the Cash balance shown on the ending balance sheet. That is your final control check.

Part B: Classifying cash flows

3. Operating activities

Relate mainly to normal revenues and expenses.

Inflows: Cash collected from customers, Interest received, Dividend income received.

Outflows: Payments to suppliers, Payments to employees, Operating expenses, Interest paid, Income tax paid.

Under the classification used in the slides: Interest received → operating. Dividend income received → operating. Interest paid → operating. Dividends paid to shareholders → financing.

4. Investing activities

Relate mainly to long-term assets.

Inflows: Sale of equipment, Sale of land or buildings, Sale of long-term investments, Collection of long-term notes receivable.

Outflows: Purchase of equipment, Purchase of buildings or land, Purchase of long-term investments, Loans made to other parties.

Long-term assets → Investing

5. Financing activities

Involve lenders and owners.

Inflows: Borrowing money, Issuing notes or bonds, Issuing common shares, Selling treasury shares.

Outflows: Repaying loan principal, Paying dividends, Purchasing treasury shares.

Long-term debt and equity → Financing

6. Quick classification table

TransactionClassificationEffect
Cash collected from customersOperatingInflow
Cash paid to suppliersOperatingOutflow
Equipment purchased for cashInvestingOutflow
Equipment sold for cashInvestingInflow
Loan receivedFinancingInflow
Loan principal repaidFinancingOutflow
Interest paidOperatingOutflow
Shares issued for cashFinancingInflow
Dividends paidFinancingOutflow
Treasury shares purchasedFinancingOutflow

7. Non-cash investing and financing activities

Some major transactions affect investing and financing accounts but use no cash — building acquired by issuing shares, land acquired by issuing a note payable, debt converted into common shares.

Building300,000
Common Stock300,000

This is not included in the main cash-flow totals because Cash effect = RM0. It is disclosed separately under non-cash investing and financing activities.

Part C: Indirect method

8. The basic indirect-method format

Starts with accrual-basis net income.

Cash Flows from Operating Activities

Net Income

Adjustments:
+ Depreciation and other non-cash expenses
− Gains on disposal
+ Losses on disposal
± Changes in current assets
± Changes in current liabilities

Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities

The aim is not to recalculate profit — the aim is to convert accrual net income into operating cash flow.

9. Indirect-method adjustment rules

ItemAdjustment
Depreciation, depletion and amortizationAdd
Gain on disposalSubtract
Loss on disposalAdd
Increase in current assetSubtract
Decrease in current assetAdd
Increase in current liabilityAdd
Decrease in current liabilitySubtract
Current assets move opposite
Current liabilities move together
Current asset increases → subtract
Current asset decreases → add

Current liability increases → add
Current liability decreases → subtract

10. Why depreciation is added back

Depreciation reduces net income (Dr Depreciation Expense / Cr Accumulated Depreciation) but does not reduce Cash. Suppose Net income = RM50,000, Depreciation = RM12,000. Net income has already been reduced by RM12,000 despite no cash payment. Therefore: RM50,000 + RM12,000 — depreciation is added back.

Depreciation does not create cash. It is added back only because it reduced net income without reducing cash.

11. Why gains are subtracted

Suppose equipment is sold and the company records a RM7,000 gain. The gain increases net income, but the equipment sale is an investing activity. The full cash received from selling the equipment belongs in the investing section.

Gain → Subtract from net income

Otherwise, part of the asset-sale effect would appear in both operating and investing sections.

12. Why losses are added

A loss reduces net income, but it is not an operating cash payment.

Loss → Add back

Memory rule: Gain increased income → subtract. Loss decreased income → add.

Part D: Current asset adjustments

13. Increase in Accounts Receivable

Suppose Sales revenue = RM100,000, Accounts Receivable increased by RM15,000. The company recognized RM100,000 of revenue but did not collect RM15,000. Cash collected = RM100,000 − RM15,000.

Subtract increase in Accounts Receivable

14. Decrease in Accounts Receivable

Suppose Accounts Receivable decreases by RM8,000. This generally means the company collected cash from customers for sales recorded previously.

Add decrease in Accounts Receivable

15. Increase in inventory

Suppose Merchandise Inventory increases by RM10,000. The company purchased more inventory than it sold. Obtaining that additional inventory required cash or created liabilities.

Subtract increase in inventory
An increasing asset may look positive on the balance sheet, but the cash-flow question is asking where cash went, not whether management looks pleased in the annual report.

16. Decrease in inventory

Suppose inventory decreases by RM4,000. The company sold inventory that had already been purchased in an earlier period. Current-period cash purchases were therefore lower than COGS.

Add decrease in inventory

17. Prepaid expenses and other current assets

The same rule applies. Increase in prepaid expense — cash was paid before the expense was recognized → Subtract.

Decrease in prepaid expense — expense was recognized using an amount paid earlier → Add.

Part E: Current liability adjustments

18. Increase in Accounts Payable

Suppose Accounts Payable increases by RM20,000. The company purchased goods or incurred expenses but has not paid RM20,000. Cash was preserved.

Add increase in Accounts Payable

19. Decrease in Accounts Payable

Suppose Accounts Payable decreases by RM6,000. The company paid more cash than the new obligations incurred during the period.

Subtract decrease in Accounts Payable

20. Accrued liabilities

Suppose salary expense is RM30,000 and Salaries Payable increases by RM5,000. The company recognized RM30,000 expense but paid only RM25,000. The unpaid RM5,000 should be added under the indirect method. If Salaries Payable decreases, the company paid obligations from an earlier period, so the decrease is subtracted.

Part F: Full indirect-method operating example

The chapter's ShopMart example provides: Net income RM40,000; Depreciation expense RM20,000; Gain on disposal of plant assets RM10,000; Accounts Receivable increased RM17,000; Merchandise Inventory decreased RM2,000; Accounts Payable increased RM40,000; Accrued Liabilities decreased RM5,000.

RM40,000 + RM20,000 − RM10,000 − RM17,000 + RM2,000 + RM40,000 − RM5,000 = RM70,000

Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities = RM70,000

Part G: Investing activities

21. Why ending balance changes are not enough

Suppose Plant Assets increased from RM250,000 to RM500,000. It does not automatically mean the company bought RM250,000 of assets — it may also have purchased assets, sold assets, or acquired assets without cash. You may need Plant Assets and Accumulated Depreciation T-accounts.

22. Plant Assets T-account formula

Beginning Plant Assets + Purchases − Cost of Assets Disposed = Ending Plant Assets
Purchases = Ending Plant Assets − Beginning Plant Assets + Cost of Assets Disposed

Only the cash portion of purchases belongs in investing cash flow.

23. ShopMart plant asset purchases

Beginning Plant Assets = RM252,000; Assets disposed at original cost = RM55,000; Ending Plant Assets = RM507,000. Acquisitions = RM507,000 − RM252,000 + RM55,000 = RM310,000. Assuming all acquisitions were paid in cash: Investing outflow = RM310,000.

24. Calculating cash received from asset disposal

Suppose an asset had: Original cost RM55,000; Accumulated depreciation RM15,000; Gain on disposal RM10,000.

Step 1 — Book value: RM55,000 − RM15,000 = RM40,000

Step 2 — Add the gain: RM40,000 + RM10,000 = RM50,000 cash received.

25. Disposal formula

Cash Received = Original Cost − Accumulated Depreciation + Gain − Loss

Equivalent to:

Cash Received = Book Value + Gain − Loss

26. Disposal entry

Cash50,000
Accumulated Depreciation15,000
Plant Assets55,000
Gain on Disposal10,000

The investing section reports RM50,000, not RM10,000. The RM10,000 is only the gain, not the cash proceeds.

27. ShopMart investing section

Cash Flows from Investing Activities

Cash paid for acquisition of plant assets    (RM310,000)
Cash received from disposal of plant assets    50,000

Net Cash Used for Investing Activities    (RM260,000)

RM50,000 − RM310,000 = (RM260,000).

A negative investing cash flow is not automatically bad. It may mean the company is expanding. Naturally, buying new productive equipment costs money; apparently factories do not materialize because management believed strongly enough.

Part H: Financing activities

28. Notes payable

Beginning Notes Payable RM80,000; New notes issued RM90,000; Notes repaid RM10,000; Ending Notes Payable RM160,000. Check: RM80,000 + RM90,000 − RM10,000 = RM160,000.

Cash-flow treatment: RM90,000 borrowing → financing inflow. RM10,000 principal repayment → financing outflow.

29. Borrowing entry

Cash90,000
Notes Payable90,000

30. Loan repayment entry

Notes Payable10,000
Cash10,000

Only principal repayment is financing. Interest paid is operating under the chapter's classification.

31. Issuing common shares

Suppose common shares increase by RM120,000 because shares were issued for cash.

Cash120,000
Common Stock120,000

This is a financing inflow.

32. Treasury shares

Suppose the company purchases RM20,000 of its own shares.

Treasury Stock20,000
Cash20,000

This is a financing outflow. Treasury Stock is contra-equity, not an investment asset.

33. Calculating dividends from retained earnings

Ending Retained Earnings = Beginning Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends

Rearrange:

Dividends = Beginning Retained Earnings + Net Income − Ending Retained Earnings

Example

Beginning RE RM80,000; Net income RM40,000; Ending RE RM110,000. Dividends = RM80,000 + RM40,000 − RM110,000 = RM10,000. Assuming cash dividends: Financing outflow = RM10,000.

34. Important dividend warning

The Retained Earnings calculation may tell you dividends declared, not necessarily dividends paid. If Dividends Payable exists, calculate cash paid separately:

Cash Dividends Paid = Dividends Declared + Beginning Dividends Payable − Ending Dividends Payable

Use this only when Dividends Payable information is given.

35. ShopMart financing section

Financing activityRM
Cash received from notes payable90,000
Cash paid on notes payable(10,000)
Cash received from common shares120,000
Treasury shares purchased(20,000)
Dividends paid(10,000)

Net financing cash flow = RM90,000 − RM10,000 + RM120,000 − RM20,000 − RM10,000 = RM170,000

Part I: Completing the statement

36. Calculate net change in cash

ShopMart: Operating RM70,000; Investing (RM260,000); Financing RM170,000. RM70,000 − RM260,000 + RM170,000 = (RM20,000). Cash decreased by RM20,000.

37. Calculate ending cash

Beginning cash RM42,000. Net decrease (RM20,000). Ending cash = RM42,000 − RM20,000 = RM22,000. This must agree with the ending balance sheet Cash account.

38. Full ShopMart cash-flow structure

ShopMart
Statement of Cash Flows
For the Year Ended 31 December 2025

Cash Flows from Operating Activities
Net cash provided by operating activities    RM70,000

Cash Flows from Investing Activities
Net cash used for investing activities    (260,000)

Cash Flows from Financing Activities
Net cash provided by financing activities    170,000

Net decrease in cash    (20,000)
Cash balance, beginning    42,000
Cash balance, ending    RM22,000

Part J: Non-cash investing and financing activities

39. Building acquired by issuing shares

Building300,000
Common Stock300,000

Disclosure: "Acquisition of building by issuing common shares: RM300,000"

40. Land acquired by issuing a note

Land70,000
Notes Payable70,000

Disclosure: "Acquisition of land by issuing notes payable: RM70,000"

41. Debt retired by issuing shares

Notes Payable100,000
Common Stock100,000

Disclosure: "Retirement of notes payable through common-share issuance: RM100,000." These affect the company significantly but do not appear inside the main cash totals because no cash moved.

Part K: Free cash flow

42. Formula

Free Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow − Planned Capital Expenditures − Cash Dividends

43. Example

Operating cash flow RM200,000; Planned long-term asset purchases RM160,000; Cash dividends RM15,000. RM200,000 − RM160,000 − RM15,000 = RM25,000.

Interpretation: RM25,000 remains after normal operations, planned long-term investments and dividends — available for debt repayment, new investment opportunities, emergencies, or expansion.

Negative free cash flow is not automatically bad. A growing company may be investing heavily. A company with persistently negative free cash flow and no convincing reason is a less charming proposition.

Part L: Direct method

44. Direct-method operating structure

Shows actual cash receipts and payments:

Cash received from customers
+ Interest received
+ Dividends received

− Cash paid to suppliers
− Cash paid to employees
− Interest paid
− Income taxes paid

= Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities

Only the operating section differs from the indirect method. Investing and financing sections remain the same.

45. Cash collected from customers

Cash Collected = Sales Revenue + Beginning Accounts Receivable − Ending Accounts Receivable

Equivalent shortcut: Cash Collected = Sales Revenue − Increase in AR, or Sales Revenue + Decrease in AR.

ShopMart example

Sales Revenue RM286,000; Beginning AR RM73,000; Ending AR RM90,000. RM286,000 + RM73,000 − RM90,000 = RM269,000. Accounts Receivable increased by RM17,000, meaning RM17,000 of sales remained uncollected.

46. Interest and dividends received

Interest revenue RM12,000; Dividend revenue RM9,000. Because no related receivable accounts are shown, the chapter assumes both amounts were fully received in cash. Total cash receipts = RM269,000 + RM12,000 + RM9,000 = RM290,000.

47. Calculating inventory purchases

Purchases = COGS + Ending Inventory − Beginning Inventory

ShopMart: COGS RM156,000; Ending Inventory RM143,000; Beginning Inventory RM145,000. RM156,000 + RM143,000 − RM145,000 = RM154,000.

48. Calculating cash paid for inventory

Cash Paid for Inventory = Purchases + Beginning AP − Ending AP

ShopMart: Purchases RM154,000; Beginning AP RM50,000; Ending AP RM90,000. RM154,000 + RM50,000 − RM90,000 = RM114,000. Accounts Payable increased by RM40,000, so the company paid RM40,000 less cash than the purchases recorded.

49. Combined cash-paid-for-inventory formula

Cash Paid for Inventory = COGS + Ending Inventory − Beginning Inventory + Beginning AP − Ending AP
The two-step method is usually safer: (1) calculate purchases, (2) calculate cash paid. One enormous formula saves approximately three seconds and can cost rather more marks.

50. Cash paid for operating expenses

Cash Paid = Expense + Beginning Related Liability − Ending Related Liability

ShopMart: Other Operating Expense RM16,000; Beginning Accrued Liabilities RM10,000; Ending Accrued Liabilities RM5,000. RM16,000 + RM10,000 − RM5,000 = RM21,000. The liability decreased by RM5,000, meaning the company paid the current expense of RM16,000 plus RM5,000 owed from earlier.

51. Total cash paid to suppliers

Cash paid for inventory RM114,000 + cash paid for other supplier-related expenses RM21,000 = RM135,000.

52. Other operating payments

Employees RM56,000; Interest RM15,000; Income tax RM14,000. Total cash payments = RM135,000 + RM56,000 + RM15,000 + RM14,000 = RM220,000.

53. Direct-method operating cash flow

Total receipts RM290,000. Total payments RM220,000. RM290,000 − RM220,000 = RM70,000. This matches the indirect method. Both methods must produce the same operating cash flow.

54. Why depreciation does not appear under direct method

The direct method reports actual cash receipts and payments. Depreciation does not use cash, so it is excluded. A gain on disposal is also excluded because the gain is not an operating cash receipt — the full cash proceeds appear under investing activities. The indirect method adjusts these only because it begins with net income.

Part M: Full practice question

Nova Berhad: Net income RM75,000; Depreciation expense RM18,000; Gain on sale of equipment RM6,000. Balance-sheet changes: Accounts Receivable increase RM12,000; Inventory increase RM8,000; Prepaid Expenses decrease RM3,000; Accounts Payable increase RM10,000; Salaries Payable decrease RM2,000.

Additional: Equipment costing RM40,000 with accumulated depreciation of RM15,000 was sold; gain on sale RM6,000. Equipment purchased for cash RM70,000. Notes payable issued for cash RM50,000. Notes payable repaid RM12,000. Common shares issued for cash RM30,000. Dividends paid RM9,000. Beginning Cash RM25,000.

Required: (1) Operating cash flow using indirect method. (2) Investing cash flow. (3) Financing cash flow. (4) Ending Cash.

55. Operating section

Start with net income RM75,000. Add depreciation RM18,000; subtract gain RM6,000; subtract AR increase RM12,000; subtract inventory increase RM8,000; add prepaid decrease RM3,000; add AP increase RM10,000; subtract Salaries Payable decrease RM2,000.

RM75,000 + RM18,000 − RM6,000 − RM12,000 − RM8,000 + RM3,000 + RM10,000 − RM2,000 = RM78,000

56. Cash received from equipment sale

Book value = RM40,000 − RM15,000 = RM25,000. Add gain: RM25,000 + RM6,000 = RM31,000.

57. Investing section

Cash received from sale of equipment    RM31,000
Cash paid to purchase equipment    (70,000)

Net Cash Used for Investing Activities    (RM39,000)

58. Financing section

Notes payable issued    RM50,000
Notes payable repaid    (12,000)
Common shares issued    30,000
Dividends paid    (9,000)

Net Cash Provided by Financing    RM59,000

RM50,000 − RM12,000 + RM30,000 − RM9,000 = RM59,000

59. Net change and ending cash

Net Change = RM78,000 − RM39,000 + RM59,000 = RM98,000. Ending Cash = RM25,000 + RM98,000 = RM123,000.

Part N: Subjective-exam workflow

60. Recommended order

Step 1 — Compare balance sheets: calculate changes in every account (Ending balance − Beginning balance). Clearly label each change as increase or decrease.

Step 2 — Prepare operating section: start with net income and adjust non-cash expenses, gains/losses, current assets, current liabilities.

Step 3 — Analyze long-term assets: use T-accounts to find cash purchases, assets disposed, cash proceeds.

Step 4 — Analyze long-term debt and equity: find borrowings, repayments, share issues, treasury shares, dividends.

Step 5 — Calculate net change in Cash: O + I + F.

Step 6 — Check ending Cash: Beginning Cash + Net Change = Ending Cash.

Step 7 — Disclose non-cash activities: keep them separate from the cash totals.

61. Useful working table

AccountIncrease/DecreaseCash-flow treatment
Accounts ReceivableIncreaseSubtract operating
InventoryDecreaseAdd operating
Accounts PayableIncreaseAdd operating
Plant Assets—Analyze investing
Notes Payable—Analyze financing
Common Stock—Analyze financing

This prevents random signs from being scattered across the page like confetti.

Part O: Common subjective-exam mistakes

  • Treating depreciation as a cash inflow — depreciation is added back, but it does not create cash.
  • Using the change in Plant Assets as cash purchased — the account may also contain disposals or non-cash acquisitions; use a T-account and additional information.
  • Reporting only the gain as investing cash received — the investing section reports the full sale proceeds: Cash proceeds = Book value + Gain.
  • Reversing the current-asset signs — correct: increase → subtract, decrease → add.
  • Reversing the current-liability signs — correct: increase → add, decrease → subtract.
  • Putting equipment purchases under operating — equipment is a long-term asset; it belongs under investing.
  • Putting loan interest with loan principal — Principal → financing. Interest → operating.
  • Including non-cash transactions in the main sections — an asset acquired by issuing shares is disclosed separately; it does not enter the net change in Cash.
  • Assuming negative investing cash flow is bad — it may indicate expansion; the issue is whether the investment is productive and financially sustainable.
  • Forgetting to reconcile ending Cash — your final answer should satisfy: Beginning Cash + Operating + Investing + Financing = Ending Cash. If it does not, something is missing or incorrectly signed.

Final formulas to memorise

Indirect current-account rules

Current asset increase → Subtract
Current asset decrease → Add
Current liability increase → Add
Current liability decrease → Subtract

Asset cash proceeds

Cost − Accumulated Depreciation + Gain − Loss

Dividends

Beginning RE + Net Income − Ending RE

Cash collected from customers

Sales + Beginning AR − Ending AR

Purchases

COGS + Ending Inventory − Beginning Inventory

Cash paid for inventory

Purchases + Beginning AP − Ending AP

Free cash flow

Operating Cash Flow − Capital Expenditures − Cash Dividends

Final cash check

Beginning Cash + Operating + Investing + Financing = Ending Cash

For the exam, the most important part is the indirect operating section. Once the current-asset and current-liability signs become intuitive, the rest is mainly T-account reconstruction and classification.

Chapter 8

Full Intuitive Explanation

🧠

Open the complete intuitive explanation

The conceptual, reasoning-first companion to the Calc-Focused tab — all content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

The income statement answers: "Did the business earn a profit?" The statement of cash flows answers: "Where did the actual cash come from, and where did it go?" Those are not the same question.

A company can report high profit while running short of cash because: it made many sales on credit but has not collected from customers; it purchased expensive equipment; it repaid loans; it paid dividends; some reported expenses, such as depreciation, did not require cash.

This chapter explains the difference between accrual-based net income and the actual movement of cash.

1. Why net income is not equal to cash

Suppose a company sells RM10,000 of goods on account:

Accounts Receivable10,000
Sales Revenue10,000

Revenue and net income increase by RM10,000, but Cash increases by RM0. The company has earned revenue under accrual accounting, but the customer has not paid. Now suppose the company records RM2,000 depreciation:

Depreciation Expense2,000
Accumulated Depreciation2,000

Net income decreases by RM2,000, but no cash is paid when depreciation is recorded. Therefore:

Net income is not the same as net cash flow

The statement of cash flows explains the difference.

2. What the statement of cash flows reports

The statement reports the company's cash receipts, cash payments, net increase or decrease in cash, beginning cash balance, and ending cash balance. It covers a period of time, just like the income statement — e.g. "Statement of Cash Flows, For the Year Ended 31 December 2025." The final relationship is:

Beginning Cash + Net Change in Cash = Ending Cash

3. The three categories of cash flows

Every cash transaction is classified into one of three sections: (1) Operating activities, (2) Investing activities, (3) Financing activities.

A useful mental picture: Operating — running the business. Investing — buying and selling long-term resources. Financing — obtaining and returning money to lenders and owners.

4. Operating activities

Relate mainly to revenue and expenses from the company's normal business operations.

Common inflows: Cash collected from customers, Interest received, Dividends received on investments.

Common outflows: Payments to suppliers, Payments to employees, Payments for operating expenses, Interest paid, Income taxes paid. Under the treatment used in this chapter, interest and dividend income are operating activities.

Simple intuition

For a grocery shop: receiving cash from customers → operating inflow; paying for merchandise → operating outflow; paying employees → operating outflow; paying electricity → operating outflow. These transactions come from running the shop itself.

5. Investing activities

Involve long-term assets and long-term investments — property, equipment, buildings, land, long-term investments, long-term notes receivable.

Inflows: Selling equipment, Selling land, Selling investments, Collecting long-term loans made to others.

Outflows: Purchasing equipment, Purchasing buildings or land, Purchasing investments, Lending money to another party.

Memory rule: investing activities usually concern what the company invests in for the future. Buying equipment is an investing outflow even though the company is not "losing" the money in the ordinary sense — it exchanges cash for another asset.

6. Financing activities

Involve obtaining money from or returning money to lenders and shareholders.

Inflows: Borrowing money, Issuing notes payable, Issuing bonds, Issuing common shares, Reselling treasury shares.

Outflows: Repaying loan principal, Paying dividends, Buying treasury shares.

Important distinction

Interest paid on a loan is classified as operating in this chapter. Repayment of the loan principal is financing. For example, suppose RM10,000 is paid: RM8,000 principal → financing outflow; RM2,000 interest → operating outflow.

Apparently one payment was not complicated enough, so accounting splits it according to what each portion represents.

7. A balance-sheet shortcut

The diagram on page 11 connects the three cash-flow categories to balance-sheet accounts.

Account category affectedUsually linked to
Current assetsOperating
Current liabilitiesOperating
Long-term assetsInvesting
Long-term liabilitiesFinancing
EquityFinancing

This is a useful starting point, but not a mindless rule. For example: Cash itself is a current asset, but every cash-flow category naturally affects Cash. Dividends reduce retained earnings but are financing. Net income affects retained earnings, but the transactions creating net income are generally operating.

8. Classification examples

TransactionClassificationDirection
Cash collected from customersOperatingInflow
Cash paid to suppliersOperatingOutflow
Cash purchase of equipmentInvestingOutflow
Cash sale of equipmentInvestingInflow
Cash borrowed from bankFinancingInflow
Loan principal repaidFinancingOutflow
Common shares issued for cashFinancingInflow
Dividends paidFinancingOutflow
Treasury shares purchasedFinancingOutflow

9. Non-cash investing and financing activities

Some important transactions affect investing and financing accounts but do not involve cash — acquiring a building by issuing shares, acquiring land by issuing a note payable, converting debt into common shares.

Suppose a company acquires a RM300,000 building by issuing common shares:

Building300,000
Common Stock300,000

The company acquired a long-term asset and issued equity, but Cash was never involved. Therefore, it does not appear in the main investing or financing cash totals. Instead, it is disclosed separately as a non-cash investing and financing activity.

10. Two methods for operating activities

The statement of cash flows can present operating activities using the Indirect method or the Direct method. Only the operating section changes — investing and financing sections are the same under both methods.

Indirect method

Starts with Net Income, then adjusts it to obtain actual operating cash flow.

The logic: begin with accrual-based profit, then remove everything that did not represent operating cash.

Direct method

Directly reports cash received from customers, cash paid to suppliers, cash paid to employees, cash paid for interest, cash paid for taxes.

The logic: ignore accrual net income and show the actual operating cash receipts and payments.

Both methods must produce the same Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities.

11. Preparing a statement using the indirect method

The chapter identifies the following information as necessary: current-year income statement, current-year balance sheet, previous-year balance sheet, additional transaction information. The comparative balance sheets show how accounts changed. The income statement explains the current year's revenues, expenses, gains, losses and net income. Additional information helps separate cash transactions from non-cash changes.

12. The indirect-method structure

Cash Flows from Operating Activities:

Net Income
+ Non-cash expenses
− Gains
+ Losses
± Changes in current assets
± Changes in current liabilities

Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities

The adjustments do not change net income itself — they merely convert net income into operating cash flow.

13. Why depreciation is added back

Depreciation expense reduces net income (Dr Depreciation Expense / Cr Accumulated Depreciation), but Cash is not credited — depreciation is a non-cash expense. Suppose Net income = RM40,000, Depreciation expense = RM20,000. Net income has already been reduced by RM20,000 even though no cash was paid. To convert net income into cash flow: RM40,000 + RM20,000. Depreciation is added back.

Important clarification: adding depreciation back does not mean depreciation creates cash. It only means depreciation reduced net income without reducing current-period cash, so its effect must be removed.

14. Why gains are subtracted

Suppose equipment is sold and a RM10,000 gain is reported. The gain increases net income. However, the cash received from selling the equipment belongs in the investing section, not the operating section. If the gain remained inside operating cash flow, part of the equipment transaction would effectively appear in both sections.

Subtract gains from net income

The gain is removed from operating activities. The full cash proceeds from the sale are reported under investing activities.

15. Why losses are added

A loss on disposal reduces net income. However, the disposal is an investing activity — the loss itself is not an operating cash payment.

Add losses back to net income

Memory rule: Gain increased net income → subtract it. Loss decreased net income → add it back.

16. Changes in current assets

Current assets other than Cash generally move in the opposite direction from operating cash flow.

Increase in current asset → Subtract
Decrease in current asset → Add
This often confuses students because an increase in an asset normally sounds positive. But the cash-flow statement is not asking whether the asset is good. It asks what happened to cash.

17. Why an increase in Accounts Receivable is subtracted

Suppose sales revenue is RM100,000, but Accounts Receivable increases by RM20,000. That means RM20,000 of the revenue has not yet been collected. Cash collected is approximately RM100,000 − RM20,000 = RM80,000. Net income includes the full RM100,000 revenue.

Subtract the increase in Accounts Receivable
The company earned the revenue, but some customers are still treating payment as an optional future hobby.

18. Why a decrease in Accounts Receivable is added

Suppose Accounts Receivable decreases by RM8,000. This generally means the business collected cash from customers for sales recorded in an earlier period. The cash collection exceeds the current period's credit sales effect.

Add the decrease in Accounts Receivable

19. Why an increase in inventory is subtracted

Suppose inventory increases by RM15,000. The company has bought more inventory than it sold during the period. That additional inventory normally required cash or created supplier obligations.

Increase in Inventory → Subtract

The additional inventory is an asset, but obtaining it used cash resources.

20. Why a decrease in inventory is added

Suppose inventory decreases by RM2,000. The company sold more inventory than it purchased during the period. Some of the COGS came from inventory already purchased in an earlier period. Therefore, current-period cash paid for inventory was lower than COGS.

Decrease in Inventory → Add

21. Other current assets

The same logic applies to prepaid expenses, supplies, short-term receivables. Increase in prepaid expense: the company paid cash before recognizing the expense → Subtract. Decrease in prepaid expense: the company recognized expense using amounts paid earlier → Add.

22. Changes in current liabilities

Current liabilities usually move in the same direction as operating cash flow.

Increase in current liability → Add
Decrease in current liability → Subtract

23. Why an increase in Accounts Payable is added

Suppose Accounts Payable increases by RM40,000. The company has recorded purchases or expenses but has not yet paid RM40,000 of them. Those costs may reduce net income or increase inventory, but cash has not yet left.

Add the increase in Accounts Payable

The company temporarily preserved cash by owing more to suppliers.

24. Why a decrease in Accounts Payable is subtracted

Suppose Accounts Payable decreases by RM12,000. The company paid suppliers more than the amount of new obligations created during the period. Some cash was used to settle debts from previous periods.

Subtract the decrease in Accounts Payable

25. Accrued liabilities

Suppose salary expense is RM30,000 and Salaries Payable increases by RM5,000. The company recognized RM30,000 of expense but paid only RM25,000. Therefore, the RM5,000 increase is added under the indirect method. Conversely, if Salaries Payable decreases, the company paid more cash than the current-period salary expense, so the decrease is subtracted.

26. The indirect-method sign table

ItemAdjustment to net income
Depreciation, depletion and amortizationAdd
Gain on sale of long-term assetSubtract
Loss on sale of long-term assetAdd
Increase in current assetSubtract
Decrease in current assetAdd
Increase in current liabilityAdd
Decrease in current liabilitySubtract

A compact memory rule: Current assets: opposite. Current liabilities: same. Asset increase → subtract. Asset decrease → add. Liability increase → add. Liability decrease → subtract.

27. ShopMart operating activities example

Net income RM40,000; Depreciation expense RM20,000; Gain on disposal RM10,000; Increase in Accounts Receivable RM17,000; Decrease in Merchandise Inventory RM2,000; Increase in Accounts Payable RM40,000; Decrease in Accrued Liabilities RM5,000.

RM40,000 + RM20,000 − RM10,000 − RM17,000 + RM2,000 + RM40,000 − RM5,000 = RM70,000

Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities = RM70,000

The operating reconciliation on pages 28–30 shows these adjustments moving from RM40,000 accrual net income to RM70,000 operating cash flow.

28. Why operating cash can exceed net income

In the example: Operating cash = RM70,000; Net income = RM40,000. Operating cash is higher mainly because depreciation reduced income without using cash, Accounts Payable increased significantly (some obligations remained unpaid), and inventory decreased (some goods sold had been purchased previously). However, Accounts Receivable increased, which reduced current cash collections. This shows why net income alone does not reveal the company's cash position.

29. Investing activities using long-term asset accounts

The investing section normally requires analyzing Plant Assets, Accumulated Depreciation, Investments, Notes Receivable, and additional disposal information. A simple comparison of beginning and ending Plant Assets is often insufficient because new assets may have been purchased, old assets may have been sold, and some assets may have been acquired without cash. The T-accounts help reconstruct the actual transactions.

30. Finding purchases of plant assets

The ShopMart Plant Assets account: Beginning balance RM252,000; Acquisitions RM310,000; Disposals at cost RM55,000; Ending balance RM507,000. Check: RM252,000 + RM310,000 − RM55,000 = RM507,000.

Investing cash outflow = RM310,000

31. Finding cash received from selling an asset

The asset sold had: Original cost RM55,000; Accumulated depreciation RM15,000; Gain on sale RM10,000. Book value = RM55,000 − RM15,000 = RM40,000. A gain of RM10,000 means the asset was sold for RM10,000 more than book value: RM40,000 + RM10,000 = RM50,000.

Cash received = RM50,000

The disposal entry is:

Cash50,000
Accumulated Depreciation15,000
Plant Assets55,000
Gain on Disposal10,000

32. Asset-disposal cash formula

Cash Received = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation + Gain − Loss

Why? Cost − Accumulated Depreciation = Book Value. Then: Gain → selling price is above book value. Loss → selling price is below book value.

33. ShopMart investing section

Cash paid for assets = (RM310,000). Cash received from sale = RM50,000. Net investing cash flow = RM50,000 − RM310,000 = (RM260,000). The negative amount means ShopMart used RM260,000 more for long-term investments than it received from disposals.
