The Calc-Focused tab already covers the ShopMart financing section, direct-method formulas, and the Nova Berhad practice question in complete detail, so the calculation content isn't lost — only some of this tab's conceptual narration past section 33 is missing. Send the rest of the intuitive notes if you'd like it appended.
Chapter 8.5

Conceptual Framework

⚖️ Accounting Equation Effects

Assets ∆ = 150,000

Liab ∆ = 80,000

Equity ∆ = 70,000

🏛️ Fin. Capital Maintenance

Calculated Profit 70,000

🔁 Asset Exchange — Why Not Every Cash Outflow Is an Expense

A machine purchased for RM600,000 cash is not an expense — it's one asset (Cash) exchanged for another (Machine):

Machine ↑
RM600,000
Cash ↓
RM600,000
Net change in assets
RM0
Common bad answer: "The RM600,000 is an expense because cash decreased." Cash decreasing does not automatically mean an expense — otherwise buying land would apparently destroy profit immediately, which would be a rather creative form of accounting. There is no expense here because the company hasn't consumed a resource or reduced equity; it has simply swapped one asset for another of equal value.

Qualitative Characteristics (CVTU)

Fundamental

Relevance: Influences decisions (Predictive/Confirmatory value. Materiality).

Faithful Rep: Complete, Neutral, Free from error.

Enhancing

  • Comparability
  • Verifiability
  • Timeliness
  • Understandability

💰 Financial vs. Physical Capital Maintenance

Financial Capital

Capital = net assets/equity. Profit is earned only when ending net assets exceed beginning net assets, excluding owner contributions/distributions. This is the commonly used approach — the calculator above uses it.

Physical Capital

Capital = productive capacity (e.g. ability to produce 1,000 loaves/day). Profit is recognised only after the company has maintained that operating capacity — wealth above that level is profit. More theoretical, less common.

Chapter 8.5

Objective & Users

🏛️ Framework vs. Standard

The Conceptual Framework is the reasoning behind IFRS Standards — closer to a constitution or design blueprint than a law itself. It is not an IFRS Standard, so when a specific Standard applies, the Standard wins. The Framework cannot overrule it.

Helps the IASB develop consistent IFRS Standards.
Helps preparers develop policies when no Standard applies or a choice exists.
Helps users understand and interpret IFRS requirements.
Exam trap: the Framework "sets accounting rules" is a weak answer — it supports rule creation/interpretation but never overrides a Standard.

🎯 The Central Objective

Financial reports provide useful information to existing/potential investors, lenders, and other creditors, so they can decide whether to provide resources (buy/sell/hold shares, give/recover loans, extend credit, vote on management decisions).

Q1: Will the company generate cash?

Amount of future cash inflows, timing, and uncertainty. E.g. can a lender expect repayment of loan + interest?

Q2: Was management a good steward?

Stewardship: did management protect assets, use resources efficiently, control costs, and follow laws/contracts?

⚠️ Limitations of Financial Reports

Reports cannot provide every piece of information every user wants; they're based partly on estimates and judgement; and they do not directly show the market value of the whole business.

Reported Equity ≠ Market Value

E.g. a company reports RM5m equity but investors value it at RM20m due to reputation, growth prospects, or unrecognised knowledge. Reports help users estimate value — they don't state it directly.

📸 Financial Position

"The photograph" — the company's position at one date.

Assets − Liabilities = Equity

E.g. "Statement of financial position as at 31 Dec 2026." Answers: what resources, what obligations, what's left for owners?

🎬 Financial Performance

"The video" — what changed during a period.

Income − Expenses = Profit or Loss

E.g. "Statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 Dec 2026." Accrual accounting records the economic effect when it occurs, not merely when cash moves.

👥 Primary Users

UserMain focus
InvestorsProfitability, growth, dividends, risk, investment value
Lenders & creditorsLiquidity, solvency, cash-flow generation, ability to repay
ManagementNOT a primary user — has access to detailed internal information
Others (regulators, employees, public)May find reports useful, but not the primary design target
Classic trap: "financial statements are mainly prepared for management" is wrong. General purpose reports are mainly for investors, lenders and other creditors.
Chapter 8.5

Qualitative Characteristics

Two Tests Information Must Pass

Relevance + Faithful Representation = Fundamental Characteristics

Enhanced by: Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, Understandability ("CVTU")

1️⃣ Relevance

Information is relevant when it's capable of influencing a user's decision.

Predictive value: helps form expectations about the future (e.g. current revenue → estimate next year's).
Confirmatory value: confirms or revises previous expectations (e.g. RM1.3m actual vs. RM2m predicted revenue).
Materiality is entity-specific relevance — omitting/misstating it could reasonably influence decisions. No universal % exists; RM10,000 may be immaterial for a multinational, hugely material for a small business. Nature can matter even when the amount is small (e.g. a small illegal payment by a director).

2️⃣ Faithful Representation

Information should represent the economic substance of what actually happened.

Complete: necessary descriptions, numbers, and explanations are included.
Neutral: not manipulated to look better or worse — unbiased, not emotionless.
Free from error: appropriate process, properly applied assumptions — not "the estimate must turn out exactly right."
Exam point: an estimate CAN still be faithfully represented. Warranty expense estimated at RM100,000, actual claims RM95,000–110,000 — still faithful if the method was reasonable, assumptions disclosed, and uncertainty explained.

🛡️ Prudence

Exercising caution under uncertainty — prevents overstating assets/income and understating liabilities/expenses. But prudence does not allow deliberate pessimism: a company cannot intentionally understate assets, overstate liabilities, or create secret reserves. That would no longer be neutral.

Both Fundamentals Must Exist

Relevant but not faithful

A highly optimistic asset value without reasonable evidence — might influence investors, but doesn't faithfully represent reality.

Faithful but irrelevant

A perfectly accurate record of stationery purchased ten years ago — accurate, but useless for current decisions.

Making irrelevant information comparable does not suddenly make it useful — it merely produces consistently irrelevant information.

Enhancing Characteristics — "CVTU"

Comparability

Identify similarities/differences between companies or across years. Comparability is the goal; consistency (same method over time) is one way to achieve it — but consistency shouldn't excuse keeping a bad policy forever. Comparability ≠ uniformity: like items should look alike, different items should look different.

Verifiability

Knowledgeable, independent observers could reach a similar conclusion (not necessarily full agreement). Direct: observe directly (count cash). Indirect: check inputs and recalculate (check quantities/costs/method, recalculate total).

Timeliness

Available early enough to affect decisions — accurate but 5-years-late is useless for today's decision. Older info may still help identify trends or evaluate past predictions.

Understandability

Clearly classified, concisely presented, properly explained — but complex matters should NOT be omitted just because "users may not understand." Reports assume users have reasonable business knowledge and analyse diligently.

💵 The Cost Constraint

Providing information isn't free (collecting, processing, checking, auditing, publishing, and users analysing it all cost money). The benefits should justify the costs.

E.g. a small company technically could get a detailed independent valuation every month, but if it costs RM100,000/month for little benefit, requiring it would be absurd. However, "too costly" should never become a convenient excuse to hide important information.

Chapter 8.5

The Five Elements

Financial PositionFinancial Performance
AssetsIncome
LiabilitiesExpenses
Equity—

🏗️ Asset

"A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events." An economic resource is a right with the potential to produce economic benefits.

Three-part test:

  1. Is there a present economic resource/right?
  2. Does the company control it?
  3. Did it arise from a past event?

Benefits can include: generating cash, being sold, helping produce goods, reducing future payments, settling a liability.

Refinement: the asset is technically the right (to use, rent, sell), not the physical object — ownership isn't always necessary (e.g. leased equipment). Ask "who controls the economic benefits?" not "who owns the object?"

⛓️ Liability

"A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events."

Three-part test:

  1. Present obligation?
  2. Must potentially transfer an economic resource?
  3. Arose from a past event?

The company is already "trapped" — it cannot realistically avoid the transfer. A future intention (e.g. plan to buy a machine next year) is NOT a liability — no past event, no unavoidable obligation.

Constructive obligation: can arise without a strict legal contract, when established behaviour/policy/promise leaves no practical way to avoid acting (e.g. a retailer that always refunds dissatisfied customers, even without contractual duty).

⚖️ Equity

Assets − Liabilities = Equity
Assets
RM800,000
− Liabilities
(RM300,000)
= Equity
RM500,000

Equity is a residual — not normally measured directly. This is why accounting equity doesn't necessarily equal market capitalisation, selling price, or liquidation value.

📈 Income

Increases in assets, or decreases in liabilities, that increase equity — excluding owner contributions.

Services for RM10,000 on credit:
AR ↑ → Income ↑ → Equity ↑

Not income: owner contributes RM50,000 → Cash ↑, Equity ↑, but NOT income (came from the owner, not performance).

📉 Expenses

Decreases in assets, or increases in liabilities, that decrease equity — excluding distributions to owners.

Electricity RM2,000 used, unpaid:
Payable ↑ → Expense ↑ → Equity ↓

Not an expense: owner withdraws RM5,000 → Cash ↓, Equity ↓, but NOT an expense (distribution, not a cost of earning income).

🔗 How the Elements Connect

Don't memorise income/expense as separate objects — they arise from changes in assets and liabilities:

Income:
Asset ↑ or Liability ↓ → Equity ↑

E.g. Customer pays:
Cash ↑ → Revenue ↑ → Equity ↑
Expense:
Asset ↓ or Liability ↑ → Equity ↓

E.g. Equipment depreciated:
Net asset value ↓ → Expense ↑ → Equity ↓

This connection lets you reason through subjective questions instead of guessing.

Chapter 8.5

Recognition & Derecognition

🎓 Definition vs. Recognition — The University Analogy

Definition

"Does the item meet the definition of an asset, liability, equity, income or expense?" — like a student qualifying to apply.

Recognition

"Should it actually be included in the financial statements with a monetary amount?" — like the university deciding whether the student is admitted.

Qualification and admission are related, but not the same decision. An item may meet the definition but still not be recognised if recognition wouldn't provide useful information — recognition requires info that is relevant, faithfully represented, and worth the cost.

🔗 Recognition Connects the Statements

Goods sold for RM10,000, originally cost RM6,000:

Cash/Receivable+RM10,000
Revenue (income)+RM10,000
Inventory−RM6,000
Cost of sales (expense)+RM6,000
Profit / Equity+RM4,000

The income statement and statement of financial position are connected, not independent universes.

🎲 Three Kinds of Recognition Uncertainty

Existence Uncertainty

Does the asset/liability actually exist? E.g. company is being sued, unclear if it committed the alleged wrongdoing.

Outcome Uncertainty

It exists, but the final result is uncertain. E.g. legal obligation exists, unclear whether it'll be RM50,000 or RM200,000.

Measurement Uncertainty

It exists, but the amount must be estimated (impairment, warranty provision, useful life, value in use).

A high level of uncertainty does not automatically prevent recognition — the estimate may still be useful when properly explained. Only in limited, extreme cases does uncertainty prevent recognition entirely.

🗑️ Derecognition

Removing all or part of a recognised asset or liability.

Asset — derecognised when the company loses control (inventory sold, receivable collected, equipment disposed).

Liability — derecognised when the present obligation no longer exists (loan repaid, payable settled, obligation legally released).

A company should NOT derecognise an asset merely because it "moved it somewhere else" while still controlling the benefits — substance over an artificial legal arrangement.

📄 Executory Contracts

Neither party has performed, or both have performed equally. E.g. 20 Dec: sign agreement to buy inventory on 15 Jan. At 31 Dec: supplier hasn't delivered, company hasn't paid.

Usually no inventory and no payable recognised yet — the company hasn't received the resource and hasn't yet incurred a separate present obligation. If the contract becomes onerous, a liability may arise under the applicable Standard.

Chapter 8.5

Measurement Bases

Once an item is recognised: at what amount should it be recorded? The Framework does not mandate one measurement basis for everything — no single basis gives the best information in every situation.

💰 Historical Cost

Starts with the original transaction price (e.g. machine purchased for RM600,000), adjusted over time for depreciation, amortisation, impairment, payments/collections, interest.

Strengths

Actual transaction, understandable, verifiable, cheaper to determine.

Weaknesses

May become outdated; doesn't reflect current market; identical assets bought at different times look different.

E.g. Company A bought land 20 years ago for RM200,000; Company B bought identical land this year for RM2m — historical cost reports very different amounts for currently similar assets.

📊 Current Value Measurement

Fair Value

Price received to sell an asset (or paid to transfer a liability) in an orderly transaction between market participants — uses the market's assumptions, not management's. E.g. shares bought at RM100,000, now worth RM130,000 → fair value RM130,000.

Value in Use

Applies to an asset — present value of future benefits this specific company expects from using and eventually disposing of it. Two companies may assign different values to identical machinery.

Fulfilment Value

Applies to a liability — present value of resources the company expects to transfer to fulfil the obligation. Entity-specific settlement amount.

Current Cost

How much would it cost today to acquire an equivalent asset? Similar to replacement cost. E.g. machine cost RM600,000 originally, equivalent now costs RM750,000 → current cost RM750,000.

Comparing the Bases

BasisMain questionPerspective
Historical costWhat did it originally cost?Past transaction
Fair valueWhat would the market pay today?Market participants
Value in useWhat is it worth through our use?Entity-specific
Fulfilment valueWhat will we need to settle it?Entity-specific
Current costWhat would an equivalent item cost today?Current entry price

🧮 Worked Example — One Machine, Four Measurements

Original cost RM600,000, accumulated depreciation RM120,000, current market selling price RM550,000, replacement cost RM700,000, entity-specific value in use RM640,000:

BasisWorkingAmount
Historical carrying amountRM600,000 − RM120,000RM480,000
Fair valueCurrent market selling priceRM550,000
Current costReplacement cost todayRM700,000
Value in usePV of entity-specific future benefitsRM640,000

The question is not merely which number is largest — it's which measurement basis is relevant to the reporting purpose. An asset used alongside others in operations often favours historical/current cost; an asset that generates cash independently often favours a current value basis.

🎯 How Is the Basis Selected?

Consider: relevance, faithful representation, characteristics of the asset/liability, contribution to cash flows, comparability, verifiability, understandability, cost.

Assets used together (equipment, factories, inventory) → historical/current cost often more useful, since users compare Revenue − Cost = Margin.

Assets producing cash independently (e.g. marketable investments) → current value often more relevant.

🧮 Measurement of Equity

Equity is normally NOT measured directly — it's a residual:

Total Recognised Assets − Total Recognised Liabilities = Total Equity

Individual components (share capital, retained earnings, revaluation reserve) may be separately presented, but total equity stays a residual — changing asset/liability measurement also changes equity.

Measurement uncertainty (future cash flows, impairment, provisions, useful life, residual value) is normal — not a reason to avoid recognition. Instead: (1) use a reasonable estimation method, (2) disclose assumptions, (3) explain the uncertainty, (4) consider the possible range of outcomes. Pretending otherwise would leave half the financial statements blank.
Chapter 8.5

Presentation & Reporting

Good accounting isn't merely obtaining the correct number — the number must also be communicated properly. The Framework focuses on classification, aggregation, avoiding inappropriate offsetting, and entity-specific disclosure.

📂 Classification

Grouping items with shared characteristics — current vs. non-current assets, operating vs. finance expenses, ordinary vs. preference shares. Similar items grouped, dissimilar items separated. Dumping everything under "other expenses" is compact, but tells users almost nothing.

➕ Aggregation

Adding similar items together — thousands of customers become "Trade Receivables," not individually listed. But excessive aggregation can hide important information; the company must balance drowning users in detail vs. hiding everything inside vague totals.

🚫 Offsetting

Presenting an asset and liability as one net amount is generally inappropriate when they're separate items — it hides the real size of both.

Wrong (offset)

Net amount: RM20,000

Correct (shown separately)

Asset RM100,000
Liability RM80,000

🎯 Entity-Specific Disclosure

Disclosures should explain the company's actual situation — generic copied wording is "boilerplate" and says essentially nothing.

Weak (boilerplate)

"The company is exposed to various business risks."

Better (entity-specific)

"The company depends on one customer for 45% of annual revenue. Loss of this customer may significantly reduce operating cash flows."

📊 Profit or Loss vs. OCI

Profit or loss is the primary source of performance information — in principle, income and expenses go here.

Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) is used in exceptional cases when certain current-value changes provide more relevant/faithful performance info there instead.

The Conceptual Framework does NOT independently decide which items go into OCI — specific IFRS Standards make that call. Some OCI items may later be reclassified into profit or loss where the Standard requires it.

🏢 Reporting Entity & Going Concern

Reporting entity — required or chooses to prepare financial statements. May be one legal entity, part of an entity, or a group. Consolidated = parent + subsidiaries as one entity. Unconsolidated = parent alone.

Going concern — statements assume the entity will continue operating, doesn't intend/need to liquidate or cease trading. If closure is expected, normal measurements may no longer be appropriate (e.g. disposal values instead of continued-use values).

Capital & capital maintenance (Financial vs. Physical) is covered with an interactive calculator in the Concepts & Capital tab.

Chapter 8.5

Exam Case Studies

The Six-Step Structure for Application Questions

1. Identify the element
Asset? Liability? Equity? Income? Expense?
2. Apply the exact definition
Present resource/obligation from a past event?
3. Separate definition from recognition
Relevant? Faithfully represented? Measurable? Worth the cost?
4. Select/discuss measurement
Historical cost, fair value, value in use, fulfilment value, current cost?
5. Discuss uncertainty
Existence, outcome, or measurement uncertainty?
6. Conclude clearly
Never end on "it depends" — state the most likely treatment.

🎓 Worked Case: Five Events to Classify

Click an event to see the full six-step-style analysis and conclusion.

Event 1: Machine purchased RM600,000

Analysis

There is a present economic resource; the company controls its use; it arose from a past purchase; it can contribute to future economic benefits.

Conclusion

Recognise an ASSET, normally initially measured at historical cost of RM600,000.

Machine600,000
Cash600,000

🚨 Common Trap: Asset Exchange ≠ Expense

Revisit Event 1 above (machine purchased RM600,000 cash). A frequent wrong answer treats the cash outflow itself as an expense. It isn't: Machine ↑RM600,000 and Cash ↓RM600,000 leave total assets unchanged (net effect RM0) and equity untouched — one asset was simply exchanged for another of equal value. An expense only arises later, as the machine is used up through depreciation. See the Concepts & Capital tab for the full asset-exchange breakdown.

📝 Likely Subjective Questions

1. Explain the purpose and status of the Conceptual Framework.

Defines objectives/concepts of general purpose reporting; helps the IASB develop consistent Standards; helps preparers when no Standard applies or choices exist; helps users understand IFRS; is NOT an IFRS Standard; does not override a specific Standard.

2. Distinguish relevance from faithful representation.

Relevance concerns whether information can influence decisions through predictive/confirmatory value (materiality is entity-specific relevance). Faithful representation concerns whether information depicts economic substance completely, neutrally and free from error. Both are necessary — relevant-but-misleading and accurate-but-irrelevant are both not useful.

3. Explain the difference between fundamental and enhancing qualitative characteristics.

Relevance and faithful representation are fundamental — information must possess both to be useful. Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability enhance information that's already relevant and faithfully represented. Enhancing characteristics cannot rescue irrelevant or misleading information.

4. Explain recognition and derecognition.

Recognition is including an item that meets the definition of an asset/liability/equity/income/expense in the financial statements, using words and a monetary amount — appropriate when it provides relevant, faithfully represented information, subject to the cost constraint. Derecognition is removing all/part of a recognised asset or liability, normally when control of an asset is lost or a present obligation no longer exists.

5. Compare historical cost and fair value.

Historical cost is based on the original transaction price, adjusted for depreciation/impairment etc. — normally understandable and verifiable, but may become outdated. Fair value reflects the current price market participants would receive to sell an asset or pay to transfer a liability — may be more current, but more uncertain and costly when no active market exists.

6. Why may several measurement bases be used in financial reporting?

No single measurement basis provides the most useful information for every asset and liability. The appropriate basis depends on relevance, faithful representation, the item's characteristics, its contribution to future cash flows, enhancing characteristics, and cost. Historical cost may suit assets used together in operations; current value may be more relevant for independently traded financial assets.

Chapter 8.5

Full Intuitive Explanation

📚

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

The easiest way to understand this chapter is to stop treating it as a collection of definitions. The whole chapter follows one logical question:

How should accountants decide what information belongs in financial statements, how much it should be recorded at, and how it should be shown?

The Conceptual Framework provides the reasoning behind those decisions. It is the foundation used to develop IFRS Standards, but it is not itself an IFRS Standard. Therefore, when a specific IFRS Standard applies, the Standard wins. The Framework cannot overrule it.

1. The whole chapter as one flow

Think of financial reporting as a factory:

Economic event
↓
Does it affect financial-statement users?
↓
Does it meet the definition of an element?
↓
Should it be recognised?
↓
How should it be measured?
↓
Where and how should it be presented?

The chapter moves through: (1) Objective — why reports are prepared; (2) Users — who needs the information; (3) Qualitative characteristics — what makes information useful; (4) Elements — what kinds of items can appear; (5) Recognition — whether the item enters the statements; (6) Measurement — what monetary amount to use; (7) Presentation and disclosure — how to communicate it; (8) Capital maintenance — how profit can be understood.

That flow is more useful for a subjective examination than memorising the slides in isolation.

2. What is the Conceptual Framework?

Intuitive meaning

Imagine that IFRS Standards are individual laws. The Conceptual Framework is closer to a constitution or design blueprint explaining the principles behind those laws. A specific IFRS Standard might tell a company exactly how to account for inventory; the Conceptual Framework explains why the information should be relevant, faithfully represented and measured appropriately.

Its three main roles

The Framework helps: the IASB develop consistent IFRS Standards; preparers develop accounting policies when no specific Standard applies or when a Standard allows a choice; users understand and interpret IFRS requirements.

Framework = guidance and concepts.
IFRS Standard = actual accounting requirement.
A common weak examination answer says that the Framework "sets accounting rules." That is not quite correct. It supports the creation and interpretation of rules, but it does not automatically override a Standard.

Good subjective-answer sentence

The Conceptual Framework provides the underlying concepts used in general purpose financial reporting. It assists the IASB in developing consistent Standards, assists preparers when no specific Standard applies and helps users interpret IFRS requirements. However, it is not an IFRS Standard and cannot override a specific Standard.

3. Objective of general purpose financial reporting

The central objective

Financial reports are prepared to provide useful information to existing and potential investors, lenders, and other creditors. These people make decisions about whether to provide resources, such as buying/selling/holding shares, giving or recovering loans, extending credit, or voting on management decisions.

What do these users really want to know?

Question 1 — Will the company generate cash? They assess the amount of future cash inflows, when those inflows may occur, and how uncertain those inflows are. E.g. a lender wants to know whether the company can repay the loan and interest.

Question 2 — Has management used the company's resources properly? This is called stewardship. Users assess whether management protected the company's assets, used resources efficiently, controlled costs, and followed laws and contractual requirements.

So financial reporting is not merely "How much profit did the company earn?" It also asks: what resources does the company have, what does it owe, and did management use those resources responsibly?

4. Limitations of financial reports

Financial reports are useful, but they are not crystal balls. They cannot provide every piece of information every user wants; they are based partly on estimates, assumptions and judgement; they do not directly show the market value of the whole business; they must be read together with external information.

E.g. a company may report equity of RM5 million, but investors may value the company at RM20 million because of reputation, future growth, or valuable knowledge that is not separately recognised.

Accounting equity is not automatically the company's market value.

The Framework specifically states that general purpose reports help users estimate an entity's value; they are not designed to state that value directly.

5. Financial position versus financial performance

Financial position: the photograph

Assets − Liabilities = Equity

Shows the company's position at a particular date — e.g. "Statement of financial position as at 31 December 2026." Answers: what resources does the company control? What obligations does it have? What is left for the owners?

Financial performance: the video

Income − Expenses = Profit or loss

E.g. "Statement of profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 2026." Explains how the company performed over time.

Why accrual accounting is used

Accrual accounting records the economic effect when it occurs, not merely when cash moves. Example: a company performs services in December but receives cash in January. Under accrual accounting, revenue belongs to December, accounts receivable is recognised in December, and January merely records collection of the receivable. Accrual accounting provides a better picture of performance than showing only cash received and paid.

6. Primary users

Investors usually focus on: profitability, growth, dividends, risk, value of their investment.

Lenders and creditors usually focus more on: liquidity, solvency, cash-flow generation, ability to repay principal and interest.

Management uses financial information too, but is not considered a primary user of general purpose reports because management can access detailed internal information.

Other users — regulators, employees, customers and the public may also find the reports useful, but the reports are not primarily designed around all their individual needs.

Examination point: do not answer "Financial statements are mainly prepared for management." That is a classic trap. Management has access to internal reports. General purpose financial reports are mainly directed at investors, lenders and other creditors.

7. The five elements of financial statements

Financial positionFinancial performance
AssetsIncome
LiabilitiesExpenses
Equity—

The Framework's definitions are more precise than the casual definitions people normally use.

7.1 Asset

Formal idea: "A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events." An economic resource is a right that has the potential to produce economic benefits.

The three-part test: (1) Is there a present economic resource or right? (2) Does the company control it? (3) Did it arise from a past event?

Intuitive meaning: an asset is not simply "something valuable" — it is something the company presently controls that may provide benefits: generating cash, being sold, helping produce goods, reducing future cash payments, settling a liability.

Example — machine: a machine is an asset because the company has a present right to use it, controls its use, obtained it through a past purchase, and it can help produce goods and cash inflows.

Important refinement — the asset is technically the right: accounting often says "the building is an asset." Strictly, the economic resource is the company's rights over the building (to use, rent, sell it). This sounds unnecessarily philosophical, because apparently accounting needed metaphysics, but it matters in leasing and contractual arrangements.

Ownership is not always necessary: a company may control an asset without legally owning it — e.g. the right to use leased equipment. The better question is not "who owns the object?" but "who controls the economic benefits from the right?"

7.2 Liability

Formal idea: "A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events."

The three-part test: (1) Does the company have a present obligation? (2) Must it potentially transfer an economic resource? (3) Did the obligation arise from a past event?

Intuitive meaning: a liability means the company is already trapped by something that has happened — it cannot realistically avoid the transfer. Examples: obligations to pay cash, deliver goods, provide services, compensate another party.

Future intention is not enough: suppose management plans to purchase a machine next year — that plan is not yet a liability because no past event has created an unavoidable obligation, and the company may still change its decision. Merely expecting to spend money does not create a liability.

Constructive obligation: may arise even without a strict legal contract when a company's established behaviour, public policy or specific promise leaves it with no practical ability to avoid acting. E.g. a retailer that has consistently promised refunds even when the written contract does not require it — customers may reasonably expect refunds, creating a constructive obligation.

7.3 Equity

Equity = Assets − Liabilities

The residual interest after liabilities are deducted from assets. Example: Assets RM800,000 − Liabilities RM300,000 = Equity RM500,000. Equity is not normally measured directly — it is what remains after recognised assets and liabilities have been measured. This explains why accounting equity does not necessarily equal market capitalisation, selling price of the business, or liquidation value.

7.4 Income

Increases in assets, or decreases in liabilities, that increase equity, excluding contributions from owners. Example: the company provides services for RM10,000 on credit — Accounts receivable increases (Asset ↑), Revenue recognised (Income ↑), Equity ↑.

Owner contribution is not income: if an owner contributes RM50,000 — Cash ↑, Equity ↑ — but this is not income because the increase came from the owner, not from financial performance.

7.5 Expenses

Decreases in assets, or increases in liabilities, that decrease equity, excluding distributions to owners. Example: electricity of RM2,000 is used but unpaid — Electricity expense increases, Electricity payable increases, Equity decreases.

Owner drawings are not expenses: when an owner withdraws RM5,000 — Cash decreases, Equity decreases — but the withdrawal is not an expense because it is a distribution to the owner, not a cost of generating income.

8. The relationship among the elements

Do not memorise income and expense as completely separate objects — they arise from changes in assets and liabilities:

Income: Asset ↑ or Liability ↓ → Equity ↑
Expense: Asset ↓ or Liability ↑ → Equity ↓

Example of income: Customer pays for a service → Cash ↑ → Revenue ↑ → Equity ↑

Example of expense: Equipment is depreciated → Accumulated depreciation ↑, Net asset value ↓, Depreciation expense ↑ → Equity ↓

This connection is extremely useful in subjective questions because it lets you reason instead of guessing.

9. Qualitative characteristics of useful information

Useful financial information must pass two main tests: (1) Relevance, (2) Faithful representation — these are the fundamental qualitative characteristics. The information becomes even more useful through comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability — the enhancing qualitative characteristics.

10. Fundamental characteristic 1: Relevance

Information is relevant when it is capable of influencing a user's decision.

Predictive value — helps users form expectations about the future. E.g. current-year revenue can help investors estimate next year's revenue.

Confirmatory value — helps users confirm or revise previous expectations. E.g. an investor predicted RM2 million revenue; actual revenue of RM1.3 million shows the earlier prediction was too optimistic. Information can have both values simultaneously.

Materiality

Materiality is an entity-specific aspect of relevance. Information is material when omitting, misstating or hiding it could reasonably influence users' decisions. E.g. an RM10,000 mistake may be immaterial for a huge multinational, highly material for a small business earning RM20,000 annually. There is no magical universal materiality percentage — it depends on amount, nature, context, and size of the reporting entity.

Nature can matter even when the amount is small: a relatively small illegal payment made by a director may still be material because of its nature and what it reveals about management.

11. Fundamental characteristic 2: Faithful representation

Information should represent the economic substance of what actually happened. A faithful representation aims to be: (1) Complete, (2) Neutral, (3) Free from error.

Complete — users receive the necessary descriptions, numbers and explanations. E.g. reporting a provision of RM500,000 without explaining the legal uncertainty or estimation method may be incomplete.

Neutral — information is not manipulated to make the company appear better or worse. Neutral does not mean emotionless or purposeless — it means unbiased.

Free from error — does not mean every estimate must later prove perfectly correct. It means the process is appropriate, assumptions are properly applied, no relevant information is deliberately omitted, and the amount is honestly described as an estimate.

Important examination point: an estimate can still be faithfully represented. Suppose warranty expense is estimated at RM100,000. The final claims may eventually be RM95,000 or RM110,000 — that does not automatically mean the original figure was wrong. It may still be faithful if a reasonable method was used, assumptions were disclosed, and the uncertainty was explained.

Prudence

Prudence means exercising caution under uncertainty. It prevents overstating assets and income, and understating liabilities and expenses. But prudence does NOT allow deliberate pessimism — a company cannot intentionally understate assets, overstate liabilities, or create secret reserves. That would no longer be neutral.

12. Fundamental characteristics must both exist

Information cannot be useful when it is relevant but misleading, or accurate but irrelevant.

Example 1 — Relevant but not faithful: a company reports a highly optimistic asset value without reasonable evidence. It might influence investors, but it does not faithfully represent reality.

Example 2 — Faithful but irrelevant: a company provides a perfectly accurate record of office stationery purchased ten years ago. Accurate, yes. Useful for current decisions, probably not.

The enhancing characteristics cannot rescue information that fails the fundamental characteristics. Making irrelevant information comparable does not suddenly make it useful. It merely produces consistently irrelevant information.

13. Enhancing qualitative characteristics

A useful memory aid: CVTU — Comparability, Verifiability, Timeliness, Understandability.

13.1 Comparability

Allows users to identify similarities and differences between different companies, and between different years of the same company.

Comparability versus consistency: comparability is the goal; consistency (using the same method from one period to another) is one method of achieving it. Consistency should not be used as an excuse to keep a bad accounting policy forever — if a more relevant and faithful method becomes available, a company may change its policy and explain the change.

Comparability is not uniformity: different transactions should not be made to look identical merely for neatness. Like items should look alike; different items should look different.

13.2 Verifiability

Knowledgeable and independent observers could reach a similar conclusion — it does not require complete agreement.

Direct verification: observe the amount directly — e.g. counting cash, inspecting inventory.

Indirect verification: check the inputs and recalculate the result — e.g. to verify ending inventory: check quantities, check unit costs, confirm the FIFO method, recalculate the total.

13.3 Timeliness

Information must be available early enough to affect decisions. A report that arrives five years late may be wonderfully accurate but rather useless for a decision today. However, older information may remain useful for identifying trends, comparing long-term performance, and evaluating previous predictions.

13.4 Understandability

Information should be clearly classified, concisely presented, and properly explained. But understandability does not mean complex matters should be omitted — removing a difficult liability because "users may not understand it" would make the report incomplete and potentially misleading. Financial statements are prepared for users who have reasonable business knowledge and analyse the information diligently.

14. Cost constraint

Providing financial information is not free. Costs include collecting information, processing it, checking it, auditing it, publishing it, and users analysing it. The benefits of information should justify the costs — this is called the cost constraint.

Example: a small company might technically be able to obtain a highly detailed independent valuation every month. But if it costs RM100,000 each month and provides little additional benefit, requiring it would be absurd. The Framework accepts that financial reporting involves practical trade-offs. However, "too costly" should not become a convenient excuse to hide important information. Naturally, companies would quite enjoy that interpretation.

15. Definition versus recognition

Definition: "Does the item meet the definition of an asset, liability, equity, income or expense?"

Recognition: "Should the item actually be included in the financial statements with a monetary amount?"

An item may meet the definition of an asset or liability but still not be recognised if recognition would not provide useful information. Recognition requires information that is relevant, faithfully represented, and worth the cost of providing.

Simple analogy: a student may qualify to apply for a university programme — that is like meeting the definition. The university still decides whether the student is actually admitted — that is like recognition. Qualification and admission are related, but they are not the same decision.

16. Recognition

Recognition means including an item in the statement of financial position or the statement of financial performance, using words and a monetary amount. The recognised amount becomes part of totals such as total assets, total liabilities, revenue, profit.

Recognition connects the statements

Suppose goods are sold for RM10,000 and originally cost RM6,000. The company recognises:

Cash/Receivable: RM10,000 increase
Revenue: RM10,000 income

Inventory: RM6,000 decrease
Cost of sales: RM6,000 expense

Profit increases by RM4,000
Equity increases by RM4,000

The income statement and statement of financial position are connected, not independent universes.

17. Recognition under uncertainty

There are three different uncertainties that students often mix together.

17.1 Existence uncertainty

Uncertainty about whether an asset or liability actually exists. E.g. a company is being sued, but it is unclear whether the company committed the alleged wrongdoing. Question: is there presently an obligation at all?

17.2 Outcome uncertainty

The asset or liability exists, but the final result is uncertain. E.g. the company has a legal obligation, but it is uncertain whether it will pay RM50,000 or RM200,000.

17.3 Measurement uncertainty

The item exists, but its monetary amount cannot be observed directly and must be estimated — e.g. estimating impairment, warranty provision, useful life, value in use.

A high level of uncertainty does not automatically prevent recognition. The estimate may still be useful when properly explained. Only in limited cases may uncertainty be so extreme that no available estimate provides useful information.

18. Derecognition

Derecognition means removing all or part of a recognised asset or liability from the statement of financial position.

Asset — normally derecognised when the company loses control. Examples: inventory is sold, a receivable is collected, equipment is disposed of.

Liability — normally derecognised when the present obligation no longer exists. Examples: loan is repaid, payable is settled, obligation is legally released.

Important point: a company should not derecognise an asset merely because it has moved it somewhere else while still controlling the benefits. Substance matters more than an artificial legal arrangement.

19. Executory contracts

An executory contract is a contract in which neither party has performed, or both have performed equally. Example: on 20 December, a company signs an agreement to buy inventory on 15 January. At 31 December, the supplier has not delivered inventory and the company has not paid — both sides still need to perform.

Usually, no inventory and no payable are recognised yet. Why? Because the company has not received the economic resource and normally has not yet incurred a separate present obligation to pay. However, if the contract becomes unfavourable or onerous, a liability may arise under the applicable Standard.

20. Measurement

Once an item is recognised, the next question is: at what amount should it be recorded? The Framework does not say one measurement basis must be used for everything. Different items may require different bases because no single basis gives the best information in every situation.

21. Historical cost

Starts with the original transaction price. Example: a machine is purchased for RM600,000 — initial historical cost RM600,000. Over time, the amount may be adjusted for depreciation, amortisation, impairment, payments or collections, interest.

Strengths: based on an actual transaction; usually understandable; often verifiable; normally cheaper to determine.

Weaknesses: may become outdated; may not reflect current market conditions; identical assets purchased at different times may appear at different amounts.

Example: two companies own identical land — Company A purchased it for RM200,000 twenty years ago; Company B purchased identical land for RM2 million this year. Historical cost reports very different amounts even though the assets are currently similar.

22. Current value measurement

Uses updated information at the measurement date. Includes: fair value, value in use, fulfilment value, current cost.

22.1 Fair value

The current price that would be received to sell an asset, or paid to transfer a liability, in an orderly transaction between market participants. Fair value uses the market's assumptions, not management's personal plans. Example: the company bought shares for RM100,000; current market value RM130,000 → fair value RM130,000. Strength: current and market-relevant. Weakness: when no active market exists, valuation may rely on subjective assumptions.

22.2 Value in use

Applies to an asset. It is the present value of the future economic benefits the specific company expects from using the asset and eventually disposing of it. Key phrase: entity-specific asset value. Two companies may assign different values in use to identical machinery because they use it differently.

22.3 Fulfilment value

Applies to a liability. It is the present value of the economic resources the company expects to transfer to fulfil the obligation. Key phrase: entity-specific liability settlement amount. It focuses on what this company expects it will need to settle the obligation itself.

22.4 Current cost

Asks: how much would it cost today to acquire an equivalent asset? Example: a machine originally cost RM600,000, but an equivalent machine now costs RM750,000 → current cost RM750,000. It is similar to replacement cost.

23. Comparing the measurement bases

BasisMain questionPerspective
Historical costWhat did it originally cost?Past transaction
Fair valueWhat would the market pay today?Market participants
Value in useWhat is the asset worth through our use?Entity-specific
Fulfilment valueWhat will we need to settle the liability?Entity-specific
Current costWhat would an equivalent item cost today?Current entry price

24. How is the measurement basis selected?

The company should consider: relevance, faithful representation, characteristics of the asset or liability, how it contributes to cash flows, comparability, verifiability, understandability, cost.

Assets used together (equipment, factories, inventory) — historical cost or current cost may be more useful, because users often want to compare Revenue − Cost = Margin.

Assets producing cash independently (can be sold independently, actively traded, change in value frequently, e.g. marketable investments) — current value may be more relevant.

Measurement trade-off: historical cost may be more verifiable but less current. Fair value may be more relevant to current conditions but less verifiable when based on estimates. The correct basis depends on the economic situation. Anyone claiming one measurement basis is always superior is trying to turn a judgement problem into a multiple-choice slogan.

25. Measurement uncertainty

Arises when an amount cannot be directly observed and must be estimated — future cash flows, impairment, legal provisions, useful life, residual value.

The correct response is not automatically "do not recognise it because it is uncertain." A better response: (1) use a reasonable estimation method, (2) disclose the assumptions, (3) explain the uncertainty, (4) consider the possible range of outcomes.

Uncertainty is normal in accounting. Pretending otherwise would leave half the financial statements blank.

26. Measurement of equity

Equity is normally not measured directly. Instead: Total recognised assets − Total recognised liabilities = Total equity. Individual components may be separately presented, such as share capital, retained earnings, revaluation reserve. But total equity remains a residual. Therefore, changing the measurement of assets or liabilities may also change equity.

27. Presentation and disclosure

Good accounting is not merely obtaining the correct number — the number must also be communicated properly. The Framework focuses on classification, aggregation, avoiding inappropriate offsetting, and entity-specific disclosure.

27.1 Classification

Grouping items with shared characteristics — e.g. current versus non-current assets, operating versus finance expenses, ordinary shares versus preference shares. Similar items should be grouped together, while dissimilar items should be separated. Putting everything under "other expenses" may be technically compact, but it tells users almost nothing.

27.2 Aggregation

Adding similar items together. E.g. a business may have thousands of individual customers — it does not list each customer, it aggregates them into "Trade receivables." But excessive aggregation can hide important information. The company must find a balance between drowning users in insignificant detail and hiding everything inside vague totals.

27.3 Offsetting

Presenting an asset and liability as one net amount. Example: Receivable from Supplier A RM100,000, Payable to Supplier A RM80,000, Net amount RM20,000. Offsetting is generally inappropriate when the asset and liability are separate items because it hides the real size of both. Users should normally see Asset RM100,000 and Liability RM80,000 rather than only RM20,000.

27.4 Entity-specific disclosure

Disclosures should explain the company's actual situation. Generic copied wording is called boilerplate.

Example of weak disclosure: "The company is exposed to various business risks." That says essentially nothing.

Better: "The company depends on one customer for 45% of annual revenue. Loss of this customer may significantly reduce operating cash flows." The second disclosure is entity-specific and decision-useful.

28. Profit or loss versus OCI

Profit or loss is the primary source of information about financial performance. In principle, income and expenses are included in profit or loss.

Other comprehensive income (OCI) — in exceptional situations, certain changes in current values may be presented in OCI when doing so provides more relevant or faithfully represented performance information. Think of OCI as a separate section for certain gains and losses that specific Standards do not place immediately in normal profit or loss.

The Conceptual Framework does not independently tell companies which exact items go into OCI. Specific IFRS Standards make that decision. Some OCI items may later be reclassified into profit or loss where the applicable Standard requires it.

29. Reporting entity and going concern

Reporting entity

An entity that is required, or chooses, to prepare financial statements. It may be one legal entity, part of an entity, or a group of entities. Consolidated financial statements show the parent and subsidiaries as one reporting entity. Unconsolidated financial statements show the parent alone.

Going concern

Financial statements are normally prepared on the assumption that the entity will continue operating for the foreseeable future, does not intend or need to liquidate, and does not intend or need to cease trading. If the company is expected to close, normal accounting measurements may no longer be appropriate — e.g. assets may need to be considered based on disposal values rather than continued business use.

30. Capital and capital maintenance

This section answers a surprisingly deep question: when can an increase be considered profit? The Framework discusses two concepts.

30.1 Financial capital maintenance

Treats capital as the company's net assets or equity. Profit is earned when ending net assets exceed beginning net assets, excluding owner contributions and distributions to owners.

Opening net assets RM500,000
Closing net assets RM620,000
Less owner contribution RM50,000
Adjusted increase (Profit) RM70,000

The RM50,000 contribution is not profit.

30.2 Physical capital maintenance

Focuses on productive capacity. Profit is recognised only after the company has maintained its ability to produce the same level of goods or services. Example: a bakery begins the year with equipment capable of producing 1,000 loaves per day. At year-end, machine prices have risen significantly. Under physical capital maintenance, the bakery must first maintain enough resources to preserve the 1,000-loaf capacity — only wealth above that level is considered profit.

Financial capitalPhysical capital
Focuses on money or net assetsFocuses on productive capacity
Profit after financial capital is maintainedProfit after operating capacity is maintained
Commonly usedMore theoretical and less common

31. How to answer subjective application questions

Use this six-step structure.

Step 1 — Identify the possible element: asset, liability, equity, income, or expense?

Step 2 — Apply the exact definition: for an asset — is there a present economic resource controlled as a result of a past event? For a liability — is there a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of a past event?

Step 3 — Separate definition from recognition: even if the item meets the definition, ask — would recognition provide relevant information? Can it be faithfully represented? Can it be measured reasonably? Do the benefits justify the cost?

Step 4 — Select or discuss measurement: historical cost, fair value, value in use, fulfilment value, current cost.

Step 5 — Discuss uncertainty: existence, outcome, or measurement.

Step 6 — Conclude clearly: do not finish with vague phrases such as "it depends on accounting standards." State what it depends on and give the most likely treatment.

32. Case from slide 20

The slide provides five events for classification.

Event 1: Machine purchased for RM600,000

Analysis: there is a present economic resource; the company controls its use; it arose from a past purchase; it can contribute to future economic benefits.

Conclusion: recognise an asset, normally initially measured at historical cost of RM600,000.

Machine600,000
Cash600,000

No immediate expense is recognised merely because cash was paid. The machine provides benefits across future periods.

Event 2: Lawsuit won, but compensation amount is uncertain

This question is less clean than the slide pretends. Analysis: because the lawsuit has been won, the company may now have a present right to compensation — an asset may exist. However, recognition depends on whether the right is sufficiently established, a useful monetary estimate can be made, and recognition would provide relevant and faithfully represented information.

Defensible conclusion

The lawsuit may create an asset and related income because the company has obtained a right to compensation. However, if the amount is subject to such extreme measurement uncertainty that no useful estimate can be made, the item may not be recognised and should instead be disclosed.

Do not simply say "not recognised because uncertain." Uncertainty by itself does not automatically prohibit recognition under the Framework.

Event 3: Contract signed to purchase inventory next month

Analysis: neither side has performed — inventory has not been delivered, payment has not been made. It is normally an executory contract.

Conclusion: usually not recognised at that point. Once the supplier delivers the inventory: Dr Inventory / Cr Cash or Accounts Payable. An exception may arise if the contract has become onerous or otherwise creates a separate asset or liability under a specific Standard.

Event 4: Customers owe RM150,000

Analysis: the company has a present right to receive cash; it controls that right; the right arose from past sales or services; it has the potential to produce economic benefits.

Conclusion: recognise an asset — accounts receivable, measured at RM150,000 subject to any required adjustment for expected non-collection.

Event 5: Expected legal loss of RM80,000

The wording does not provide enough information for an automatic answer. Analysis: ask — (1) did a past event create a present obligation? (2) does the company have no practical ability to avoid settlement? (3) can the amount be reasonably estimated?

Conclusion: if a present obligation exists and RM80,000 provides a useful estimate — recognise a liability and a related expense.

Legal expense80,000
Legal provision80,000

If it is genuinely uncertain whether any present obligation exists, recognition may not be appropriate, but the matter may require disclosure.

33. Likely subjective examination questions

Question 1: Explain the purpose and status of the Conceptual Framework.

Answer structure: (1) Defines objectives and concepts of general purpose financial reporting. (2) Helps IASB develop consistent Standards. (3) Helps preparers when no Standard applies or when choices exist. (4) Helps users understand IFRS. (5) Is not an IFRS Standard. (6) Does not override a specific Standard.

Question 2: Distinguish relevance from faithful representation.

Model answer

Relevance concerns whether information is capable of influencing users' decisions through predictive or confirmatory value. Materiality is an entity-specific aspect of relevance. Faithful representation concerns whether information depicts the economic substance completely, neutrally and free from error. Both characteristics are necessary because relevant but misleading information, and accurate but irrelevant information, are not useful.

Question 3: Explain the difference between fundamental and enhancing qualitative characteristics.

Model answer

Relevance and faithful representation are fundamental because information must possess both to be useful. Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability enhance information that is already relevant and faithfully represented. Enhancing characteristics cannot make irrelevant or misleading information useful.

Question 4: Explain recognition and derecognition.

Model answer

Recognition is the inclusion of an item that meets the definition of an asset, liability, equity, income or expense in the relevant financial statement using words and a monetary amount. Recognition is appropriate when it provides relevant information and a faithful representation, subject to the cost constraint. Derecognition is the removal of all or part of a recognised asset or liability, normally when control of an asset is lost or when a present obligation no longer exists.

Question 5: Compare historical cost and fair value.

Model answer

Historical cost is based on the original transaction price and is adjusted for matters such as depreciation and impairment. It is normally understandable and verifiable but may become outdated. Fair value reflects the current price that market participants would receive to sell an asset or pay to transfer a liability. It may provide more current information but may be more uncertain and costly when no active market exists.

Question 6: Why may several measurement bases be used in financial reporting?

Model answer

No single measurement basis provides the most useful information for every asset and liability. The appropriate basis depends on relevance, faithful representation, the characteristics of the item, its contribution to future cash flows, enhancing qualitative characteristics and cost. Historical cost may be appropriate for assets used together in operations, while current value may be more relevant for independently traded financial assets.

34. Final memory framework

For the examination, remember this sequence:

Why → Who → Quality → What → Record → Value → Show

Why? Provide useful financial information.

Who? Investors, lenders and other creditors.

Quality? Relevant and faithfully represented, enhanced by comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability.

What? Assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses.

Record? Recognise only when doing so provides useful information.

Value? Choose an appropriate measurement basis.

Show? Classify, aggregate and disclose clearly without inappropriate offsetting.

That is essentially the entire chapter compressed into one reasoning chain.

Chapter 9

Managers & Ethics

🏛️ Organisational Structure

Board of directors (elected by shareholders, sets strategic goals) → CEO (overall responsibility for implementing short/long-term plans) → senior officers & divisional managers.

Line Position

Directly involved in providing goods/services — production manager, sales manager, software dev manager.

Restaurant analogy: chefs, waiters, cashiers — they directly prepare or deliver the service.

Staff Position

Supports the line positions — accounting, payroll, HR, legal support.

Restaurant analogy: accountants, HR, IT support — don't serve the meal, but the restaurant would collapse without them.

🎯 The Three Managerial Functions

1. Planning

Choosing goals and deciding how to achieve them.

Strategic: long-term (entering a country, new factory). Operational: short-term day-to-day (units to produce, material orders).

2. Directing

Managing daily operations — assigning employees, approving purchases, scheduling production, coordinating departments. Planning decides what should happen; directing makes it happen.

3. Controlling

Monitoring performance — comparing actual vs. planned results and investigating differences. Not about punishing employees; it's identifying differences and correcting problems.

Budgeted material costRM100,000
Actual material costRM115,000
DifferenceRM15,000 unfavourable

⚖️ Four IMA Ethical Standards

Competence

Maintain professional knowledge/skills; follow relevant laws; provide accurate, clear, timely info; identify/manage risk. Don't advise on what you don't understand and hope confidence substitutes for competence.

Confidentiality

Keep information confidential; disclose only when authorised/legally required; prevent misuse; never use it for personal benefit (e.g. don't trade shares on inside knowledge of an upcoming acquisition).

Integrity

Avoid conflicts of interest; act ethically; avoid conduct that damages the profession; professional integrity above personal interest (e.g. refuse a bonus offered for hiding an unfavourable variance).

Credibility

Communicate fairly, objectively, completely, with limitations disclosed. If information is delayed/incomplete/unreliable, say so — don't present a weak assumption as highly certain.

🚨 Ethical Dilemma: The December Sale

Two customer orders will only be completed and shipped on 3 January, but the controller suggests recording them on 31 December to hit the year's profit target.

Why it's wrong: the goods were not completed, not shipped, and not properly earned as revenue in December. Recording them early manipulates income.

Appropriate response: first explore whether production can genuinely finish in December. If not — don't record the revenue in December, explain the ethical/accounting problem, and escalate if the controller refuses.

Management pressure does not change the economic event. Moving a number across a calendar date does not create revenue. It creates fiction with a spreadsheet.

Company Types & Cost Concepts

🏢 Three Types of Companies

TypeWhat it doesInventory accounts
ServiceSells time, knowledge, skills, expertise (law firm, salon, consultancy)Normally none
MerchandisingBuys finished products, stores, resells (supermarket, retailer)Merchandise Inventory (one account)
ManufacturingBuys raw materials, uses labour/equipment to convert into finished products, sellsRaw Materials, WIP, Finished Goods (three accounts)

The key difference: the manufacturer makes the product.

📦 The Three Manufacturing Inventories

Raw Materials

"Ingredients waiting outside the kitchen."

Wood, screws, fabric, varnish — waiting to be used.

Work-in-Process (WIP)

"Inside the factory, but not ready."

A table with legs but not painted; a cake baking but not decorated.

Finished Goods

"Ready, but not yet sold."

Completed tables in the warehouse, packaged tablets ready for sale.

Raw Materials → Work-in-Process → Finished Goods → Cost of Goods Sold

🎯 Cost Object

Anything for which management wants a separate measurement of cost — one product, one department, one customer, one project, one branch, one service. E.g. if a company wants to know the cost of producing Product A, Product A becomes the cost object.

↔️ Direct vs. Indirect Costs

Direct: easily & cost-effectively traced to a cost object (wood traced to a specific table). Indirect: cannot be easily/economically traced (factory electricity supporting many products).

"Can physically be traced" isn't the only test — it must also be economical to trace. A tiny amount of glue could technically be measured per unit, but tracking every drop costs more than the info is worth → treated as indirect.

❓ "Direct or Indirect to What?"

The same cost may be direct in one situation and indirect in another. E.g. the production manager's salary may be direct to the production department, but indirect to one individual product. Without identifying the cost object, the classification may be meaningless.

Income Statement Differences

TypeStructure
ServiceService Revenue − Operating Expenses = Operating Income (no COGS)
MerchandisingSales − COGS = Gross Profit − Op. Exp. = Operating Income
ManufacturingSame structure as merchandising — but COGS must first be calculated via COGM, not just purchased

🛂 The Factory Cost "Passport"

Each cost carries a passport through: Raw Materials → WIP → Finished Goods → COGS. The cost begins as an asset and stays an asset while the product is unused, unfinished, or finished-but-unsold.

Only when the product is sold does the cost become an expense.

Chapter 9

Business Trends & Value Chain

📊 Six Trends Affecting Managerial Accounting

Service Economy Shift

More businesses provide services — managerial accounting calculates cost per consultation, per hospital patient, per hotel guest, per transaction.

Global Competition

Managers need info on pricing, quality, delivery speed, efficiency, cost reduction. A company can't charge more for internal inefficiency.

Time-Based Competition

Faster production, delivery, shorter waits, quicker responses. Helps identify delays and non-value-adding activities.

ERP Systems

Integrates data from sales, inventory, purchasing, production, accounting, HR — shared through one system instead of disconnected departments.

E-Commerce

Selling globally — analysing online sales, delivery cost, customer acquisition cost, platform fees, returns, profitability by region.

Just-in-Time (JIT)

Obtain/produce inventory close to when needed — reduces storage costs, excess inventory, waste, obsolete products. But less protection if suppliers fail.

"No unnecessary inventory" sounds lovely until the only supplier stops shipping.

🔗 The Value Chain

Activities involved in creating, producing, selling, delivering, and supporting a product. Total Quality Management (TQM) — continuous improvement, cooperation, waste reduction, defect prevention — runs across every stage.

R&D → Design → Production → Marketing & Sales → Distribution → Customer Support

Managers analyse which activities add value, which waste resources, where quality can improve, where cost can be cut. E.g. if production is efficient but customer support is terrible, the whole value chain is still weak.

🌍 Triple Bottom Line

Profit

Economic performance

People

Employee treatment, labour practices, community, customer welfare

Planet

Pollution, waste, energy use, sustainable materials

Business performance is not evaluated solely through profit.

💇 Service Company Unit Cost

$3,900 ÷ 1,950 services = $2 per service

Used for pricing, budgeting, evaluating efficiency, comparing branches, estimating profit.

🛍️ Merchandising Unit Cost

$90,800 ÷ 260 items = $349.23 per item

Helps decide selling price, product profitability, whether supplier costs are rising, whether to keep selling the product.

📝 Likely Subjective Questions

1. Distinguish financial accounting from managerial accounting.

Identify users → explain purpose → compare past/future focus → compare rules → compare detail/frequency → mention behavioural effect. (See the comparison table on the Intro & Classes tab.)

2. Explain planning, directing and controlling.

Planning involves setting organisational goals and deciding how to achieve them — strategic (long-term direction) vs. operational (short-term activities). Directing involves managing daily operations. Controlling involves monitoring actual performance, comparing it with plans, and taking corrective action.

3. Distinguish direct and indirect costs.

A direct cost can be easily and cost-effectively traced to a particular cost object. An indirect cost cannot be traced conveniently or economically. Classification depends on the selected cost object — e.g. a factory supervisor's salary may be direct to the production department but indirect to an individual product.

4. Explain the three manufacturing costs.

Direct materials become part of the finished product and can be conveniently traced to it. Direct labour is employee cost traced directly to production. Manufacturing overhead includes all indirect manufacturing costs — indirect materials, indirect labour, factory rent, utilities, depreciation.

5. Distinguish product costs and period costs.

Product costs (direct materials + direct labour + manufacturing overhead) are initially recorded as inventory and become COGS when sold. Period costs (selling and administrative expenses) are expensed in the period incurred.

6. Explain Cost of Goods Manufactured.

COGM represents the manufacturing cost of goods completed during the period. Calculated by adding beginning WIP to manufacturing costs incurred during the period and subtracting ending WIP.

7. Explain the movement of manufacturing costs.

Costs begin in Raw Materials Inventory. When materials are used with direct labour and overhead, their cost enters WIP. When production completes, cost moves to Finished Goods as COGM. When products are sold, cost moves from Finished Goods to COGS.
