🚨 Six Mistakes to Avoid

  • Treating all labour as direct labour — factory supervisors/maintenance workers are normally indirect labour.
  • Treating every factory cost as overhead — direct materials and direct labour are factory costs, but NOT overhead.
  • Treating product cost as an immediate expense — unsold product costs remain inventory assets.
  • Treating office rent as manufacturing overhead — office rent is an administrative period cost.
  • Confusing COGM with COGS — COGM means completed; COGS means sold.
  • Subtracting beginning inventory — beginning inventory is normally ADDED (available this period); ending inventory is subtracted (unused/unfinished/unsold).
Chapter 9

Full Intuitive Explanation

📚

Open the complete intuitive explanation

All content from the notes is preserved here, but collapsed so quick revision stays quick.

▼

This chapter is easier once you realise that it is mainly about following costs through a business.

Financial accounting asks: "What happened to the company?"

Managerial accounting asks: "What should managers do next?"

The central flow of this chapter is:

Managers need information
↓
Costs are identified and classified
↓
Manufacturing costs enter inventory
↓
Inventory moves through production
↓
Finished products are sold
↓
Costs become Cost of Goods Sold
↓
Managers use the information to make decisions

The chapter covers managerial accounting, cost classification, manufacturing financial statements, ethical responsibilities and current business trends.

1. What is managerial accounting?

Managerial accounting provides financial and non-financial information to people inside the organisation — production managers, sales managers, department managers, senior management, employees involved in planning and control. It helps them plan, direct operations, control performance, make decisions.

Intuitive example

Suppose a company manufactures tablets. Financial accounting reports: "The company earned RM500,000 profit last year." Managerial accounting asks: Which tablet model was most profitable? How much does one tablet cost to manufacture? Is labour cost increasing? Should the company produce more units? Which department exceeded its budget? Can the selling price be reduced?

Financial accounting describes the business mainly for outsiders. Managerial accounting helps insiders run the business.

2. Financial accounting versus managerial accounting

This is one of the most likely subjective questions.

AreaFinancial accountingManagerial accounting
Main usersInvestors, creditors, authoritiesManagers and employees
Main purposeInvestment and credit decisionsPlanning, directing, controlling
Time focusMainly past performanceMainly future decisions
RulesMust follow accounting standardsNot required to follow GAAP
ScopeUsually whole companyProducts, departments or territories
FrequencyQuarterly or annuallyDaily, weekly or whenever needed
DetailSummarisedHighly detailed
BehaviourBehavioural effect is secondaryReports may influence employee behaviour
Intuitive difference: financial accounting is like a company's official report card. Managerial accounting is like the teacher's private notes — which student needs help, which topic is weak, what should be taught next, how to improve performance. The report card must follow a formal format. The teacher's notes can be designed however the teacher finds useful.

Good subjective answer

Financial accounting provides information mainly to external users such as investors and creditors. It focuses primarily on past performance, usually reports the company as a whole and must comply with applicable accounting standards. Managerial accounting provides detailed information to internal users. It is used for planning, directing and controlling operations, often focuses on future decisions and is not required to follow a fixed external reporting format.

3. Why managerial accounting is important

Managers cannot make good decisions using instinct alone. They need answers to questions such as: How much does the product cost? Which activity wastes resources? Is the department meeting its target? Should the company increase its price? Should a product be discontinued? Is the company producing too much inventory?

Managerial accounting turns business activity into information that supports these decisions. It is not simply "recording transactions." It connects:

Business data → Analysis → Management decision → Action

4. Managers in an organisation

Companies are normally divided into departments or divisions. An organisational chart shows who reports to whom, who has responsibility, how departments are connected. The slide's organisational chart places the board of directors at the top, followed by the CEO, and then senior officers and divisional managers.

Board of directors

Elected by shareholders. Its role includes developing the corporation's strategic goals.

Chief executive officer

Has overall responsibility for implementing the organisation's short-term and long-term plans.

Line positions versus staff positions

Line position — directly involved in providing goods or services to customers. E.g. production manager, sales manager, software development manager.

Staff position — supports the line positions. E.g. accounting, payroll, human resources, legal support.

Intuitive comparison: imagine a restaurant. Line employees include chefs, waiters, cashiers — they directly prepare or deliver the service. Staff employees include accountants, HR staff, IT support — they do not serve the meal, but the restaurant would probably collapse without them.

5. Managerial accounting functions

The chapter gives three major functions: (1) Planning, (2) Directing, (3) Controlling.

5.1 Planning

Choosing goals and deciding how to achieve them. Strategic planning focuses on long-term direction — entering another country, opening a new factory, developing a new product line, becoming the market leader within five years. Operational planning focuses on short-term, day-to-day actions — how many units to produce next month, how many employees are needed, how much material to order, monthly sales targets.

Strategic planning = Where are we going?
Operational planning = What are we doing next?

5.2 Directing

Managing daily operations — assigning employees, approving purchases, scheduling production, solving operational problems, coordinating departments. Planning decides what should happen. Directing makes it happen.

5.3 Controlling

Monitoring performance and keeping the organisation on track. Managers compare actual result versus planned result:

Budgeted material costRM100,000
Actual material costRM115,000
DifferenceRM15,000 unfavourable

Management then investigates why the cost was higher — material price increased, too much material was wasted, the supplier changed, or production was inefficient.

Controlling is not merely punishing employees. It is identifying differences and correcting problems.

6. Ethics in managerial accounting

Managerial accountants often handle confidential and decision-sensitive information. A dishonest number may cause managers to approve the wrong project, pay an unfair bonus, hide a loss, overproduce inventory, or mislead investors. The chapter presents four ethical standards from the Institute of Management Accountants: (1) Competence, (2) Confidentiality, (3) Integrity, (4) Credibility.

6.1 Competence

Maintain professional knowledge and skills; follow relevant laws and standards; provide accurate, clear, concise and timely information; identify and help manage risk.

Do not advise management on something you do not understand and then hope confidence will substitute for competence. It usually does not.

6.2 Confidentiality

Keep information confidential; disclose it only when authorised or legally required; prevent misuse of confidential information; avoid using confidential information for personal benefit. Example: an accountant learns that the company will purchase another company next month — the accountant must not use the information to trade shares.

6.3 Integrity

Avoid conflicts of interest; act ethically; avoid conduct that damages the profession; place professional integrity above personal interest. Example: a manager promises an accountant a bonus for hiding an unfavourable cost variance — accepting the request violates integrity.

6.4 Credibility

Communicating information fairly, objectively, completely, with relevant limitations disclosed. If information is delayed, incomplete or unreliable, the accountant should say so. A number should not be presented as highly certain when it is based on weak assumptions.

7. Ethical dilemma from the chapter

The company wants to report a profit this year. Two customer orders will only be completed and shipped on 3 January, but the controller suggests recording them on 31 December.

Why is this wrong?

The goods were not completed, not shipped, and not properly earned as revenue in December. Recording them early would manipulate income.

Appropriate response

The accountant could first explore whether production can genuinely be completed and the goods shipped in December. If that cannot happen: the revenue should not be recorded in December, the accountant should explain the ethical and accounting problem, and if the controller refuses, the matter should be reported to a higher level.

The lesson is: management pressure does not change the economic event. Moving a number across a calendar date does not create revenue. It creates fiction with a spreadsheet.

8. Three types of companies

Before classifying costs, identify what type of company is involved.

8.1 Service company

Sells time, knowledge, skills, expertise — law firm, accounting firm, salon, consultancy, repair company. Service companies generally do not carry goods inventory in the same way as merchandising or manufacturing companies.

8.2 Merchandising company

Buys finished products, stores them, resells them — supermarket, clothing retailer, electronics shop. The product is already finished when purchased.

8.3 Manufacturing company

Purchases raw materials, uses labour and equipment, converts materials into finished products, sells the completed products — furniture factory, automobile manufacturer, food manufacturer, electronics manufacturer.

The key difference is that the manufacturer makes the product.

9. The three manufacturing inventories

Manufacturing companies use three inventory accounts: (1) Raw Materials Inventory, (2) Work-in-Process Inventory, (3) Finished Goods Inventory.

9.1 Raw Materials Inventory

Materials waiting to be used in production — wood, screws, fabric, varnish for a furniture factory.

Think of raw materials as: "Ingredients waiting outside the kitchen."

9.2 Work-in-Process Inventory

Products that have entered production but are not complete — a table with legs attached but not painted; a tablet with internal parts installed but no screen; a cake being baked but not decorated.

Think of WIP as: "The product is inside the factory, but it is not ready."

9.3 Finished Goods Inventory

Completed products that have not yet been sold — fully completed tables in the warehouse, packaged tablets ready for sale, finished cakes waiting for customers.

Think of finished goods as: "Ready, but not yet sold."

Inventory flow

Raw Materials → Work-in-Process → Finished Goods → Cost of Goods Sold

This flow is the heart of the chapter.

10. Cost object

A cost object is anything for which management wants a separate measurement of cost — one product, one department, one customer, one project, one branch, one service. Suppose a company wants to know the cost of producing Product A — Product A becomes the cost object. The company then classifies costs based on whether they can be traced to Product A.

11. Direct and indirect costs

11.1 Direct cost

Can be easily and cost-effectively traced to a cost object. Example: wood used to produce a specific table can be traced to that table — therefore the wood is a direct cost of the table.

11.2 Indirect cost

Cannot be easily or cost-effectively traced to a specific cost object. Example: factory electricity supports many products — it would be impractical to identify exactly how much electricity belongs to each table, so factory electricity is an indirect cost.

Important exam logic

"Can physically be traced" is not the only issue — the cost must also be economical to trace. Example: a tiny amount of glue is physically used in one product; technically it could be measured for every unit, but tracking every drop would cost more than the information is worth. Therefore, glue is often treated as indirect material.

Direct or indirect depends on the cost object

The same cost may be direct in one situation and indirect in another. Example: the production manager's salary may be direct to the production department, but indirect to one individual product.

Therefore, always ask: "Direct or indirect to what?" Without identifying the cost object, the classification may be meaningless.

12. Three manufacturing costs

Manufacturing costs are divided into: (1) Direct materials, (2) Direct labour, (3) Manufacturing overhead.

12.1 Direct materials

Raw materials that physically become part of the finished product and can be traced conveniently to the product — wood in a table, processor in a computer, fabric in a shirt, flour in bread.

12.2 Direct labour

The cost of employees who work directly on the product — assembly workers, machine operators working on the product, carpenters making furniture, bakers producing bread.

12.3 Manufacturing overhead

All indirect manufacturing costs — indirect materials, indirect labour, factory rent, factory utilities, factory insurance, depreciation on factory equipment, factory property tax, production supervisor's salary.

Manufacturing overhead = All factory costs other than direct materials and direct labour

Be careful: "overhead" does not mean every expense in the company. Only indirect costs connected to manufacturing are manufacturing overhead. Office rent is not manufacturing overhead. Advertising is not manufacturing overhead. Sales commission is not manufacturing overhead.

13. Indirect materials and indirect labour

Indirect materials — materials used in production that are difficult or uneconomical to trace to individual products: glue, cleaning supplies, lubricants, small screws (depending on practicality).

Indirect labour — employees who support production but do not work directly on individual products: factory supervisor, maintenance employee, factory cleaner, security guard at the factory.

Indirect materials and indirect labour are included in manufacturing overhead.

14. Prime costs and conversion costs

These two classifications rearrange the same three manufacturing costs.

Prime costs = Direct materials + Direct labour
Conversion costs = Direct labour + Manufacturing overhead

Conversion costs represent the cost of converting raw materials into finished goods.

Why direct labour appears in both

Direct labour works directly on the product and also helps convert raw material into a finished product. Therefore it belongs to both prime costs and conversion costs. The diagram on page 25 shows direct labour in the overlapping section between prime costs and conversion costs.

Example

Direct materials RM80,000; Direct labour RM50,000; Manufacturing overhead RM30,000.

Prime costs = RM80,000 + RM50,000 = RM130,000

Conversion costs = RM50,000 + RM30,000 = RM80,000

Do not add all three for either calculation.

15. Product costs versus period costs

This distinction affects when a cost becomes an expense.

15.1 Product costs

The costs of purchasing or manufacturing products. For a manufacturer: Product costs = Direct materials + Direct labour + Manufacturing overhead. Product costs are initially recorded as inventory assets and become expenses only when the products are sold.

Cost incurred → Inventory asset → Product sold → Cost of Goods Sold expense

15.2 Period costs

Non-manufacturing costs — selling expenses, administrative expenses, advertising, office rent, CEO's salary, delivery expense, interest expense, income tax expense. Period costs are expensed in the period in which they are incurred; they do not enter inventory.

Product cost: recorded as inventory first, expensed when product is sold
Period cost: expensed immediately in the period incurred

16. Common cost-classification traps

CostClassification
Depreciation on manufacturing equipmentManufacturing overhead
Depreciation on office equipmentPeriod cost
AdvertisingPeriod cost
Factory property tax and insuranceManufacturing overhead
Office property tax and insurancePeriod cost
Production supervisor's salaryManufacturing overhead
CEO's salaryPeriod cost
Assembly-line workers' wagesDirect labour
Materials used in tabletsDirect materials
Factory suppliesManufacturing overhead
Freight on purchased materialsDirect materials cost
Delivery expense to customersPeriod cost

Factory versus office rule

When uncertain, ask: "Does the cost happen inside production?" If yes, it is normally a product cost. If it relates to sales, administration, head office, or delivery to customers, it is normally a period cost.

Freight-in versus delivery expense

Freight-in on materials: the cost of bringing materials to the factory is part of the cost of acquiring those materials — it enters product cost.

Delivery to customers: occurs after production and relates to selling or distribution — it is a period cost.

17. Balance sheet differences among the three company types

Service company — normally has no product inventory. Typical assets: cash, receivables, equipment.

Merchandising company — has one main inventory account: Merchandise Inventory.

Manufacturing company — has three inventory accounts: Raw Materials Inventory, Work-in-Process Inventory, Finished Goods Inventory. The balance sheet comparison on page 31 shows this distinction directly.

18. Income statement differences

Service company: Service revenue − Operating expenses = Operating income. Generally does not report Cost of Goods Sold.

Merchandising company: Net sales revenue − COGS = Gross profit; Gross profit − Operating expenses = Operating income.

Manufacturing company: uses the same broad structure as a merchandiser (Net sales revenue − COGS = Gross profit). The difference is how COGS is calculated — a merchandiser buys completed goods, a manufacturer must first calculate how much it cost to produce the goods.

19. The factory cost journey

Imagine each cost carrying a passport. It moves through: Raw Materials Inventory → Work-in-Process Inventory → Finished Goods Inventory → Cost of Goods Sold. The cost begins as an asset. It remains an asset while the product is unused, unfinished, or finished but unsold. Only when the product is sold does the cost become an expense. The flow diagram on page 34 illustrates this movement from raw materials, direct labour and overhead into WIP, then finished goods and finally Cost of Goods Sold.

20. Cost of Goods Manufactured

Cost of Goods Manufactured (COGM) is: the manufacturing cost of goods completed during the period. It does NOT mean all goods started, all goods sold, all manufacturing costs paid, or all goods remaining in the factory. It specifically means goods that finished production.

21. The three-step COGM calculation

The chapter uses three steps: (1) Calculate direct materials used. (2) Calculate total manufacturing costs incurred. (3) Calculate Cost of Goods Manufactured.

22. Step 1: Direct materials used

Beginning Direct Materials Inventory
+ Purchases of Direct Materials
= Direct Materials Available for Use
− Ending Direct Materials Inventory
= Direct Materials Used

Using the chapter's figures: Beginning direct materials $70,000; Purchases $350,000; Available for use $420,000; Less ending direct materials $(65,000); Direct materials used $355,000.

Intuitive logic

You had RM70,000 at the beginning. You bought RM350,000 more. Therefore RM420,000 was available. But RM65,000 remains unused. So RM420,000 − RM65,000 = RM355,000 used. Ending inventory is subtracted because it was not used in production.

23. Step 2: Total manufacturing costs incurred

Direct materials used
+ Direct labour
+ Manufacturing overhead
= Total manufacturing costs incurred

Direct materials used $355,000; Direct labour $169,000; Manufacturing overhead: Indirect materials $17,000, Indirect labour $28,000, Factory depreciation $20,000, Factory utilities/insurance/taxes $18,000 → Total overhead $83,000. Total manufacturing costs incurred $607,000. This represents production costs added during the current period.

24. Step 3: Cost of Goods Manufactured

Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory
+ Total Manufacturing Costs Incurred
= Total Manufacturing Costs to Account For
− Ending Work-in-Process Inventory
= Cost of Goods Manufactured

Beginning WIP $80,000; Total manufacturing costs incurred $607,000; Total to account for $687,000; Less ending WIP $(27,000); Cost of Goods Manufactured $660,000.

25. Why beginning WIP is added

Beginning WIP consists of unfinished products from the previous period. These goods are still being completed this year. Therefore, their cost contributes to goods finished this year — so beginning WIP is added.

26. Why ending WIP is subtracted

Ending WIP is still incomplete. COGM should contain only completed goods. Therefore: Total costs inside production − Cost still unfinished = Cost completed. This is the logic behind subtracting ending WIP.

27. Full Schedule of Cost of Goods Manufactured

Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory

Direct Materials:
  Beginning Direct Materials Inventory
  + Purchases of Direct Materials
  = Direct Materials Available for Use
  − Ending Direct Materials Inventory
  = Direct Materials Used

+ Direct Labour

+ Manufacturing Overhead
  Indirect materials, Indirect labour, Factory depreciation, Factory rent and utilities, Other indirect factory costs

= Total Manufacturing Costs Incurred

+ Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory
= Total Manufacturing Costs to Account For
− Ending Work-in-Process Inventory
= Cost of Goods Manufactured

Be careful with presentation. Beginning WIP may appear at the top of the schedule, but mathematically it is added after total current manufacturing costs are calculated.

28. Cost of Goods Sold for a manufacturer

After COGM is calculated, it enters Finished Goods Inventory.

Beginning Finished Goods Inventory
+ Cost of Goods Manufactured
= Cost of Goods Available for Sale
− Ending Finished Goods Inventory
= Cost of Goods Sold

Beginning Finished Goods $0; COGM $660,000; Cost of Goods Available for Sale $660,000; Less ending Finished Goods $(60,000); Cost of Goods Sold $600,000.

29. COGM versus COGS

Students often confuse these. Cost of Goods Manufactured — the cost of goods that finished production (Work-in-Process → Finished Goods). Cost of Goods Sold — the cost of finished goods sold to customers (Finished Goods → Cost of Goods Sold).

One product can be manufactured but not sold

Suppose 2,200 tablets are completed but only 2,000 are sold. Then: cost of all 2,200 units enters COGM; cost of only 2,000 units enters COGS; cost of 200 units remains in Finished Goods Inventory.

30. One formula pattern controls all inventories

The slide on page 42 gives the same basic structure for all three inventory accounts:

Beginning balance + Additions − Ending balance = Amount used, manufactured or sold

Apply it three times.

Raw materials: Beginning raw materials + Purchases − Ending raw materials = Direct materials used

Work-in-process: Beginning WIP + Manufacturing costs added − Ending WIP = Cost of Goods Manufactured

Finished goods: Beginning finished goods + Cost of Goods Manufactured − Ending finished goods = Cost of Goods Sold

This is the best way to remember the calculations. It is the same pipe used three times.

31. Visual flow of the calculations

RAW MATERIALS
Beginning RM + Purchases − Ending RM = Direct Materials Used
↓
WORK-IN-PROCESS
Beginning WIP + Direct Materials Used + Direct Labour + Manufacturing Overhead − Ending WIP = Cost of Goods Manufactured
↓
FINISHED GOODS
Beginning Finished Goods + Cost of Goods Manufactured − Ending Finished Goods = Cost of Goods Sold

32. Unit product cost

Managers may calculate the average cost of one unit produced.

Unit product cost = Cost of Goods Manufactured ÷ Units produced

$660,000 ÷ 2,200 tablets = $300 per tablet

If 2,000 tablets are sold: 2,000 × $300 = $600,000 Cost of Goods Sold

The remaining 200 tablets are finished but unsold: 200 × $300 = $60,000 Finished Goods Inventory. This agrees with the chapter's ending Finished Goods Inventory.

33. Complete numerical flow

Raw materials: Beginning $70,000 + Purchases $350,000 − Ending $(65,000) = Materials used $355,000

Manufacturing costs: Direct materials used $355,000 + Direct labour $169,000 + Manufacturing overhead $83,000 = Current manufacturing costs $607,000

Work-in-process: Beginning WIP $80,000 + Current manufacturing costs $607,000 − Ending WIP $(27,000) = COGM $660,000

Finished goods: Beginning $0 + COGM $660,000 − Ending $(60,000) = COGS $600,000

34. Manufacturing income statement

Net Sales Revenue − Cost of Goods Sold = Gross Profit

Gross Profit − Selling and Administrative Expenses = Operating Income

Operating Income ± Other Income and Expenses = Income Before Tax

Income Before Tax − Income Tax Expense = Net Income

Product costs appear in Cost of Goods Sold. Period costs appear as selling and administrative expenses or other expenses.

35. Likely subjective calculation format

A question may give beginning/ending raw materials, purchases, direct labour, overhead costs, beginning/ending WIP, beginning/ending finished goods. Use this order:

Part 1 — Direct materials used: Beginning RM + Purchases − Ending RM

Part 2 — Total manufacturing costs: Direct materials used + Direct labour + Manufacturing overhead

Part 3 — Cost of Goods Manufactured: Beginning WIP + Total manufacturing costs − Ending WIP

Part 4 — Cost of Goods Sold: Beginning finished goods + COGM − Ending finished goods

Do not jump directly into one giant formula. That is how signs get mixed up and ending WIP mysteriously becomes beginning finished goods.

36. Business trends affecting managerial accounting

The chapter identifies several trends.

36.1 Shift toward a service economy

More businesses now provide services rather than only physical products. Managerial accounting is also used to calculate cost per consultation, cost per hospital patient, cost per hotel guest, cost per banking transaction, cost per delivery.

36.2 Global competition

Businesses compete with companies around the world. Managers need information on pricing, product quality, delivery speed, efficiency, cost reduction.

A company cannot simply charge more because its internal process is inefficient. Customers do not usually feel sentimental about poor cost control.

36.3 Time-based competition

Companies compete through speed — faster production, faster delivery, shorter waiting times, quicker response to customers. Managerial accounting helps identify delays and activities that do not add value.

36.4 Enterprise Resource Planning systems

An ERP system integrates data from different parts of the organisation — sales, inventory, purchasing, production, accounting, human resources. Instead of separate departments maintaining disconnected information, the data can be shared through one system.

36.5 E-commerce

Allows companies to sell products globally. Managerial accountants may analyse online sales, delivery cost, customer acquisition cost, platform fees, returns, profitability by region.

36.6 Just-in-Time management

JIT aims to obtain or produce inventory close to the time it is needed. The goal is to reduce storage costs, excess inventory, waste, obsolete products. However, JIT also means the company has less protection when suppliers fail or deliveries are delayed.

"No unnecessary inventory" sounds lovely until the only supplier stops shipping.

37. Total Quality Management

TQM is a philosophy of continuous improvement in products and processes. It encourages cooperation, quality improvement, waste reduction, prevention of defects, continuous learning. The chapter's value chain diagram presents:

Research and development → Design → Production → Marketing and sales → Distribution → Customer support

Each stage should add value to the final product or customer experience.

38. Value chain

The value chain includes the activities involved in creating, producing, selling, delivering, supporting a product. Managers analyse the value chain to determine which activities add value, which activities waste resources, where quality can be improved, where cost can be reduced.

Example: if production is efficient but customer support is terrible, the full value chain is still weak.

39. Triple bottom line

Considers three areas: Profit, People, Planet.

Profit — economic performance of the company.

People — social impact: employee treatment, labour practices, community contribution, customer welfare.

Planet — environmental impact: pollution, waste, energy use, sustainable materials.

The idea is that business performance is not evaluated solely through profit.

40. Managerial accounting in service companies

Service companies still need cost information. Example: Total operating costs $3,900; Number of services provided 1,950. Unit cost per service = $3,900 ÷ 1,950 = $2 per service. Managers can use this for pricing, budgeting, evaluating efficiency, comparing branches, estimating profit.

41. Managerial accounting in merchandising companies

A merchandising company may calculate unit cost per item sold. Example: Cost of Goods Sold $90,800; Number of items sold 260. Unit cost = $90,800 ÷ 260 = $349.23 per item. This helps managers decide selling price, product profitability, whether supplier costs are increasing, whether the product should continue to be sold.

42. How to answer a cost-classification question

Step 1 — Identify the company type: service, merchandising, or manufacturing?

Step 2 — Identify the cost object: one product, one department, one customer?

Step 3 — Ask whether the cost is traceable: if easily and economically traceable → Direct cost. If not → Indirect cost.

Step 4 — Ask whether it relates to manufacturing: if yes → direct materials/direct labour/manufacturing overhead. If no → period cost.

Step 5 — Explain when it becomes an expense: Product cost → inventory first, expense when sold. Period cost → expense in the current period.

43. Model classification answers

Factory rent: Indirect manufacturing cost. Manufacturing overhead. Product cost. Included in inventory before sale.

Office rent: Non-manufacturing cost. Administrative period cost. Expensed when incurred.

Assembly worker wages: Direct labour. Product cost. Prime cost. Conversion cost.

Factory supervisor salary: Indirect labour. Manufacturing overhead. Product cost. Conversion cost.

Wood used in furniture: Direct material. Product cost. Prime cost.

Advertising: Selling expense. Period cost. Expensed when incurred.

44. Likely subjective examination questions

Question 1: Distinguish financial accounting from managerial accounting.

Answer structure: (1) Identify users. (2) Explain purpose. (3) Compare past and future focus. (4) Compare rules. (5) Compare detail and frequency. (6) Mention internal behaviour.

Question 2: Explain planning, directing and controlling.

Model answer

Planning involves setting organisational goals and deciding how to achieve them. Strategic planning concerns long-term direction, while operational planning concerns short-term activities. Directing involves managing the organisation's daily operations. Controlling involves monitoring actual performance, comparing it with plans and taking corrective action when necessary.

Question 3: Distinguish direct and indirect costs.

Model answer

A direct cost can be easily and cost-effectively traced to a particular cost object. An indirect cost cannot be traced conveniently or economically to that cost object. The classification depends on the selected cost object. For example, a factory supervisor's salary may be directly traceable to the production department but indirect to an individual product.

Question 4: Explain the three manufacturing costs.

Model answer

Direct materials are materials that become part of the finished product and can be conveniently traced to it. Direct labour consists of employee costs that can be traced directly to production. Manufacturing overhead includes all indirect manufacturing costs, including indirect materials, indirect labour, factory rent, utilities and depreciation.

Question 5: Distinguish product costs and period costs.

Model answer

Product costs include direct materials, direct labour and manufacturing overhead. They are initially recorded as inventory and become Cost of Goods Sold when the product is sold. Period costs are non-manufacturing costs such as selling and administrative expenses. They are expensed in the period in which they are incurred.

Question 6: Explain Cost of Goods Manufactured.

Model answer

Cost of Goods Manufactured represents the manufacturing cost of goods completed during the accounting period. It is calculated by adding beginning Work-in-Process Inventory to the manufacturing costs incurred during the period and subtracting ending Work-in-Process Inventory.

Question 7: Explain the movement of manufacturing costs.

Model answer

Manufacturing costs begin in Raw Materials Inventory. When materials are used together with direct labour and manufacturing overhead, their costs enter Work-in-Process Inventory. When production is completed, the cost moves to Finished Goods Inventory as Cost of Goods Manufactured. When the finished products are sold, the cost moves from Finished Goods Inventory to Cost of Goods Sold.

45. Examination mistakes to avoid

  • Treating all labour as direct labour — factory supervisors and maintenance workers are normally indirect labour.
  • Treating every factory cost as overhead — direct materials and direct labour are factory costs but not overhead.
  • Treating product cost as an immediate expense — unsold product costs remain inventory assets.
  • Treating office rent as manufacturing overhead — office rent is administrative period cost.
  • Confusing COGM with COGS — COGM means completed. COGS means sold.
  • Subtracting beginning inventory — beginning inventory is normally added because it is available this period. Ending inventory is subtracted because it remains unused, unfinished or unsold.

46. Final memory framework

Remember the chapter through four ideas.

1. Managerial purpose

Plan → Direct → Control

2. Manufacturing costs

Direct Materials + Direct Labour + Manufacturing Overhead

3. Inventory flow

Raw Materials → Work-in-Process → Finished Goods → Cost of Goods Sold

4. Inventory formula

Beginning inventory + Additions − Ending inventory = Amount transferred out

Applied three times: Raw Materials → Materials Used. Work-in-Process → Cost of Goods Manufactured. Finished Goods → Cost of Goods Sold.

That single pattern covers most of the calculations in this chapter.

Master CVP Calculator

🧭 The Master CVP Equation — Where Every Formula Comes From

Start here. Almost every calculation in this chapter is a rearrangement of one equation:

Profit = Revenue − Total cost
= SP(Q) − [VC(Q) + FC]
= (SP − VC)Q − FC
= Contribution margin/unit × Q − Fixed costs

Breakeven sets Profit = 0 and solves for Q. Target profit sets Profit = a chosen number and solves for Q. Sensitivity analysis changes SP, VC or FC and re-solves. Margin of safety and operating leverage both describe how far from — and how sensitive profit is around — this same line. One equation, many questions.

Unit Contribution Margin225
CM Ratio45%
Breakeven (Units)60
Breakeven ($)30,000
Target Profit (Units)80
Target Profit ($)40,000
Margin of Safety (Units)40
Margin of Safety ($)20,000
Margin of Safety Ratio40.0%
Operating Income (at Expected Sales)9,000
Degree of Operating Leverage2.50

High-Low Method

Separates mixed costs.

  • 1. Var Rate = ∆ Cost / ∆ Activity
  • 2. Fix Cost = Total Cost − (Var Rate × Act)

Operating Leverage

Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) = CM / Op. Income

∆ Profit % = DOL × ∆ Sales %

Live DOL for the inputs above: 2.50 — a 10% sales change ≈ 25.0% profit change.

Chapter 10

Cost Behaviour: Variable, Fixed & Mixed

🔑 Why Cost Behaviour Matters

CVP analysis only works once managers know how costs behave as activity changes. The chapter splits every cost into variable, fixed or mixed — and the single biggest source of exam mistakes is confusing total cost with cost per unit.

📱 Variable Costs — the Battery Example

Constant per unit, changes in total. Every tablet needs a RM55 battery:

TabletsCost / tabletTotal battery cost
0RM55RM0
25RM55RM1,375
50RM55RM2,750
75RM55RM4,125
100RM55RM5,500
Total variable cost = Variable cost/unit × Units
e.g. RM55 × 80 = RM4,400

Like movie tickets: RM20 each — 1 ticket = RM20, 5 = RM100, 10 = RM200. Price per ticket never changes, only the total.

🏭 Fixed Costs — the Factory Rent Example

Constant in total, changes per unit. Monthly fixed cost RM13,500:

TabletsTotal fixed costFixed cost / tablet
25RM13,500RM540
50RM13,500RM270
75RM13,500RM180
100RM13,500RM135
Fixed cost/unit = Total fixed cost ÷ Units
e.g. RM13,500 ÷ 25 = RM540

Like a RM10,000/month factory rent: whether it makes 1, 100 or 1,000 units, the rent stays RM10,000 — but rent per unit keeps shrinking.

↔️ Variable vs. Fixed — the Reversal Trap

BehaviourTotal costCost per unit
VariableChanges with volumeStays constant
FixedStays constantChanges inversely with volume

Students often assume "fixed" means fixed per unit. It does not — it's the total that's fixed.

"Variable varies in total. Fixed is fixed in total."

🧩 Mixed Costs

Contains both a fixed portion and a variable portion: Y = a + bX (a = fixed, b = variable rate/unit, X = activity).

E.g. RM2,000 monthly service fee + RM25 per tablet sold. At 100 tablets:

RM2,000 + RM25(100) = RM4,500

Even at zero tablets, cost = RM2,000 — this is why the mixed-cost line begins above zero rather than at zero.

📏 Relevant Range

The activity band within which total fixed cost and variable cost/unit stay constant. CVP does not assume costs behave the same forever — only predictably within a range.

E.g. a factory producing 0–4,000 units pays RM100,000 rent. At 4,001 units, a second factory may be needed and fixed cost jumps — a step, not one flat line forever.

Better exam phrasing: "Fixed costs remain constant in total within the relevant range and for the specified period" — not "fixed costs never change."
Chapter 10

High-Low Method & Regression

✂️ Splitting a Mixed Cost

The high-low method separates a mixed cost into its variable-per-unit rate and fixed portion, using only the observations with the highest and lowest activity (not the highest/lowest cost — those usually line up, but the selection rule is activity).

📋 Source Data — Maintenance Cost

QuarterMaintenance costTablets produced
FirstRM1,630360
SecondRM1,935415
Third (highest activity)RM1,960480
Fourth (lowest activity)RM1,480240

🧮 High-Low Calculator

Variable Rate / Unit2
Fixed Cost1,000
Total cost = 1,000 + 2 × Activity
Predicted Cost at Test Activity1,800

High-Low vs. Regression

High-LowRegression
Uses two pointsUses all observations
Easy to calculateMore statistically reliable
May be distorted by unusual pointsBetter reflects overall relationship
Suitable for simple examsOften done with software

Example regression estimate: variable cost ≈ RM2.18/tablet, fixed cost ≈ RM936.76.

⚠️ Weakness of High-Low

It uses only two observations and ignores everything else. If the highest or lowest month was unusual (machinery breakdown, electricity surcharge, extraordinary repairs, a temporary production problem), the estimate may be misleading. Useful for quick analysis — not the height of statistical sophistication.

Chapter 10

Contribution Margin

💡 Why "Contribution"?

Contribution margin = Sales revenue − Variable costs. It is not automatically profit — it first contributes toward fixed costs, and only what's left over becomes operating income.

Contribution margin   RM45,000
Fixed costs         (RM13,500)
─────────────────────
Operating income   RM31,500

The first RM13,500 of contribution margin covers fixed costs; only the remaining RM31,500 becomes profit.

🔺 Three Forms of Contribution Margin

FormFormulaUse
Total CMSales − Total variable costsOverall profit calculation
Unit CMSelling price − Variable cost/unitRequired sales in units
CM RatioUnit CM ÷ Selling priceRequired sales in RM

Chapter figures: RM500 − RM275 = RM225 unit CM; RM225 ÷ RM500 = 45% CM ratio. That means for every RM1 of sales, RM0.45 goes toward fixed costs & profit, RM0.55 covers variable cost (45% + 55% = 100%).

Traditional Income Statement

Sales
− Cost of Goods Sold
= Gross profit
− Selling & admin expenses
= Operating income

Classifies costs by function (product vs. period).

Contribution Margin Income Statement

Sales
− Variable costs
= Contribution margin
− Fixed costs
= Operating income

Classifies costs by behaviour — this is the format CVP analysis actually needs, because it separates what changes with sales from what doesn't.

📐 The 6 CVP Assumptions

  1. Selling price per unit remains constant.
  2. Costs can be classified as variable, fixed or mixed.
  3. Variable cost per unit remains constant.
  4. Total fixed costs remain constant.
  5. Volume is the main factor affecting cost.
  6. Inventory levels do not change.
In reality, price may fall as volume rises, suppliers may offer bulk discounts, overtime may raise labour cost, another factory may be needed... CVP is a planning model, not divine revelation — useful when the assumptions are reasonably realistic within the relevant range.
Chapter 10

Breakeven & Sensitivity Analysis

⚖️ The Breakeven Point

The sales level where Operating income = RM0 — Total revenue = Total costs, or equivalently Contribution margin = Fixed costs. No profit, no loss.

Three Ways to the Same Answer (60 tablets)

ApproachFormulaWorking
EquationSPQ − VCQ − FC = 0RM225Q = RM13,500 → Q = 60
Contribution marginFC ÷ Unit CMRM13,500 ÷ RM225 = 60 units
CM ratioFC ÷ CM ratioRM13,500 ÷ 45% = RM30,000 = 60 units
Rule of thumb: question asks for units → divide by unit CM. Question asks for RM revenue → divide by CM ratio. Never divide fixed costs by CM ratio to get units directly.

🎯 From Breakeven to Target Profit

Target profit uses the exact same formula as breakeven — just add the desired profit to fixed costs before dividing:

Required units = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ Unit CM
Required sales (RM) = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM ratio

Breakeven is simply the special case where Target profit = RM0. E.g. with a target profit of RM4,500: (RM13,500+RM4,500)÷RM225 = 80 units — versus 60 units at breakeven.

📊 The CVP Graph

Three lines on one chart:

  • Sales revenue line — starts at zero (zero sales = zero revenue), slope = selling price/unit.
  • Fixed cost line — horizontal, since fixed costs are constant within the relevant range.
  • Total cost line — begins at the fixed-cost amount (not zero); equation = Fixed cost + Variable cost/unit × Units.

Breakeven = where the revenue line crosses the total-cost line. Before it, total costs > revenue (loss). After it, revenue > total costs (profit).

🔁 Sensitivity Analysis — "What If?"

Base case: SP RM500, VC RM275, FC RM13,500 → unit CM RM225 → breakeven 60 units.

ScenarioNew CM/unitNew breakeven
Selling price falls to RM475RM475−RM275 = RM200RM13,500÷RM200 = 67.5 → 68 units
Variable cost rises to RM285RM500−RM285 = RM215RM13,500÷RM215 = 62.79 → 63 units
Fixed costs rise to RM16,500RM225 (unchanged)RM16,500÷RM225 = 73.33 → 74 units

Required sales are always rounded up — a company can't sell half a tablet, and rounding down would fail to actually reach breakeven. (Note: the source slide for the fixed-cost scenario correctly states RM16,500 and correctly concludes 74 units, but its displayed numerator briefly shows RM13,500 — a typo in the slide, not in the concept; RM13,500÷RM225 would still be 60, not 74.)

Directional Effects

ChangeUnit CMBreakeven
Price ↑IncreasesDecreases
Price ↓DecreasesIncreases
Variable cost ↑DecreasesIncreases
Variable cost ↓IncreasesDecreases
Fixed cost ↑No changeIncreases
Fixed cost ↓No changeDecreases

Anything that raises contribution margin makes breakeven easier; anything that lowers it makes breakeven harder. Fixed costs don't move CM/unit, but they change how much total contribution is needed.

🍯 Cost Stickiness

CVP assumes costs move symmetrically with volume. In reality costs are often sticky — they rise faster when sales increase than they fall when sales decrease. When demand rises, management hires staff/leases space; when demand later falls, they hesitate to cut those resources (rehiring cost, lease terms, hope of recovery). So CVP models can overestimate how quickly costs will fall when sales decline.

Chapter 10

Margin of Safety & Operating Leverage

🛡️ Margin of Safety

How far expected sales exceed breakeven sales — how much sales can fall before the company starts losing money.

Units: Expected − Breakeven = 100 − 60 = 40
RM: 40 × RM500 = RM20,000
Ratio: 40 ÷ 100 = 40%

High MOS

Lower operating risk — comfortably above breakeven, sales can decline a lot before a loss.

Low MOS

Higher operating risk — close to breakeven, a small sales dip can create a loss.

⚡ Operating Leverage

Measures how strongly operating income responds to a change in sales — driven by the mix of fixed vs. variable costs.

DOL = Contribution margin ÷ Operating income
% change in OI ≈ DOL × % change in sales
High fixed / low variable cost structure → high DOL → bigger reward when sales rise, bigger risk when sales fall.

✈️ Company A vs. Company B — Same Profit, Different Risk (at 500 passengers)

Company ACompany B
SalesRM12,500RM12,500
Variable costsRM2,500RM7,500
Contribution marginRM10,000RM5,000
Fixed costsRM6,000RM1,000
Operating incomeRM4,000RM4,000
DOL10,000÷4,000 = 2.505,000÷4,000 = 1.25
If sales fall 20%...2.50 × 20% = −50% OI1.25 × 20% = −25% OI

Both companies earn the identical RM4,000 profit at 500 passengers — but Company A's higher fixed / lower variable structure makes it far more sensitive to a downturn. When sales fall, Company A's RM6,000 fixed cost doesn't budge, while much of Company B's cost base (mostly variable) falls along with revenue.

Chapter 10

Sales Mix & Multiproduct Breakeven

🐱 Why Sales Mix Matters

Most companies sell more than one product, and products have different contribution margins. A company selling more high-CM products earns more profit than one selling mostly low-CM products — even at the same total unit volume. Multiproduct CVP must therefore account for the mix (e.g. 3 cat beds : 2 scratching posts).

🧮 Multiproduct Breakeven Calculator

Product 1 — Cat Bed

Product 2 — Scratching Post

Cat Bed CM/unit20
Scratching Post CM/unit70
Package CM (per mix bundle)200
Weighted-Avg CM/unit40
Required Total Units1,000
↳ Cat Beds600
↳ Scratching Posts400

🪜 The 5-Step Method

  1. Calculate each product's unit CM — Selling price − Variable cost.
  2. Apply the sales mix — Unit CM × mix quantity for each product.
  3. Calculate the weighted-average CM — Total package CM ÷ Total package units.
  4. Calculate required total units — (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ Weighted-average CM.
  5. Allocate total units back to each product — Total units × each product's mix proportion.
Most marks are lost at Step 5 — students calculate the weighted-average CM correctly, get the required total units correctly, and then simply forget to split that total back into individual products using the mix ratio.
The weighted-average method assumes the sales mix stays constant. If customers start buying relatively more cat beds and fewer scratching posts (the higher-CM product), the average CM falls and the breakeven requirement rises. Multiproduct breakeven is only valid for the assumed mix — which is exactly why companies use data analytics to monitor which products customers are actually buying, since two companies can post identical revenue yet very different profit if one sells more high-margin products.

Given: SP RM80, VC RM50, FC RM24,000, Expected sales 1,200 units.

2. CM ratioRM30 ÷ RM8037.5%
3. Breakeven unitsRM24,000 ÷ RM30800 units
4. Breakeven revenueRM24,000 ÷ 37.5%RM64,000
5. Operating income @1,200(1,200×RM30) − RM24,000RM12,000
6. Margin of safety1,200−800=400u; ×RM80=RM32,000; 400÷1,200400u / RM32,000 / 33.33%
